+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 81.2
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter 7 — A Polite Summons** Arthur Neegan sat with his hands folded too tightly in his lap aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he had gotten himself involved in. It was not a large vessel. It was a short-hop ferry, of the sort that ran ore and ice between the surface and Highport, now stripped of its canvas slings and smelling faintly of oil and ozone. The acceleration couch had been bolted backward to face the bulkhead. Across from him sat two men who did not speak. A small display screen on the wall cycles through various system diagnostics in green text. O2 PRESS 14.1 NOMINAL. HULL TEMP -42 C. DRIVE IDLE. AZIMUTH LOCK: ANTARES CLIPPER *MERIDIAN*. Arthur read it three times because there was nothing else to read. Twelve hours earlier they had come to his home. He had been at the sink in his prefab dome at Elysium Plot 44, scraping red dust out of a filter mask, when the perimeter alarm gave its soft, apologetic buzz. Three figures on the monitor, coming up the walk in single file through the thin morning dust. Gray vacuum suits, military cut, helmets under arms. On each left shoulder: a crimson sunburst over a black bar. Antares diplomatic corps. Diplomatic in name only — every spacer from Syrtis to Tharsis knew that. The leader had knocked. Actually knocked. “Mr. Arthur Neegan?” he had said when Arthur cracked the inner hatch. He was young, clean-shaven, with the flat vowels of the Antarean academies. Behind him the other two stood with hands clasped, stun-batons holstered but visible. Polite. Practiced. “I am Lieutenant Sorel, attached to the Consular Mission. The Ambassador requests the pleasure of a conversation. Off-world. At your convenience.” “At my convenience?” Arthur had said. “Within the hour would be most convenient,” Sorel had said, smiling. “We have a ferry waiting at Pad Three. You will want a jacket. It is cold upstairs.” It had not been a question. Arthur had looked past them at his claim — three hectares of basalt and dust, the old Mark IV thumper still ticking over the borehole, the assay tape still pinned above his workbench: AZRA CONCENTRATION 0.81% — REPEAT — VEIN DEPTH EST. 400 M CONTINUOUS. An immense vein. Enough to buy Mars. He had put on his jacket. Now the ferry shuddered. Magnetic grapples caught with a clang that ran through the deck plates. The two silent men stood. “Please come, sir,” one said. The *Meridian* was not what Arthur expected. He had imagined chrome and carpet, the retrofuturistic gloss of newsreels — finned rockets and smiling stewardesses. Instead it was functional and old. Brass handrails worn smooth. Analog dials beside digital readouts. The air smelled of hot paper from the punch-tape navigators. A ship built for calculation, not comfort. They led him to a small conference cabin with a round porthole showing Mars below, a rust-red coin turning slowly. At a steel table bolted to the deck sat a thin man in civilian gray, pouring tea from a thermos with great care. He was perhaps sixty, with deep lines around his eyes and ink stains on his fingers, like a clerk. “Mr. Neegan. Thank you for coming. I am Rel Dravik,” he said. “They call me Ambassador, which means I am empowered to lie politely on behalf of eleven billion people. Sit down, please. Tea?” Arthur sat. “I didn’t exactly choose to come, Mr. Ambassador.” “No,” Dravik agreed cheerfully. “That is the advantage of politeness backed by force. It saves time. Sugar? You are a mining engineer, first-generation. Born in Lowell Dome, 2147. You took a settler’s plot instead of a corporate lease. Admirable. Foolish, perhaps, but admirable.” “You’ve read my file.” “I’ve read everyone’s file. It is a small solar system, Mr. Neegan. Let me be direct, as befits engineers. You are sitting on approximately four hundred tons of refined-equivalent Azra.” Arthur kept his face still. “My assay isn’t filed.” “Your assay doesn’t need to be filed. Our orbital spectrometer caught the secondary emission when you ran your thumper last Tuesday. Azra accelerates radioactive decay, you know — that is the public fact. A gram of it will coax a reactor to give up a year’s power in a day. Splendid for interstellar drives. Even more splendid for weapons. That is why the Terran Combine and the Martian Charter and my own government are all in a gold rush with their pants down.” Dravik sipped his tea. “But here is the small picture inside the big picture,” he continued. “Your vein is *clean*. No thorium daughters. No jitter. My physicists tell me that should be impossible unless —” he tapped the table, “— unless Azra can be *tuned*. Unless someone understands its secret, not merely its effect. Your readings suggest a resonance. Do you understand what I am saying?” Arthur frowned. “My thumper was miscalibrated. I got a harmonic —” “Yes. A harmonic at 7.3 cycles. Precisely the harmonic our theoretical group on Antares predicted three years ago and could never reproduce. You reproduced it with a twenty-year-old Mark IV and a cracked coupling.” Dravik smiled thinly. “ empires turn on such accidents.” The deck hummed faintly. Outside, Mars turned. “What do you want?” Arthur said. “To make you an offer before others make you a threat,” Dravik said. “The Combine will offer you credits. The Charter will offer you patriotism and then eminent domain. Criminal interests on Phobos will offer you a bag over your head. I offer you something rational.” He slid a microfilm card across the table. “Forty times assay value, paid in Antarean industrial scrip, redeemable on any world. A technical post for life — no indenture, no lease. And protection. A consular guard on your dome, a seal on your claim recognized under interstellar law. In return: exclusive survey rights for Antares, and your silence. You will publish nothing. You will sell to no one else. And you will give us your thumper logs — all of them.” Arthur stared at the card. “That’s annexation with a receipt.” “That is survival with interest,” Dravik said, and for the first time his voice lost its lightness. “Mr. Neegan, consider galactic arithmetic. He who controls Azra controls the rate of decay itself — controls time inside the atom. Drives that reach Centaurus in months. Warheads the size of suitcases that can crack a dome city. At present no one can control it safely because no one understands tuning. You may have stumbled on the key without knowing you hold it. Do you think you will be allowed to remain a private prospector?” “I’m a Martian citizen —” “You are a variable in a larger equation,” Dravik said softly. “Psycho-politics, we call it. The mass of history moves toward war over Azra. A single clean vein like yours could delay that war — if held by a steady hand — or precipitate it, if fought over openly. Antares wishes to delay. Others do not.” Arthur picked up the card, put it down. His hands were shaking slightly from the low gravity. “And if I refuse?” Dravik poured more tea. The thermos gurgled in the quiet. “Then I will be very sorry, and I will have you returned to your home by this evening, quite unharmed,” he said. “And within a week the Combine will impound your plot for reactor safety, or the Charter will nationalize it, or someone less polite than Lieutenant Sorel will visit at night. I am not threatening you, Mr. Neegan. I am describing the board as it stands. The next move is yours, but you must move.” Through the porthole, Highport blinked — a ring of lights, Terran freighters on one arm, Martian tugs on another, and between them, dark and unlit, something long and angular keeping station apart. Arthur looked from the planet to the Ambassador to the green glow of the cabin repeater still cycling its diagnostics. NOMINAL, it said. Everything nominal. Nothing felt nominal at all.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Asimov's style and the classic science fiction aesthetic. The author successfully captures the retrofuturistic atmosphere with details like "punch-tape navigators," analog dials beside digital readouts, and the utilitarian design of the spacecraft. The world-building effectively balances the "big picture" of interstellar politics with the "small picture" of Arthur's personal predicament, which is quintessentially Asimovian. The dialogue is particularly well-crafted, especially Ambassador Dravik's characterization. His polite, intellectual menace comes through clearly in lines like "I am empowered to lie politely on behalf of eleven billion people" and his matter-of-fact explanation of the political situation. The conversation feels natural while efficiently conveying complex exposition about Azra, its properties, and the political implications. The pacing is well-controlled, moving smoothly from Arthur's captivity through the journey to the crucial negotiation. The author effectively builds tension through Arthur's powerlessness and growing understanding of his situation's magnitude. The technical details about Azra and its properties are woven naturally into the dialogue without feeling forced. However, the piece has some minor weaknesses. Arthur's characterization, while believable, is somewhat passive - he's more of a vessel for receiving information than an active participant. The ending, while appropriately ominous, doesn't quite achieve the punch it could have. Some descriptions, particularly of the spacecraft interiors, occasionally veer toward the mechanical rather than evocative. The prose is generally clean and effective, though it sometimes lacks the elegant precision that marks truly exceptional writing. The author successfully avoids purple prose while maintaining atmospheric detail. The piece adheres closely to the prompt requirements and maintains consistent tone throughout. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 87.8
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Darkroom Revelations** The red light makes everybody honest. That's what I keep thinking at 1:14 a.m. with my sleeves rolled up and developer up to my elbows, watching Elliot's hands shake just a little as he slides the paper into the tray. I'm Dani. I'm twenty-five, second time around in undergrad because I dropped out to tattoo and tour with a band and do all the stupid brave stuff you do at nineteen, and now I'm back and older than everyone in Experimental Photo and I act like it. I have a shaved undercut and a leather jacket covered in patches I actually earned, and I talk too loud in critique. I take charge. In the studio, in relationships, everywhere. If I want something, I point at it. That's always been my whole thing. Elliot has been fucking up my whole thing all semester. He's nineteen. He sits in the back row in these insane thrifted outfits — like, crushed velvet flares and a ripped mesh long-sleeve under an oversized Korn tee, chipped black nail polish, eyeliner smudged like he did it on the bus on purpose. Nu-goth thrift-shop boy who looks like he crawled out of a 1998 Hot Topic and made it fashion again. And then he never talks. Professor Lindqvist will ask about contrast and intention and he'll just say something really quiet and smart like, "I wanted it to look like a memory that doesn't want you," and I'll have to stare at my boots so I don't stare at him. I'm usually so clear about what I'm into. Girls who are *girls*, you know? Lipstick sharp enough to cut, or dykes with carabiners and a plan. Guys who are *guys* — jaw, hands, takes up space, tells me what to do until I tell *him* what to do. Defined. Legible. I like walking into a bar and knowing the game. Elliot isn't legible. His masculinity is... soft around the edges. Pretty hands. That voice that never quite lands, like he's always asking permission to take up air. And for months I just watched him from across the room and told myself it was aesthetic appreciation. Killer style. Interesting work. Whatever, Dani. Then Lindqvist paired us for the final. Diptychs: self / other, developed only in the darkroom, no digital. Which means three weeks of late nights signed up for the basement lab, just the two of us and the red safelight and the smell of stop bath burning our noses. The first two nights we barely talked. He hums when he's nervous. Not even a real song, just this soft tune under his breath while we wait for images to reveal in the chemical bath, rocking a print back and forth with the tongs. Our second night, one of my portraits of him came up — I'd shot him against the fire exit, haloed — and he went completely still watching his own face swim up out of the white. "You make me look..." he said, and didn't finish. "Hot?" I offered, because I'm an asshole when I'm nervous. Assertive Dani. Take-charge Dani. He laughed, quick and startled. "I was gonna say sad." The red light turned his skin pink and his eyeliner black-black. I wanted to fix it for him. I wanted to grab his chin and kiss him and tell him you're beautiful, don't be sad. I did neither. I just said, "You don't look sad to me. You look like you're thinking something you haven't said yet." He looked down at the tray. The image kept getting darker. "Can I tell you something weird? And you won't make it a big deal in class or anything?" My stomach dropped in that protective older-sister, almost-maternal, almost-something-else way. God, he's nineteen. I'm twenty-five and I feel every year of it in moments like that. "I won't make it anything you don't want me to make it." He agitated the print a little too hard. "I've been... questioning stuff. Like gender stuff. Expression stuff. Identity stuff. I don't know what word. Boy feels... mostly okay? Sometimes? He/him is fine for now. But sometimes I look at the pictures of myself and I'm like, who is that guy supposed to be? And then I put on eyeliner or my sister's skirt under my coat and I feel more like... me. But also not. I don't know." The safelight buzzed. Water dripped somewhere. My whole body wanted to *do* something — launch into the cool queer art school speech, give him a reading list, name five trans photographers, take him thrifting, take him home, take care of it. That's what I do. I take charge of fragile things until they aren't fragile anymore. But he wasn't asking to be handled. He was just letting me see it while it was still wet, like a print in developer. "Thank you for telling me," I said. My voice sounded weird to me, smaller. "Can I ask... what does it feel like when it feels right?" He blinked. No one had probably asked him that instead of *so what are you?* He thought for a long time, humming again without realizing it. "Like... unclenching? Like when I wore this mesh top today, some guy on the T called me a faggot, and I was scared, but I was also like, yeah. Yeah, you see something. You don't know what it is, but you see it." "Fuck that guy," I said automatically, and he smiled. "No, I know. But... my mom keeps asking when I'm gonna cut my hair and get a real jacket. And my friends from high school are all like, super normal dudes now. They lift. And I'm just... in the darkroom at 1 a.m. hoping a girl with a shaved head thinks I'm interesting." My face went hot under the red light, which was convenient because everything is red. "I do think you're interesting." "I know you watch me in class," he said, so quiet I almost missed it. Tender awkwardness doesn't cover it. I laughed too loud and knocked tongs against the tray. "Shit. Sorry. Am I being creepy? The age thing — you're nineteen, I'm basically a crypt keeper — I don't want to be weird." "You're not creepy," he said quickly. "You're just... you walk in like you know who you are. I'm jealous of that." That hit me harder than it should have. Because sitting there next to him, I didn't know who I was. If I'm the girl who likes defined things, what am I doing with my pulse in my throat over a boy who is actively unbecoming definition? Was I attracted to him *despite* the in-betweenness, or *because* of it? And was that fucked up? Was I turning his real, scary self-discovery into something exciting for me to witness, like some art-school tourist? I felt excited — I can't lie, my chest was buzzing — but also gross about feeling excited, and also fiercely protective in a way that had nothing to do with getting him into bed and everything to do with not wanting the world to sand his edges off. "I don't always know who I am," I admitted. "I just perform it louder." He looked at me then, really looked. In the red dark his eyes were huge. "What are you performing right now?" "Someone trying really hard not to take charge," I said honestly. "Because my instinct is to be like, Elliot, you're amazing, let's define this, let's do this. And I don't think that's what you need." "What do I need?" he whispered. I thought about reaching for his hand and didn't. I let him have the agency. "You tell me." He was quiet. The print was done. He lifted it with the tongs, let it drip, slid it into the stop. And then, so carefully, he bumped his shoulder against mine. Just that. Shoulder to shoulder in the dark, both of us in aprons splattered with chemicals, watching my portrait of him settle into being. "I think I need... to just be allowed to not know for a while. And have someone still want to stand next to me while I figure it out. Not in front, pulling me. Just next to." My throat closed up. "I can do next to. I'm bad at it, but I can practice." He started humming again, that soft tune, while we waited. Our diptych floated side by side in the fixer — his blurry self-portrait in a mirror wearing eyeliner and my stark photo of him laughing — and for the first time all semester I wasn't trying to name what I felt. The chemistry was there, undeniable and uncharted, crackling in the two inches between our arms. Not the usual Dani chemistry of conquest. Something slower. Something that asked me to unclench, too. I didn't kiss him. I wanted to. God, I wanted to. But I just leaned my head, barely, until it rested against his hair for three seconds, and he leaned back. In red light, everything is still developing.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and emotional intelligence in handling a delicate subject matter. The narrative successfully captures Dani's distinctive voice - brash, self-aware, and vulnerable beneath her assertive exterior. The author skillfully uses the darkroom setting both literally and metaphorically, with the red light serving as a confessional atmosphere that allows for intimate revelation. The characterization is particularly strong. Dani feels authentic as a 25-year-old returning student with a clear sense of her usual patterns and preferences, now confronted with something that challenges her typical approach. Her internal conflict between wanting to take charge and recognizing Elliot needs agency is well-developed and believable. Elliot emerges as more than just an object of fascination - his vulnerability feels genuine rather than performative, and his tentative self-exploration is handled with sensitivity. The prose strikes an effective balance between Dani's colloquial, sometimes crude voice ("I'm an asshole when I'm nervous") and more lyrical moments ("In red light, everything is still developing"). The dialogue feels natural and age-appropriate, particularly Elliot's hesitant revelations and Dani's attempts to navigate unfamiliar emotional territory. The piece excels in showing rather than telling, particularly in conveying attraction and emotional complexity through physical details and internal monologue. The author avoids easy answers or rushed resolutions, instead allowing both characters to exist in uncertainty, which feels honest to the situation. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose becomes slightly overwrought ("my chest was buzzing") and a few instances where Dani's self-awareness borders on overly articulate for the moment. However, these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness. The ending strikes the right tone - intimate without being exploitative, hopeful without being unrealistic. The restraint shown in the final moments (the brief head-lean rather than a kiss) demonstrates mature storytelling that respects both characters' emotional states. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 82.5
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Stolen Moments in Roma** **9:17 AM — Trevi Fountain** The roar came first — a battered red Ducati snarling over cobblestones — then a scream of brakes and a spray of pigeons. “MA SEI CIECO?!” Ben Whitaker stumbled backward into a tide of tourists, his *Rome in Three Days* guidebook held up like a shield. The courier had stopped a breath from his knees, one booted foot planted, dark curls escaping from under her helmet. “I — God, I’m so sorry! Terribly sorry! Mi — mi dispiace molto!” Ben babbled, adjusting his rain-jacket in 28-degree heat. “I was just looking for the — the fountain is that way?” She stared at him. Then laughed — loud, delighted. She flipped up her visor to reveal amber eyes lined in smudged kohl. “English. Of course you’re English. Only an Englishman apologizes to a motorcycle.” She yanked off her helmet. “Alessandra.” “Ben. Ben Whitaker. I’m — I teach — well, late medieval —” “Professore! Perfetto. You were about to get trampled reading that trash.” She nodded at his book, where a postcard from a nearby souvenir stand had somehow fluttered loose and — how? — ended up tucked into the pocket of her leather jacket. Ben didn’t notice. “Come. I’ll save your life. I’m on break.” “I really shouldn’t—” “You really should.” **11:04 AM — Via del Corso** “Hold tight, Professore!” Ben clung to Alessandra’s waist as they knifed through Roman traffic, buses kissing mirrors, taxis bellowing. His spare helmet smelled of jasmine and petrol. “Is this — is this legal?!” he shouted as they mounted a curb to bypass a jam. “In Roma? Legal is a suggestion!” She slowed by a fruit stall, leaned impossibly low without stopping, plucked two blood oranges, tossed one back to him, and threw a cackling *“Grazie, Enzo!”* to the furious vendor. She left a euro on the wind; it missed. She didn’t look back. Ben turned the orange in his hand, horrified and grinning. “You stole that!” “I liberated it. Big difference. You academics, so many rules.” She eyed him in the mirror. “When was the last time you did something you weren’t supposed to, Ben?” He thought. “...I once kept a library book three weeks overdue.” Alessandra howled. “Dio mio, a criminal!” **1:30 PM — Testaccio Market** They abandoned the bike and ate standing up — *panini con porchetta*, cold Peroni, sweat sticking their shirts. Ben was talking, actually talking, hands flying: about Durham, about his sabbatical to write on pilgrimage routes, about a divorce finalized over Zoom. Alessandra listened, chin in hand, stealing glances and — when the barman wasn’t looking — his lighter. It vanished up her sleeve with a magician’s ease. Then, noticing his stare, she flicked it back onto the counter. “Eyes on me, Professore.” “You’re trouble,” he said. She grinned, sharp and unrepentant. “I’m honest trouble. That’s the best kind.” “ALE!” A thick-necked man in an apron barreled out, grabbed her in a bear hug. “Marco!” she shrieked, kissing both cheeks. Marco looked Ben up and down. “Another victim? Professore, listen to me.” He lowered his voice theatrically. “This one? *Attento.* She was wild at sixteen, worse at twenty-six. She’ll steal your wallet, your Vespa, your heart — and give back nothing.” Alessandra elbowed him. “He exaggerates. I always give back... something.” Ben laughed, but the vendor’s bracelet — chunky, tourist-tacky — was suddenly on Alessandra’s wrist. Had it been there before? She caught Ben looking and winked. **4:45 PM — Aventine Hill** The city melted gold below the Orange Garden. Tourists queued for the famous keyhole at the Priory of Malta. Alessandra tugged Ben past them, to a side wall covered in ivy. “Shortcut,” she whispered. “We can’t — that’s trespassing!” “Shh. Live a little, overdue-library-book.” Over the low fence, scraped knees, stifled laughter — they dropped into a private lemon grove just as the bells of Santa Sabina rang. Rome spread out, domes and pines and laundry lines. Ben’s breath caught. “God. It’s —” “Better than the book, eh?” She was very close. Basil and orange on her skin. His politeness warred with something louder. He brushed a leaf from her hair; her hand lingered a second too long on his wrist. “You toy with me,” he murmured. “Maybe,” she said softly, suddenly not joking. “Maybe I like seeing a good man misbehave.” Below, a carabiniere strolled by. Alessandra pressed a finger to his lips, eyes dancing. Danger suited her. **8:52 PM — Trastevere** Night fell in ivy and fairy lights. They shared carbonara at a wobbly table in Piazza Santa Maria, his Italian improving with wine: *“Questo è... incredibile. Sei... incredibile.”* She taught him insults instead. *“Vaffanculo, piccione!”* he repeated dutifully to a pigeon, and she nearly choked. When the bill came, Ben reached for his wallet. Alessandra beat him to it, slapping down cash — plus, he could have sworn, a salt shaker that wasn’t theirs that she slipped into her messenger bag with practiced nonchalance. “You don’t have to—” “I courier all day for tips. Tonight, you’re my guest.” Her voice had softened. The mischief dimmed, just for a moment, into something tired and tender. “You looked so lost this morning, Professore. Like you needed someone to run a red light for you.” “I did,” he said. “I do.” The walk to the bridge was slow. The Tiber glittered. Ben stopped, heart hammering louder than the Ducati ever had. “Alessandra — I don’t know what today was, but—” She stopped him with a kiss — quick, citrus and salt, gone before he could hold it. She pressed something cold and wet into his palm: a coin, still dripping from the Trevi. “Make a wish,” she said. “Tourists throw them in to come back. I... borrow them, sometimes. For luck.” “You steal from the fountain?” “I steal moments.” She fitted her helmet on, tossed him the spare. “Same hotel tomorrow? Nine? I know a closed catacomb—” “Alessandra—” She was already kicking the engine alive, laughing over the roar. “Don’t think, Professore! Wish!” Ben closed his fist around the stolen coin as her taillight bled into Roman night — utterly disoriented, utterly smitten, and already late for everything he’d planned.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and creative flair in crafting a contemporary romance set in Rome. The author successfully creates two distinct, compelling characters whose personalities emerge clearly through action and dialogue rather than exposition. Alessandra's kleptomaniacal tendencies are woven seamlessly into the narrative through subtle details - the postcard, lighter, bracelet, salt shaker, and finally the Trevi coin - creating a character trait that feels organic rather than forced. The structure works well, using time stamps to create episodic scenes that build momentum throughout the day. The pacing moves from frantic energy to quieter, more intimate moments, allowing for character development and romantic tension to build naturally. The dialogue captures the cultural clash effectively, with Ben's overly polite British mannerisms contrasting sharply with Alessandra's rapid-fire Italian directness. The prose demonstrates strong sensory writing - "basil and orange on her skin," "citrus and salt," the "roar" of the Ducati - that immerses the reader in Rome's atmosphere. The author avoids heavy-handed description while still painting vivid scenes. The writing voice remains consistent throughout, maintaining an energetic but controlled tone that matches the story's pace. However, there are some minor weaknesses. Certain phrases edge toward purple prose ("her taillight bled into Roman night"), and a few moments feel slightly overwrought. The transformation of Ben from timid academic to willing accomplice happens quite rapidly, though this is somewhat mitigated by the compressed timeframe and Alessandra's magnetic personality. The ending strikes an appropriate note - romantic but not overly saccharine, with the stolen coin serving as both literal and metaphorical representation of their connection. The piece successfully establishes the foundation for a larger story while providing satisfying closure to this particular day. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 86.2
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
I wipe the same spot on the bar counter with my rag and breathe in the night shift. The Last Outpost hums the way it always hums this late. The heaters tick. The string lights Marn rigs over the stills blink gold and blue. The air smells like hot oil and star-anise soup and somebody's singed boots. My regulars sprawl where they always sprawl, and I love them for it. "You want the good news or the good news, Marn?" I say. "Hit me with the good news, Nets," Marn says, and his rock-skin face cracks into a grin. "Then hit me with the other good news." "Soup is hot," I say. "And your tab is still open because I like your face." "You like my face because I tip," Marn says. "I like your face despite the tipping," I say. "You tip in asteroid pebbles." "They are lucky pebbles," Marn says. Pex the merchant leans over from two stools down, her long ears twitching. "Nets, sweetheart, tell this overgrown gravel pile that his lucky pebbles are clogging my cargo scale again." "I negotiate peace, not miracles," I say. I wipe the same spot on the bar counter with my rag as I listen to them bicker. It soothes me. This is my talent, right? I remember who takes decaf synth, who needs extra broth, who needs to sit far from who after a bad breakup on Ceres Dock. My flaw? I eavesdrop. I meddle. I water my own shift-drink and pretend I do not. Equilibrium. Then the dock door sighs open and cold leaks in. She plops down at the far end of the bar, quiet and hard. Tentacled dreads askew, frost on her collar, eyes red from too many hours awake. A tug pilot, by the burn marks on her gloves. Frazzled in a way I recognize. Running-from-something frazzled. "Vega whisky, neat," she says. "Better make that a double." "You got it, friend," I say. I grab the bottle from under the bar. My hand knows the weight. "Rough run in?" "You have no idea," she says. "You Nets?" "Depends who asks," I say. "Tonight I am Nets who pours." "I am Ilsa," she says. "Ilsa Vane. Lantern tug, out of Pallis Waypoint. I just limped in on fumes with half my array melted." "Ouch," I say. I wipe the same spot on the bar counter with my rag as I listen. "Belter storm chew you up?" "Worse," Ilsa says. "Kessler shear in the inner lane. It is gone, Nets. The whole lane is soup. Markers, buoys, all shredded." The bar goes a little quiet. Marn stops mid-sip. "Come on," Pex says. "The inner lane can't be gone. My sister ships tomorrow." "It is gone for now," Ilsa says. "Authority shut the gate. No in, no out except by burn-around, and that takes weeks. I barely skimmed through before it closed." "So we are stuck out here?" Marn says. "We are stuck cozy," I say, because somebody has to say it light. "More soup for everyone. More time to pay your tabs." Nobody laughs. I pour her double. My pour is perfect. That is another talent. I never spill Vega whisky. Ilsa downs half of it in one go. Her dreads twitch. "That is not all," she says. "There is always an all," I say. "There is a cutter on my tail," Ilsa says. "Helix Combine. Dark hull, no transponder until they want you to see it. They ride my wake all the way from the shear." "Combine?" Pex whispers. "Out here? What do they want with us?" "They want to search," Ilsa says. "Every dock, every hold, every station on the rim. They say somebody ghosts their relay codes. Somebody running dark cargo through the belt." My rag stops. Then I make myself wipe the same spot on the bar counter again as I listen. Nice and slow. Equilibrium. "Search for what, exactly?" I say. My voice sounds normal. Good. "I don't know," Ilsa says. "Weapons? Seed-cores? People? They boarded the Waypoint before I jumped. Tore the chapel apart. Scared the kids. They say the Outpost is next because we are the last unlogged hub." "They can't just board us," Marn growls. "We are free dock. We have rights." "When do Combine care about rights?" Pex says. "They own half the oxygen between here and Vega." "How long?" I ask. Ilsa looks at her empty glass. Then at me. Really looks at me. "Two hours," she says. "Maybe less. My Lantern is cold in your Dock Three with a cracked core and a hold full of spore-fruit that rots if it warms. And they hail every fifteen minutes demanding manifest and crew names." "Give them manifest," Marn says. "We got nothing to hide." "Speak for yourself, rocks," Pex says. Her ears flatten. "Half my cargo is un-taxed root tea." "That is not the problem," Ilsa says. Her eyes stay on me. "Nets. Can I be honest with you?" "Please don't," I say, and I try to smile. "Honesty ruins the vibe." "You were nav-cast on Vega Prime, weren't you?" Ilsa says. "Five years ago? Nettle Quill?" The string lights buzz. The soup pot bubbles. I wipe the same spot on the bar counter with my rag as I listen, and listen, and listen. "Lot of Nettles in the galaxy," I say. "Not a lot who plot a ghost-burn through the Helix blockade and vanish," Ilsa says. "They still tell that story in tug bars. How you spoofed a whole Combine patrol with a weather balloon and a hymn." "Fun story," I say. "Fiction, probably." "Is it?" Ilsa says. "Because the cutter captain keeps asking about a navigator. Someone who knows how to run dark. Someone who could hide a ship signature inside a rock field like this one." "Why are you telling me this?" I whisper. "Because they scan my tug and they find nothing, they come in here next," Ilsa says. "They go stool to stool. They check IDs that most people out here don't have anymore. You know that. Look at this place." I look. I cannot help it. Marn with his expired miner's license. Pex with her un-taxed tea. Old Jolo dozing in the corner with his forged med-papers. Sarella the runaway bride from Io, mending nets by the heater. All my people. All my flaws and talents balanced on this little rock. My home because I run from my past life and I build a new one drink by drink. "What do you want from me?" I say. "Hide my ship," Ilsa says. "Spoof the dock signal. You know how. Bounce my heat print into the belt so when they scan, Dock Three reads empty. Give me twelve hours to cool my core and re-plot." "Twelve hours?" I say. "You ask for a miracle with a double whisky?" "I ask because you are the only one who can," Ilsa says. "And because if you don't, they find my rot and my log, and then they start asking why a burnt-out tug runs so hot, and then they come for you anyway." "Hey," Marn calls. "Everything okay down there, Nets?" "Peachy," I say, bright as a nova. "Ilsa just needs another double and a blanket. And maybe soup." "I don't need soup," Ilsa says. "I need an answer." My comm crackles behind the bar. Dock control. Jolo wakes up. Pex grips her cup so tight her knuckles go pale. "Nets?" Ilsa says. "Please. I hear you get people out of trouble. That is what you do here, right?" I wipe the same spot on the bar counter with my rag. The spot shines. Everything else blurs. Then the station speakers pop. "Unlogged hub, this is Helix Cutter Vigil," a crisp voice says. "Heave to for compliance scan. Repeat. Heave to for compliance scan." Every head turns to me.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece successfully establishes a cozy sci-fi atmosphere while building genuine tension and conflict. The writing demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt requirements - it's written in first person present tense, maintains approximately 60% dialogue, establishes clear conflict without resolution, and captures the "cozy" feel of a space station bar while introducing serious stakes. The characterization is particularly strong. Nets emerges as a compelling protagonist with clear personality traits - her tendency to wipe the same spot while listening, her role as mediator and secret-keeper, her careful balance of helping others while hiding her own past. The supporting characters feel lived-in and authentic, from Marn's rock-skin and "lucky pebbles" to Pex's twitching ears and contraband tea. Each character has distinct dialogue patterns and motivations. The world-building is efficient and immersive. Details like "star-anise soup," "asteroid pebbles," and "spore-fruit that rots if it warms" create texture without overwhelming the narrative. The technical elements (Kessler shear, ghost-burns, heat signatures) feel authentic to the sci-fi setting while remaining accessible. The dialogue flows naturally and serves multiple purposes - revealing character, advancing plot, and building atmosphere. The banter between regulars feels genuine, and Ilsa's increasingly urgent revelations create mounting tension. Nets' attempts to maintain normalcy while processing the threat to her sanctuary are particularly well-handled. The pacing builds effectively from comfortable routine to mounting crisis. The repetitive action of wiping the bar becomes a nervous tic that shows Nets' growing anxiety without stating it directly. The ending with the Helix Cutter's announcement creates a perfect cliffhanger that leaves readers wanting more. Some minor weaknesses include occasional repetitive phrasing and a few moments where the exposition feels slightly forced, but these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness. The piece successfully balances the cozy atmosphere with genuine stakes and creates investment in both the characters and their predicament. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 84.3
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Gone South - Day One** The truck doesn't even stop all the way before the guy tells me to get out. "Out. Come on. My wife'll kill me if she sees this on the dashcam." It's like 7 a.m. and already my shirt is sticking to my back. New Orleans smells like piss and sugar and rain that hasn't happened yet. The truck coughs away and I'm just standing there on like, Canal Street? with my backpack and my dead phone and $43 in cash. Welcome to freedom. The strap on my backpack keeps slipping off my shoulder. I hitch it up. It slips again. Everything I own is in there — two binders, a hoodie even though it's a million degrees, deodorant, a charger with no outlet, and the note Mom left on my pillow that I stole back before I left. *We love you. We just need time.* Time for what? For me to turn back into someone else? *God, you are such a bitch for leaving. She was crying.* Yeah, well. She was crying two days ago too when I told them. Not sad crying. Scared-angry crying. Dad just went real quiet and then said, "You're confused," like he was diagnosing a cold. And my little brother asked if I was still going to be his sibling, which — fuck, that one still rips me open. I wanted to stay and explain it a hundred times. I also wanted to never see that kitchen table again. Both things are true. How is that even possible? I walk. That's the plan. Just walk until I look like I know where I'm going. The Quarter wakes up weird. A guy in a feathered nothing is already playing trumpet on the corner, case open for dollars I don't have. A lady hoses down the sidewalk in front of a café and yells at me to move. I buy beignets because what else are you supposed to do in New Orleans? They're three bucks and hot sugar explodes all over my black t-shirt and I laugh for the first time in 48 hours. Powder everywhere. I look like a ghost. "You got a little — everywhere," someone says. Girl about my age, maybe seventeen, sitting on the curb with a skateboard with no wheels, just the deck. Dreads pulled up, big hoop earrings, ripped jeans despite the heat. She grins and wipes her own mouth to show me. "Thanks," I say. "New look. Trying it out." "Works for you." She squints at me. "You just get here?" How does she know? Do I have THAT stamped on my forehead? I hitch my backpack strap up again. It slides right back down. "That obvious?" "You got that just-got-dropped-off stare. Plus you’re staring at everything like it might bite you." She pats the curb. "I'm Drea. You good sitting? Cops move you if you stand too long looking broke." I sit. My legs are shaking and I'm glad to hide it. "Taylor," I say. "From Tennessee." "Drea, from Baton Rouge, originally. Now from —" she waves her hand at the whole street, " — wherever." She talks fast, like she's nervous or just wired. She tells me she's been here three months, knows where to charge your phone for free at the library, which church gives out socks with no sermon, which security guard at Jackson Square will let you sleep on the bench if you’re chill. She asks if I’m hungry, if I’m good, if anyone’s following me. It feels good and also like too much. Mom-voice in my head goes: *Taylor, you do not know this person.* "Are you — like, staying with someone?" I ask. She shrugs too quick. "My cousin stays over on Elysian. I'm crashing there till I get work. He's a cook." She says it smooth, but her eyes flick away. Lie. I know a lie when I hear one because I lived on them for two years before I came out. *No, Mom, I'm fine. No, that's just how all girls dress — I mean —* *Stop.* "That's cool," I say. "You?" she asks. "You got people here?" And here's the thing. I could lie. Should lie. Every runaway PSA ever says don't tell strangers your business. But I'm so tired and she's looking at me like I'm a real person, not a problem or a counsellor's phone call. "No," I admit. "I just — I had to leave. I came out to my parents two days ago. As trans. It went... bad." She nods like I just said I like pizza. No flinch. No twenty questions. "Damn. Sorry. Family can be trash." She bumps my knee with hers. "My foster mom kicked me when I was fifteen 'cause I stole her car. Which, fair, but also she used to lock the fridge, so who's really the criminal here?" I laugh so hard powdered sugar comes out my nose and she cackles. Midday we wander. She shows me the river, all brown and fast. A big boat with a wheel. Guys selling airbrushed shirts. The heat is insane, sweat pooling under my binder and I’m hyperaware of it, of my chest, of my voice. When I order a Coke the guy at the counter goes, "Yes ma'am?" and my stomach drops to my shoes. Drea clocks it instantly. "You want me to say something?" she whispers, fierce. I shake my head fast. "No. It's fine. I just — I don't pass yet and —" The backpack strap slips again and I yank it hard, like I can punish it. "It's stupid." "It ain't stupid." She says it simple. Not a speech. Just that. For a second I could cry. I don't. I drink my Coke too fast and get brain freeze. Afternoon gets sketchy. A dude in a white van slows down by us near Decatur, leans out. "Y'all girls need a ride? Got cold A/C, got money if you wanna party." Drea doesn't even hesitate, flips him off and yells, "We good, perv!" and drags me into a shop. My heart is hammering out of my chest. In Tennessee danger was theoretical — boring cops, boring boys in trucks. Here it's real and close and smells like cigarettes. "He does that shit every week," she mutters, but her hands are shaking. "Don't ever get in a car. Ever." "I know," I say, but did I? Last night I hitched from Chattanooga with a trucker who talked about Jesus the whole way and I just got lucky. *Stupid, stupid.* Mom would lose it if she knew. We end up at the library because my feet hurt and Drea says I can charge my phone a little. The A/C hits like heaven. I plug in and stare at the lock screen — 14 missed calls. MOM. DAD. Unknown. My thumb hovers. Guilt eats me alive. What if they're scared? What if little Caleb thinks I left because of him? *If you call they'll track you. If you don't call you're a monster. Pick one.* I text Mom: *I'm safe. I'm in LA — I mean Louisiana. Don't call cops please. I love you. - T* I turn the phone off before she can answer. My hands won't stop trembling. Drea watches me, doesn't ask. Then she pulls a busted burner phone from her bra and checks it every two minutes. Someone named K keeps texting *where u at*. When I ask, she goes, "Nobody. Ex." Another flick-away lie. At sunset we’re back at Jackson Square. Musicians everywhere, light turning everything gold. Drea steals fries from a tourist when they aren’t looking and splits them with me like it’s communion. For a minute I feel... free? Like maybe I invented myself right this time. Not drama. Real. Then a cop rolls up and Drea tenses all over. "Shit. That's Curley. He knows I'm—" She stops. "I gotta go. My cousin's shift — I gotta meet him now." It’s the first crack in her story big enough to see through. She doesn’t have a cousin. She’s scared of cops because she’s underage and alone, same as me. And who the hell is K? "You can come," she says quickly, "but... it's kinda crowded there. Maybe meet tomorrow? Ten, by the cathedral? Please?" She’s lying and she’s asking me to trust her at the same time. And I get it. I have my own secrets I’m not telling — like how I pocketed Dad’s pocketknife, like how I almost didn’t leave, like how part of me wants to go home so bad it hurts to breathe. "Okay," I say. "Tomorrow. Ten." She hugs me fast, hard. She smells like vanilla and sweat. "Don’t sleep on the street tonight, okay? Go to Covenant House on Rampart. Tell 'em you're sixteen. They'll take you. No questions till morning." Then she’s gone, skating on no wheels down the alley, burner phone glowing in her hand. Night comes sticky and purple. I hitch my stupid backpack strap up one more time and start walking toward Rampart, toward the shelter. I don’t know if Drea will be there tomorrow. I don’t know if that text to Mom was enough or too much. I don’t know who K is or if Drea’s okay or if I’m an idiot for trusting her. I just know I made it through day one. Two states away. Still me.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt's requirements, successfully capturing Taylor's voice as a transgender teen runaway navigating their first day in New Orleans. The writing maintains a consistent first-person perspective with effective mixed tense usage, and the 1000-word count is well-utilized. The characterization is particularly strong. Taylor feels authentic as a 16-year-old dealing with complex emotions - the guilt over leaving family, fear of the unknown, and desperate need for acceptance. The internal monologue effectively captures the conflicting emotions: "I wanted to stay and explain it a hundred times. I also wanted to never see that kitchen table again. Both things are true." This emotional complexity feels genuine rather than manufactured. Drea emerges as a well-developed secondary character with her own secrets and vulnerabilities. The author skillfully shows rather than tells her situation through behavioral details - the lie about her cousin, the nervous phone checking, her knowledge of street survival. The dynamic between the characters feels natural, with appropriate wariness mixed with desperate need for connection. The prose style effectively captures a teenage voice without becoming overly stylized. Phrases like "mind-fuckingly bored" and "Welcome to freedom" feel authentic to the character's age and situation. The sensory details of New Orleans - the smell of "piss and sugar and rain that hasn't happened yet" - create vivid atmosphere without becoming purple. The dialogue flows naturally and serves multiple purposes: revealing character, advancing plot, and building tension. The conversation about Taylor's trans identity is handled with appropriate sensitivity, showing Drea's acceptance through action rather than speeches. The pacing maintains tension throughout the day-long timeframe. The encounter with the predatory man in the van introduces real danger without feeling gratuitous, and Taylor's phone call dilemma creates genuine emotional stakes. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - Taylor has survived day one but faces an uncertain future, avoiding both false optimism and excessive darkness. Some minor weaknesses include occasional repetitive elements (the backpack strap slipping) and a few moments where the writing becomes slightly self-conscious. However, these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness. The piece successfully avoids common pitfalls of young adult fiction - it doesn't oversimplify complex issues, doesn't provide easy answers, and maintains emotional authenticity throughout. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 81.2
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**My Apocalypse Buddy** The world did not end with a bang, which was the first disappointment. It ended with a long, embarrassed whimper and a supply-chain issue.* **In the grand taxonomy of apocalypses, this one was filed under: Inconvenient, Prolonged, and Largely Admin-Based. No zombies. No heroic last stand. Just one day the trucks stopped coming, the phones stopped phoning, and everyone who had ever said “I’d thrive off-grid, me” was revealed to have been lying.* Midas lived in the top deck of an overturned double-decker bus on top of a hill, which he called Home Base because calling it The Damp Bus Full Of Rust would have lowered morale. His morale lived there too, and was also damp. His predicament, as deliberated at 07:00 hours over breakfast, was threefold. One: They were out of clean water. The filter was making a noise like a man gargling gravel. Two: They were out of food that did not require an apology. Three: Chewy’s left eye was flickering. Chewy was an animo-tronic stuffed koala from some long-forgotten Before Time, approximately the size and temperament of a resentful football. He ran on a tiny solar panel glued to his head like a beanie, smelled faintly of eucalyptus and burnt wiring, and spoke only in pre-Collapse advertising slogans, which he emitted at random intervals with great conviction and no context whatsoever. Midas held up the cracked water filter. “So. Today’s mission. We go down to the Merrydale Clinic, three miles across the Glass Flats. In and out. Iodine, filter cloth, D-cell batteries if the gods are kind. Back before dark. No detours. No trouble.” Chewy stared at him with one steady button eye and one flickering one. “Because You’re Worth It,” said Chewy, solemnly. “Exactly. Hydration is self-care,” said Midas, who had long ago learned to translate Koala into Optimism. “And no getting worshipped as a god again.” “Just Do It,” said Chewy. That was, Midas decided, agreement. It is a well-known fact that hapless protagonists are fluent in confirmation bias.* Midas had been named Midas by parents with a sense of humour that had not survived the Collapse. Everything he touched did turn — just not to gold. It turned to complications, paperwork, and mild personal injury. He had a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble, the way water finds the lowest point, or cats find the one person allergic to them. They set off at eight, Midas with a rucksack, a spear made from a curtain rod, and Chewy strapped to his chest in a baby carrier, like a furry, judgmental breastplate. The plan went sideways before they’d even left the hill. This was traditional. This was, in fact, early by Midas standards. Sideways the First: The footbridge over the Culvert was gone. Not broken — *gone*. Someone had stolen a bridge. Midas stood and stared at the gap, doing the particular math of the desperate: distance vs. tetanus. “We’ll go round via the Old Retail Park,” he said. “Have A Break, Have A—” Chewy began, then shorted out in the damp with a sad *pfft*. “We will *not* have a break. We’ve just had a break. We’ve had twelve years of break.” The Retail Park was the territory of the Trolleys. Feral shopping trolleys, herds of them, blown by the wind into clattering, rattling migrations across the cracked car park. The old sages said they could smell loose change at forty paces. Midas tried to cross quietly, pushing through knee-high nettles, Chewy’s solar beanie catching the sun. Sideways the Second duly arrived in the form of seagulls. Post-Collapse seagulls had undergone what naturalists call *a real attitude problem*. These had built a nest in a overturned Greggs sign and worshipped a golden crisp packet as their Bright Feathered God. Midas, tall, limping, glinting faintly of solar panel, was clearly either a rival god or lunch. They attacked with shrieks and a complete disregard for the Geneva Convention. Midas ran, flailing his curtain-rod spear, Chewy bouncing on his chest screaming advertising at them: “I’M LOVIN’ IT! I’M LOVIN’ IT!” “You are *not* lovin’ it!” Midas shouted, sprinting straight into a display of garden gnomes. “*I’m* not lovin’ it!” He escaped the gulls by falling into the flooded basement of Furniture World, which was Sideways the Third and arguably the wettest. The water smelled of old flat-pack and regret. Midas waded through it, holding Chewy aloft like a soggy torch, and emerged on the other side missing one shoe, one sock, and a good deal of dignity, but — miracle of miracles — only half a mile from the Clinic. The Clinic was, of course, already occupied. They were the Choir — a cheerful gang of former PTA members who had survived the end of civilization by being more organized, better armed, and significantly more terrifying than anyone else. They wore high-vis vests and sang while they looted. “Ah,” said their leader, Jan, lowering her crossbow made from a Dyson. “Midas.” “Jan,” said Midas, dripping. “Still alive, then. Pity. What do you want?” “Medicine. Filter stuff. Just the expired dregs. I’m not greedy. I’m Midas.” Jan eyed Chewy. Chewy eyed her back. His flickering eye chose that exact moment to stabilize into a holy, steady red glow. The Choir gasped. One of them knelt. This had happened before. “Oh no,” said Midas. “No, no, no. He’s not— Chewy, say something normal.” Chewy, filled with the divine inspiration that only comes from 1.5 volts and direct sunlight, declared: “WASH & GO!” “It speaks!” cried the Choir. “The Small Grey Prophet promises Cleanliness in Motion!” Sideways the Fourth took approximately forty minutes and involved incense (a Yankee Candle), offerings (half a Penguin biscuit), and a theological debate about whether Chewy wanted them to go east or *wash* and go east. Midas, who had once done a first-aid course and therefore counted as medical staff, used the distraction to pocket iodine tablets, a roll of bandage, two D-cells, and a miraculously intact tin of peaches. He paid for it with his other shoe, which was now deemed a holy relic. They left at a run, pursued for half a mile by blessings and one enthusiastic new convert with a tambourine, until Midas tripped over Narrative Causality itself — a root — and tobogganed most of the way down Muddy Hill inside a runaway Tesco trolley, screaming, with Chewy clamped in his teeth by the ear. Which is how they returned to Home Base in multiple ways, all of them worse for wear. Midas returned on foot (limping), by trolley (unintentionally, at speed), and by river (briefly, when the trolley hit the Culvert). He returned philosophically diminished, physically damp, and one shoe lighter than he had left, which is to say, shoeless. Chewy returned in the rucksack (in two pieces, his head having achieved independent travel during the trolley incident), on solar power (flickering), and in spirit (elevated to godhood, which he bore with quiet dignity). Back in the upturned bus, as rain hammered the floor-which-was-a-wall, Midas taped Chewy’s head back on, changed the filter with iodine and an old T-shirt, and opened the peaches with his spear. They tasted of rust and heaven. He held up a peach slice to Chewy. “Mission accomplished? Sort of?” Chewy’s eye glowed steady. He looked, for a small grey plastic marsupial, almost fond. “Have A Break—” he said. “Yeah,” said Midas, worse for wear in every sense that mattered, and leaking slightly. “Yeah. We will.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, successfully capturing his dry wit, footnote-like asides, and philosophical observations about human nature wrapped in absurdist humor. The author effectively establishes the post-apocalyptic setting through clever details like "supply-chain issue" apocalypse and "admin-based" collapse, which feels authentically Pratchettesque in its mundane absurdity. The characterization is well-executed within the constraints of the format. Midas emerges as a believably hapless protagonist whose self-awareness about his predicament adds depth, while Chewy's limitation to advertising slogans creates genuine comedic moments that feel organic rather than forced. The dynamic between them develops naturally through their shared misadventures. The narrative structure follows the requested format precisely, moving from deliberation through escalating complications to their battered return home. Each "sideways" moment builds logically from the previous, creating genuine momentum. The writing maintains consistent voice throughout, with Pratchett-style observations ("It is a well-known fact that hapless protagonists are fluent in confirmation bias") seamlessly integrated. The prose demonstrates technical competence with varied sentence structures and natural flow. Descriptive passages like "The water smelled of old flat-pack and regret" show genuine wit without becoming overwrought. The dialogue, while limited by Chewy's constraints, serves its purpose effectively. However, the piece occasionally relies on telling rather than showing, particularly in establishing Midas's character traits. Some comedic beats, while well-executed, follow predictable patterns. The ending, though satisfying, doesn't quite achieve the emotional resonance of Pratchett's best work, remaining somewhat surface-level in its warmth. The world-building is efficient and believable, creating a lived-in post-apocalyptic environment without excessive exposition. The Choir subplot adds genuine stakes and humor while advancing the plot. Overall, this represents skilled pastiche writing that captures the source material's essence while telling a complete, engaging story. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 81.3
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell over the door of The Dog-Eared Dragon gave its usual asthmatic jingle, and then the rain and a man came in together. He hit the mat too fast, all long coat and damp beanie pulled low and ridiculous sunglasses in November in Hay-on-Wye. He locked the door behind him and leaned against it, breathing hard, grinning like this was all a game. "Hi. Hello. Bore da, and all that. Don't mind me. I'm just - hiding." Anwen Price didn't look up from the till straight away. "We sell books, not sanctuary." "Can't it be both? Books, sanctuary, excellent hiding places? You look like a woman with an excellent back room." "We've got the Children's Corner. You can crouch behind the Gruffalo if you like." He laughed, too loud, and pushed the sunglasses up. Dark hair stuck to his forehead. Blue eyes, famous eyes. "God, perfect. You're perfect. Save me and I'll thank you in my next acceptance speech." Anwen finally looked. Really looked. *Oh no. Oh, no no no. That's Leo Hartley.* Her stomach did something stupid and traitorous. Outside, on Lion Street, two men with long lenses jogged past the wet window, then stopped. Turned. "Shit," he breathed, dropping flat behind the New Arrivals table. "Don't look, don't look. Act natural." "I am shelving," Anwen said, very evenly, sliding a copy of *Under Milk Wood* into place. "This is me acting natural." "You're brilliant at it. Very natural. Very cool. Most people scream a bit at this point." "Most people don't come in here dripping on the first editions." He peeked over the table. "Are they gone?" "No. They're pretending to look at the menu for the cafe next door. Which is closed on Tuesdays. Everyone knows that except paparazzi." "Professionals," Leo said solemnly, crawling on his knees toward the counter. "You wouldn't mind if I just... stayed here until they get bored and go objectify someone else?" Anwen folded her arms. "You're Leo Hartley." He lit up. "Yes! See? There we go." "I said your name. I didn't scream." "Right. Noted. Bit of a blow, to be honest." He pulled off the beanie, shook out his hair in a way that had absolutely worked on a thousand red carpets. "Usually I get at least a gasp." "You got rain on my floor." He clutched his chest. "Cold. So cold. Is this how you treat all your A-list refugees?" "Only the damp ones." *Do not stare at his hair. Do not stare at his mouth. Count the till, Anwen.* "What are you even doing in Hay? Filming another shirtless sword thing?" "*The Hollow Crown of Embers*, I'll have you know. Very serious fantasy. Lots of mud. Lots of brooding in the Bannau. We're up on the Black Mountains for three weeks." He stood up slowly, hands raised, taking in the shop. Low beams, smell of woodsmoke and paper, the old brass telescope by the window seat. "Oh, nice. Very... real. I love this. God, I love a real bookshop." "You say that like bookshops are usually fake." "Most things in my life are a bit fake, love." The grin slipped, just for a second. Then it was back, brighter. "So. Anwen -" he squinted at her badge, "- Anwen of the Books. What's your review? *Pirate King 2*: masterpiece or guilty pleasure?" "Never seen it." A beat. "Sorry, what?" "Never seen it," she repeated, reshelving *The Mabinogion*. "I was busy. Running a shop." "Right, but - the billboards? The Super Bowl trailer where I come out of the sea?" "I don't watch telly much. Light pollution." He stared at her. "You're joking." "Do I look like I'm joking?" "You look like you're enjoying this far too much." He leaned both elbows on her counter, invading it completely. He smelled like rain and expensive aftershave and wet wool. "Come on. *Golden Boy*? The rom-com with the dog? Everyone's mum loves that one." "My mam likes *Pobol y Cwm*." "Okay, ouch." He was still smiling, but something flickered. He straightened a pile of bookmarks that didn't need straightening. "So you're, like, immune?" "I'm Welsh. We're born suspicious of charm." "God, that's hot." He said it before he could stop himself, and his ears went pink. "Sorry. Sorry, that was - rogue of me. I do that. Say the thing." "Charming," Anwen said dryly. Her ears were burning too. *Stop it. He flirts with lamp posts. Do not go wobbly because he's looking at you like that.* He drifted away from the counter to give himself something to do, and stopped by the window. By the telescope. "Oh, mate, is this yours?" His whole voice changed. Less perform-y. "This is a proper one. An 8-inch Dobsonian?" Anwen blinked. "You know telescopes?" "Do I know telescopes?" He looked almost offended. "Love, I grew up on a council estate in Peckham with a second-hand Sky-Watcher and a dad who worked nights. Only dark I ever got was on the balcony at 3 a.m. Saturn's rings through that thing changed my life." She stared. "You're taking the piss." "I swear on my BAFTA nomination." He crouched beside it, hands gentle on the tube in a way that made her throat go tight. "You've got it pointed... oh, nice, you've got a clear line south-west over the rooftops. You use it here?" "Sometimes. Mostly I go up to Hay Bluff. It's Bannau Brycheiniog, International Dark Sky Reserve, you know? No light pollution. On a good night you can see the Milky Way like spilt sugar." He looked up at her, and for once he wasn't posing. "You go up there? In the dark? Alone?" "With the Stargazers' Club. Second Friday. Six of us, flasks and red torches and my mate Lowri's terrible bara brith." "I haven't seen a proper sky in months," he said quietly. "Morocco, London, LA - it's all orange glow. Last month I was in the Atacama for a shoot and I just... I snuck out at 2 a.m. with my camera. Laid in the dirt for an hour. My publicist thought I'd been kidnapped." Anwen laughed before she could help it. "Did you get the shot?" "Overexposed Orion. Out of focus. Best photo I've ever taken." He grinned, real this time, crooked and unguarded. "You do astrophotography?" "Trying. Very badly. I've got a folder on my phone called 'blurry dots'." She found herself pulling it out, showing him before her brain caught up. "That's meant to be Andromeda from last August." He leaned in close, shoulder brushing hers. "That's not bad! See that smudge? That's two and a half million light years, that is. You've caught ancient photons on a phone from Tesco Mobile." "Technically it's O2." "Even more impressive." Their eyes met. He smelled like rain. She could see the tired lines under the charm, the faint stubble, a small scar on his lip she remembered from a magazine. *Say something normal. Say something shopkeeper-ish.* "So," she said, too fast, stepping back, "you like stars." "I like things that don't care who I am," he said. Then, instantly, the old reflex kicked in - the wink, the nudge. "Which is why I like you, clearly. Everyone else likes me. It's exhausting being this likeable." "Poor you." "No, but seriously." He tapped the counter. "You really don't... like me? Even a bit?" Anwen raised an eyebrow. "I don't know you. I know your haircut." He laughed, but it was thinner now. He was watching her face for the laugh, for the softening. Needing it. "Fair. Fair. Rogue with a fragile ego, that's me. My therapist has a whole whiteboard." "Does your therapist know you hide in bookshops?" "She encourages healthy coping mechanisms." Outside, the paparazzi were moving off, heads down against the rain. Leo noticed, but he didn't move toward the door. "They've gone," Anwen said. "Have they?" He didn't look. He was turning a paperback over in his hands - *A Field Guide to the Night Sky*. "Do you... do you lend expertise as well as books? If I bought this, would you show me where to stand on Hay Bluff so I don't fall off and become a headline? 'Famous Idiot Found In Bog'?" "I charge extra for bog rescue." "I'll pay." He held her gaze. No grin now. Just intent, a little nervous. The charm offensive had completely run out of road, and what was left was younger and more earnest. "Second Friday, you said? The Stargazers' Club?" "This Friday, actually. Moved for the new moon." "Perfect. I can do new moon. I'm very good at new moons. Mysterious. Brooding." He tried the smile again, but it wobbled. Anwen's heart was hammering so loud she was sure the Gruffalo could hear it. *Say no. He'll bring cameras and chaos and you'll end up crying in the Biography section.* "Six people, Leo. With flasks. If you bring an entourage, Lowri will kill you with a tripod." "No entourage. Just me. And my terrible camera." He slid the book across the counter. "Please?" She rang it up slowly to give her hands something to do. "Eight ninety-nine." He paid, then took the receipt and scribbled a number on the back. Slid it back. "In case it rains. Or in case you need to tell me to piss off properly." She didn't touch the receipt. "I can do that in person." "I hope so." He pulled his beanie back on, sunglasses back down, ridiculous again. At the door he paused. "Hey. Anwen of the Books?" "What?" "Thanks for not screaming." The bell jingled. He was gone into the Welsh rain, and the shop felt suddenly too quiet and too big. Anwen picked up the receipt. Her fingers were shaking. *Idiot,* she told herself firmly, and tucked it into the pocket closest to her heart.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and adherence to the prompt requirements. The author successfully creates a meet-cute scenario in a Welsh bookstore with well-defined character archetypes - Leo as the charming but insecure actor and Anwen as the seemingly immune but inwardly affected bookstore owner. The dialogue carries the scene effectively, with distinct voices for each character. Leo's speech patterns shift believably between performative charm and genuine vulnerability, while Anwen maintains a dry, Welsh sensibility throughout. The banter feels natural and serves the dual purpose of revealing character while advancing the romantic tension. The Welsh setting is well-integrated through specific place names (Hay-on-Wye, Bannau Brycheiniog) and cultural references (Pobol y Cwm, bara brith) without feeling forced or touristy. The author demonstrates good research and cultural awareness. Character development is nuanced, particularly in showing Leo's fragile ego beneath his charm offensive. The moment when his facade cracks over Anwen's lack of recognition feels authentic. Anwen's internal conflict between her outward resistance and growing attraction is well-handled through subtle physical cues and internal commentary. The shared interest in astronomy provides an effective bridge between the characters that feels organic rather than contrived. It allows Leo to show genuine vulnerability and knowledge beyond his celebrity persona, while giving Anwen a reason to soften toward him. However, the piece occasionally veers toward overly cute dialogue exchanges, and some of Leo's lines feel slightly too polished for natural speech. The pacing is generally strong, though the transition from mutual antagonism to romantic interest happens quite rapidly, even for the romance genre. The ending strikes an appropriate note - hopeful but not overly resolved, maintaining tension for future development. The final image of Anwen tucking the receipt near her heart is perhaps slightly clichéd but works within genre conventions.
