+ Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The door gave before Aya touched it. It sighed inward on oiled hinges, too well-kept for a thieves' hold, and exhaled a breath of cold air that smelt of brine and tallow and old iron. Beyond lay the underhold of the Morska — a vaulted gut of black stone ribbed with the picked-clean bones of a bull leviathan, each rib arching overhead and bound with brass. Whale-oil sconces burned low along the walls, their flames guttering blue at the edges, as if the air itself were thin down here. In the centre, upon a plinth of rusted chain and Scythan basalt, rested the thing they had come for. Aya had expected a coffer. A reliquary. Instead the artifact was a spine — a length of jointed, black glass vertebrae, faintly translucent, strung with hair-fine copper wire that sweated frost. It hummed, very faintly, a note felt more in the teeth than heard. It was too quiet. That was her first true thought. After a night of running alarms and constables' whistles and the frantic clatter of the upper guildhall emptied by the raid, this silence was staged. *Mother above, we have walked into a jaw.* "Close it," said a woman's voice from the dark. Katra swore under her breath. Simeon fumbled at his waistcoat — and then Aya heard it, loud in the stillness: the tick of his pocket watch, too loud, frantic brass clicking marking each second. *Tick. Tick. Tick.* Gaslight flared. They stood in a half-circle of lamplight, and she stood at its heart. Mistress Odelia Morska. Decidedly not in Newgate irons. Decidedly not arrested in the early hours of the morning. She wore a greatcoat of tarred canvas over a corset of whalebone and steel, her grey hair pinned back severe as a ship's prow. In her right hand she held a brass-barrelled revolver, oiled and gleaming; at her left hip hung a bone-saw short sword. Behind her, four dock-built men loomed with whale-harpoons and cudgels tipped in iron, their faces daubed with soot against the lamplight. The muzzles of two more pistols, held steady by her bodyguards, found Aya and Katra and Simeon in turn. Odelia smiled, and it did not reach her eyes. "Well," she said, her voice Morska dockside, gravel rubbed in gin. "Look at my little rats, come sniffin' after the cheese. Masks an' all." Aya felt Katra shift beside her, coiled to run or to draw. Aya's gloved hand shot out and gripped her wrist, hard. *No. Not now. Not against powder.* Simeon's watch ticked on. *Tick. Tick. Tick.* His breath came shallow and fast. "Easy, loves," Odelia crooned. "Brass don't miss down here. Steel don't jam like your pretty tricks do. Hands up, gentle-like. Jemi, take their teeth." One of the bodyguards stepped forward — a wall of oilskin and scar — and stripped them with practised efficiency. Katra's knives clattered to the flagstones. Simeon's wrench and powder-flask followed. Aya's own belt of vials, her compass, her spring-lancet — all taken. She did not resist. She had read enough natural philosophy to know the velocity of a ball at ten paces. Men trusted brass and oil and steel in this city because brass and oil and steel never lied. Then the man's great hand closed on her domino mask, the black silk she had sewn herself with silver thread, and tore it away. The lamplight struck her face bare. A collective intake of breath. Even Odelia paused. "Oh," Odelia said softly. "Oh, ain't you a pretty treason." Aya stood exposed, her pale hair plastered to her forehead with sweat, her aristocrat's cheekbones and scholar's ink-stained fingers suddenly obscene in this place. *Lady Aya Harlowe of Bellweather Row.* The name rang in her skull like a chapel bell. Third daughter of Lord Harlowe, patron of the Royal Society of Engines, guest at the Duchess's winter ball not three nights past. And here, unmasked, in the underhold of thieves. Her stomach turned to water. If her father learned — when he learned — it would not be disownment. It would be the gallows-trap and the short drop. Immateria magick was outlawed. Her mother had swung at Tyburn Dock for less than what Aya had done in the last month alone. She could still see it when she closed her eyes: her mother's feet kicking above the crowd, the crowd holding their noses against whale-oil and buying hot pies, as if it were theatre. *They hanged her by the neck until dead, and they will hang me, and Katra and Simeon will hang beside me for harbouring a witch.* Simeon's watch ticked louder. *Tick. Tick. Tick.* "On your knees," Odelia said. They knelt. The stone was ice through Aya's trousers. Katra's jaw worked, fury and fear warring in her scarred face. "You set us up," Katra spat. "The raid — bloody play-acting?" "The raid were real enough," Odelia said. "Bluecoats took my tithe-boys and my second cellar. I let 'em. Needed to see which of my own pups would turn and bite while the bitch were caged." Her gaze settled, heavy and cold, on Aya. "And you bit deep, my masked philosopher. Summonin' things from the black to pick my locks and sniff my wards. I felt 'em scratchin', girl. The immateria leaves a stink, like rot under perfume." Aya forced her chin up. Her voice, when it came, was steadier than she deserved — clipped, Bellweather-educated, even now. "Then you know what I am. And you know what I'm worth." Odelia raised an eyebrow. "Do I?" "You cannot kill us. Not yet." The words tasted of copper. "I am Lady Aya Harlowe. My father sits on the Admiralty Board for Whale Oil and Engine Standards. If I disappear in the night, there will be inquiries. Constables with warrants, not bribes. Journalists. My face was at the opera on Thursday — people will notice its absence." *Liar. Father would pay to have me quietly buried if he knew. But she doesn't know that.* She pressed on, the scholar in her cataloguing her own pulse as if it belonged to someone else. "Keep me breathing, and you keep a hostage of the blood. Ransom me. Use me. The Harlowe vaults could buy you three ships and a pardon writ in gold leaf. Kill me — kill any of us — and you trade a quiet knife for a very loud noose." Beside her, Simeon made a small, strangled sound. *Tick. Tick. Tick.* His watch beat like a second heart in his waistcoat pocket, marking each tense second as it bled away. She could feel his terror radiating off him in waves; gentle, gear-handed Simeon who could mend any engine but could not mend this. Katra hissed, low: "Aya, don't —" "Quiet," Aya whispered, without looking. *Forgive me. If they know my name, you are dead with me. If they don't, we are dead now.* Odelia stepped closer, her boots ringing on stone. She leaned down until her gin-breath warmed Aya's bare cheek, until the muzzle of that brass revolver hovered a hand's breadth from Aya's temple. The metal smelt of oil. Real. Certain. No spell, no whisper from the dark, only powder and physics. "A hostage, eh?" Odelia murmured. "A little lordling witch, offerin' herself up like a gilt purse. You think your blood'll keep you warm down here, dearie? Your mother thought her blood were special too. Immateria blood. I remember her dancin' at the end of a rope while the gulls cried." Aya's throat closed. Behind her eyes, something in the dark stirred — the old cold things she called without meaning to, pressing against the membrane of the world, eager. She bit the inside of her cheek until she bled, forcing them back. *Not now. If I summon now, she will see, and we are damned for witchcraft as well as thievery.* "Name your price," Aya said hoarsely. Odelia smiled then, truly smiled, and cocked the hammer back with a click that swallowed, for one awful instant, even the ticking of Simeon's watch. "Oh, I will, my lady," she said.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and atmospheric worldbuilding within the "whalepunk" fantasy setting. The author successfully creates a vivid, immersive environment using whale bone architecture, brass fixtures, and industrial Victorian elements that feel authentic to the genre. The opening description of the underhold with its leviathan ribs and whale-oil sconces immediately establishes the unique aesthetic. The writing adheres closely to the prompt's requirements, delivering all requested story beats: the trio's entry, the confrontation with the un-incarcerated guild leader, Aya's unmasking and capture, and her attempt to negotiate using her aristocratic value as leverage. The author skillfully avoids writing a fight scene as instructed, instead building tension through dialogue and psychological maneuvering. Character voices feel distinct and authentic to their backgrounds. Odelia's rough dockside dialect ("ain't you a pretty treason," "my little rats") contrasts effectively with Aya's educated speech patterns, even under duress. The internal monologue reveals Aya's complex psychology - her fear, calculation, and the weight of her mother's execution haunting her decisions. The prose demonstrates sophisticated control, balancing rich descriptive passages with sharp dialogue and internal tension. Sensory details like Simeon's frantically ticking watch, the smell of brine and tallow, and the physical sensation of cold stone create immersive atmosphere without becoming overwrought. The author shows restraint in magical elements, keeping them mysterious and feared rather than flashy. However, some elements feel slightly predictable - the "too quiet" setup clearly telegraphs the trap, and Aya's aristocratic reveal, while well-executed, follows expected patterns. The piece also relies heavily on exposition through dialogue in places, though this serves the worldbuilding effectively. The emotional complexity is strong, particularly in Aya's internal struggle between her privileged background and criminal activities, complicated by her mother's execution and her own magical abilities. The ending maintains appropriate tension without false resolution. + Fanfic-crossover: Gunpowder Rendezvous — Score: 78.8
Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bar on the edge of Tharsis Down sweats heat and bad decisions. Neon buzzes pink against cracked tile. A fan turns slow overhead and moves nothing but smoke. The air tastes like cheap whiskey and old fry oil. Spike Spiegel sits at the counter with his legs stretched long and his boots hooked on the rail. He is tall and loose-limbed in a blue suit that hangs rumpled off his frame. His hair sticks up in a dark cloud. One eye is brown and sharp. The other eye is calm and false, a prosthetic that never quite tracks right and messes with his depth perception. He spins a lighter between his fingers. A ring of rust on Spike’s lighter suggests it’s been dropped in water more than once. He flicks it open, flicks it shut. Click. Click. He wants a cigarette and food and money, in that order, and he has none of the three. The door bangs open and Revy walks in like she owns the oxygen. She is short and hard and loud in motion. She wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the dust storm outside. Sweat shines on her collarbones. A dragon tattoo covers her right arm from wrist to shoulder, scales and teeth flexing when she moves. Twin Berettas ride in holsters at her hips, worn low for a fast draw. She is Chinese-American, foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, famous from Roanapur to the colonies as Two Hands for the way she fires both pistols at once with surgical accuracy. Right now she wants a drink. She drops onto the stool next to Spike and slaps the counter. “Whiskey. Double. Leave the bottle,” she says. Spike looks at her sideways and grins that lazy grin. “You drink like you mean it,” he says. “You stare like you want to lose an eye,” she says. “The other one looks fake enough already.” He laughs, low and unbothered. “It is. You got a good eye.” “Two good eyes. Two good hands. You do the math.” The bartender sets down her glass and her bottle and hurries away. Spike watches her drink. She drinks heavily and without pause, throat working, then slams the glass down and lights a cigarette with a snap of her Zippo. Smoke curls up around her face. “I’m Spike,” he says, and offers his empty glass toward her bottle in a silent, broke, chronically hungry question. She eyes him. “Revy. And that bottle ain’t charity.” “Just a taste. I hunt better hydrated.” “You hunt?” She pours, a bare inch, and keeps her thumb on the neck. “Who?” “Dario Venn. Syndicate skimmer. Eight million woolongs, dead or alive. Last seen drinking his profit in this piss-pot.” Her smile goes sharp. “No shit. I take the same contract. Cash from a Roanapur cleaner who wants Venn’s head in a bag.” Spike sighs and finally gets his cigarette lit. He inhales deep. He is addicted to the burn, to the pause it gives him. “Of course,” he says. “Universe loves a joke.” “So walk away, cowboy,” Revy says. “I work alone and I shoot first.” “I’m already dead once,” he says, easy. “Whatever happens, happens.” She snorts. “What kind of fatalist bullshit is that?” “The free kind. I value freedom above all else. Bounties, women, crews — I don’t hold on. Holding on gets you killed.” “Good philosophy,” she says, and her voice drops a fraction. “I’m not a good person, not a bad person. I’m just here.” For a second something vulnerable flickers behind her bravado, quick as a muzzle flash. Then it is gone. She pours herself another and pushes his inch toward him. “Drink up, pretty boy. Loser buys dinner.” They drink. The game starts simple. Shots for information. He knows Venn favors back exits. She knows Venn travels with four bodyguards and a taste for underage girls and overpriced vodka. He matches her shot for shot. She chain-smokes and curses beautifully with every toss. He stays loose, all long lines and casual balance, a Jeet Kune Do practitioner even sitting still, weight centered, ready to explode. “You fight?” she asks, noticing the way he shifts when a drunk gets too close behind her. “When I have to,” he says. “Guns are louder.” “You any good?” “Good enough to stay broke.” She laughs despite herself. The attraction sits thick between them, hot as the bar air. He looks at her mouth when she licks whiskey off her lip. She looks at his hands, scarred and steady, and at the way his shirt pulls across his chest. Neither trusts it. Trust gets you shot. Both of them live with that knowledge in their bones — him with the syndicate enforcer past he never talks about and the woman he still sees in dreams, her with the childhood abuse that lives in her fists and her anger that never cools. “So how do we do this?” Spike asks. “Share the bounty? Split the eight mil and get noodles?” “I don’t share,” Revy says. “I compete.” “Competitive, huh? I like that.” “You like anything with tits.” “Only the dangerous ones.” She leans in close enough that her hair brushes his cheek. Her breath smells like smoke and whiskey. “Then you must love me,” she whispers. His heart kicks. He does not move away. The front window shatters. Four men push through the door with rifles up, Venn’s crew, nervous and loud. The bar erupts in screams. Tables flip. The bartender drops flat. Spike and Revy move at the same instant and in opposite directions. Revy is already standing on her stool, both Berettas clear of leather. She is Two Hands in full glory, arms extended, firing simultaneously left and right with impossible precision. Glass explodes. A rifle flies from a man’s grip. She screams profanity the whole time, alive in violence, solving the problem the only way she knows. Spike dives sideways off his stool, draws his Jericho with one smooth motion, and fires from the floor. His false eye flattens the room a little, so he compensates with instinct, with years of practice. He shoots the lights out, then shoots a gunman in the knee. He rolls up, sweeps another man’s legs with a perfect Jeet Kune Do kick, disarms him, and pistol-whips him cold. It lasts eleven seconds. Silence rings. Smoke drifts. Four men groan on the sticky floor. Revy stands in the middle of it breathing hard, crop top riding up, dragon heaving, eyes bright and wild. Spike stands across from her, gun still up, chest heaving, cigarette somehow still clinging to his lip. They point their guns at each other and start laughing. “You’re good,” she says. “You’re better,” he says. “And meaner.” “Buy me another drink and I show you mean.” Venn himself is not among the dead. But one groaning man taps his jacket pocket. A motel key card. Room 12, Starlight Rest, two blocks down. Venn hides there now. Spike sees it. Revy sees it. They look at each other. The race is on. Twenty minutes later the motel room door swings open under Revy’s kick. The room smells like mildew and sex. The bed sags. The AC rattles. Venn is gone — window open, curtain flapping, a bag of cash left behind in his panic and a data chip with his accounts on the nightstand. The real bounty. Spike dives for the chip at the same moment Revy does. They collide on the edge of the bed, hands tangling, bodies slamming close. He ends up half on top of her. She ends up with a Beretta under his chin. He ends up with his Jericho pressed hard into her ribs. They freeze. Breathing fills the small room. Fast. Hot. Her leg hooks around his hip from the fall. His free hand grips her wrist. Sweat slides down her throat. His eyes drop to it, then snap back up. Her eyes drop to his mouth, then snap back up. The guns do not waver. “This is cozy,” Spike murmurs. “Move and you die,” Revy murmurs back, but she does not pull the trigger. She does not push him off. “Same to you.” Unresolved sexual tension crackles louder than the AC. He could kiss her. She could shoot him. She wants to do both. He wants to let her. Neither trusts enough to lower the gun first. Competitive instinct screams to win. Something else, lonelier and hungrier, screams to stay right here. “You gonna shoot me, Two Hands?” he whispers. “You gonna let me?” she whispers. Neither moves. The night stretches.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and character understanding within the crossover fanfiction framework. The author successfully captures the distinctive voices and mannerisms of both Spike Spiegel and Revy, translating their anime/manga personalities into prose effectively. The dialogue feels authentic to both characters, with Spike's laconic fatalism ("Whatever happens, happens") and Revy's aggressive profanity coming through naturally. The narrative structure is well-paced, moving from initial meeting through escalating tension to the climactic standoff. The bar fight sequence is particularly well-executed, showcasing each character's fighting style distinctively - Revy's dual-wielding aggression versus Spike's more fluid, adaptive approach. The action writing is clear and kinetic without becoming overwrought. The prose style effectively balances descriptive detail with narrative momentum. Phrases like "walks in like she owns the oxygen" and "The bar on the edge of Tharsis Down sweats heat and bad decisions" establish atmosphere efficiently. The writing maintains a noir-influenced tone appropriate to both source materials. However, the piece suffers from some predictability in its setup and resolution. The "two bounty hunters after the same target" premise, while fitting the characters, follows expected beats. The sexual tension, while well-executed, builds to a fairly conventional standoff scenario. The characterizations, though accurate, don't reveal new depths or surprising facets. The ending feels somewhat abrupt, cutting off at the moment of maximum tension without resolution. While this creates dramatic impact, it leaves the narrative feeling incomplete rather than artfully open-ended. The piece also occasionally relies on exposition-heavy character descriptions rather than revealing traits through action and dialogue. The technical craft is solid throughout, with consistent point of view, clear action sequences, and authentic character voices. The integration of specific details from both source materials (Spike's prosthetic eye, Revy's dragon tattoo) demonstrates thorough knowledge of the characters. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 86.3
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
I don't think about that autumn much now, unless October comes too early and the light goes flat in the afternoons. Then I remember Storliden. We had moved in August 1994. My dad got transferred from Stockholm to the forestry office in Lycksele, which meant a rented red house outside a village that wasn't even on most maps, a school with forty kids in my year, and me, fifteen, furious in a way that felt permanent. I missed the T-bana and Sergels torg and people who didn't stare. My mum kept saying it was only for a couple of years, like that helped. Astrid Lundqvist sat next to me in class because the teacher thought a local girl would settle me. She had pale braids to her waist and chewed kicker licorice until her tongue was black, and she laughed at everything I said about Stockholm like it was a fairy tale. Her family had lived in Storliden forever. Her mormor, who'd died the spring before, had taught her things, she said. Old things. At first it was just what she called midnight games. Stupid stuff, except she never treated it like it was stupid. We melted lead over a candle in her garage to read shapes for who liked who. We wrote Jonas Lindgren's name backwards on a piece of birch bark and buried it by the football field so he'd stop picking on me — he got glandular fever the next week and Astrid raised her eyebrows at me like, see? We held a sieve and scissors over a photo of our class to find out who'd stolen Emma's Walkman. It worked, sort of. Or we wanted it to work. That was the point. We smoked her brother's Marlboros and listened to No Need to Argue on my Discman with one earphone each, and the rituals gave us an excuse to be out and to know things adults didn't. Then that Friday she told me about útiseta. We were behind the ICA, waiting for her brother to finish buying snus for their dad. "It's sitting out," she said. "You sit on a burial mound at midnight to get knowledge. My mormor said the women used to do it if they needed an answer. You cover your head and you wait until something comes." She said it the way other girls talked about Ouija boards, matter-of-fact and half-bored. "You have to ask a real question. Not like, will I pass maths. Something you actually want." I asked what she wanted. She shrugged. "To know if my mum's going to leave. She's been crying on the phone." I didn't tell her my question right away. I finally said I wanted to know if we'd ever move back to Stockholm. Which was true, but not all of it. What I really wanted was to know if there was something wrong with me, why I couldn't stand being touched anymore, even by friends. Astrid laid down rules that night on the phone, her voice low so her parents wouldn't hear. No food after six, she said. Mormor said you had to come empty. Wash your face in cold water but don't brush your hair after. Wear wool, nothing that crackles. No iron — leave your keys, your coins, the little cross my aunt gave me for confirmation. And no talking once we left the road. "And don't laugh," she said. "She said people laugh because they're scared, and they get angry about that. Them." I sneaked out at half past eleven. It was the 14th of October, black and cold enough to see my breath. My parents were asleep with the TV still on. I left a pillow in my bed in case my mum checked, which was idiotic, but I was fifteen. I wore my dad's thick sweater and my winter boots and carried the grey wool blanket from the sofa. Astrid was waiting by the bus stop with a plastic bag. Inside was salt, a stub of candle in a jam jar, and her mormor's shawl that smelled of smoke and mothballs. We didn't talk on the path, because she'd said not to, but also because it felt wrong to break the quiet. The village ended fast. Past the last streetlight there was only the gravel road to the lake, then the forest thinning into the old pasture where the mound was. Everyone knew it. Gravhögen. The teachers said it was Iron Age, protected, don't dig. The kids said if you took a stone you'd dream bad for a week. Wind occasionally rustles the pine trees, sounding almost like faint whispers. That night it did that, and then stopped, and then did it again. I told myself it was just air moving through needles. Astrid walked ahead like she wasn't cold, her breath puffing out. Twice she stopped and tipped her head, listening. I wanted to ask what for, but the rule held my mouth shut. The mound was bigger than I remembered from daytime, a long dark rise covered in moss and lingonberry, with a flat stone on top like a table. Astrid set the jar down and poured a thin ring of salt around the base. Her hands shook, whether from cold or excitement I couldn't tell. "You go up first," she whispered. "Walk round it three times, against the sun. Then sit facing north. That's toward the lake." "Why against the sun?" "Because the dead go the other way. Mormor said. Don't step inside the salt after." She lit the candle. It guttered immediately. She cupped it until it held, a tiny yellow eye. "Put the shawl over your head so you can't see anything. Then ask out loud. Then wait. Don't answer if you hear your name the first time." "That's insane," I said, and giggled before I could stop it. It sounded too loud. Astrid didn't smile. "I'm serious, Linnea. No iron, no names, no looking. If you get scared, pull the shawl tighter and think about your question. I'll do it after you." I wanted to say this was just a game, that we'd go home and drink the vodka she'd stolen and laugh about how nothing happened. But her face stopped me. She looked older in the candlelight, impatient and a little afraid. I climbed up. The moss gave under my boots. I walked around the stone three times, counting in my head, feeling ridiculous and watched at the same time. Then I sat with my back to Astrid, the blanket around my shoulders, the shawl pulled over my head. Wool scratched my forehead. The world narrowed to my own breathing and the smell of smoke. "Will we move back to Stockholm?" I whispered. My voice shook. It felt like lying. Under the shawl I thought, harder, *what's wrong with me?* Then I waited. At first there was nothing but cold seeping up through my jeans and the blood thumping in my ears. I heard Astrid shift below me. An owl called far off. I tried to be still the way Mormor must have meant, empty. After a while the cold got strange. Not just my fingers. A patch at the back of my neck, under the shawl, like someone had lifted the wool away. I pulled it tighter. Then the wind came again through the pines, longer this time. Inside it — and I know how this sounds — there were shapes, almost words, too low to catch. I thought of the radio between stations. My scalp prickled. I told myself it was my brain making patterns because Astrid had told me to listen. I counted my breaths to prove I was in control. Something brushed the shawl. Light, like a twig falling. I froze. I wanted to look, and remembered: don't look. Don't answer if you hear your name the first time. "Linnea." It wasn't Astrid's voice. Or it was, thinned by the wool and the wind. I can't still tell. My whole body went hot then cold. I bit the inside of my cheek until it hurt. Under the shawl I was crying without meaning to. I thought about my question and saw, very clearly and stupidly, our apartment in Bagarmossen, the balcony with my mum's tomatoes, and then the red house here, and I couldn't tell which one I was homesick for. The candle went out. I heard Astrid swear softly, a real sound, and strike a match that wouldn't catch. The darkness under the shawl got complete. "Time's up," Astrid said quickly, too loudly. "Come down. Your turn's over." I tore the shawl off. The night rushed back, pine and lake and my own loud breathing. The mound looked exactly the same, moss and stone and salt scattered by wind. Astrid's face was white, her eyes fixed not on me but just past my shoulder. She grabbed my wrist hard. We didn't do her turn. We left the jar and the salt and half-ran all the way to the road, breaking every rule about silence, our boots loud on gravel. At the bus stop we stopped, panting, and laughed until we almost puked, saying it was nothing, just wind, just us scaring ourselves. Astrid said she hadn't called my name. She said the matchbox was damp. She said Mormor always said you shouldn't do it for fun. I never asked if her mum left. We never did another midnight game.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and atmospheric control while delivering an authentic folk horror experience. The author successfully captures the specific cultural and temporal setting of mid-1990s rural Sweden, incorporating genuine folklore elements like útiseta alongside period-appropriate details (No Need to Argue album, Discman, specific Swedish locations and products). The narrative voice is particularly well-crafted, maintaining the promised transparency of adult recollection while preserving the immediacy of teenage experience. The prose strikes an effective balance between literary sophistication and accessibility, with natural sentence rhythms and evocative imagery that serves the story rather than calling attention to itself. Character development is nuanced, especially in portraying Linnea's complex motivations - her surface desire to return to Stockholm masking deeper questions about her changing relationship with physical intimacy. Astrid emerges as more than a simple catalyst, showing genuine vulnerability beneath her confident facade. The friendship feels authentic, built on shared rebellion and mutual need. The horror elements are expertly handled, maintaining the crucial ambiguity between supernatural and psychological explanations. The ritual preparations feel researched and authentic, while the climactic scene on the burial mound builds tension effectively through sensory details and psychological pressure rather than cheap scares. The piece adheres closely to the prompt's requirements, delivering exactly the requested word count, perspective, and thematic elements. The ending appropriately avoids resolution while suggesting lasting impact, and the final detail about never doing another midnight game provides satisfying closure to their supernatural experimentation. Minor weaknesses include some slightly predictable elements in the setup and a few moments where the adult narrator's voice becomes slightly more apparent than ideal, but these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness. **"Therapeutic Boundaries"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a former professional athlete undergoing mandatory physical therapy after a career-destroying injury, harboring resentment toward recovery itself. Their physiotherapist is not only unnervingly attractive but also a former training partner from their competitive days who has successfully transitioned to a new career while the protagonist's identity remains shattered. We'll lean into the sexual tension of the scene by having her be attracted to him, but both of them attempting to maintain mental distance while being in physical contact as he shows her stretches & movements & manipulates her body, navigating the thresholds of pain. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—every movement, stretch, and manipulation must be anatomically precise and spatially consistent. Paint an exceptionally vivid sensory picture through detailed attention to pain thresholds, involuntary responses to touch. Capture the suppressed, flaring tension of physical proximity, touch, and the controlled infliction of uncomfortable movements. Physical clarity is essential — readers must understand exactly what is happening with the body during each therapeutic technique. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Therapeutic Boundaries** I don't want to get better. That's the thing no one writes on the intake form. The table vinyl is cold through the thin paper sheet under my back. I am supine, head to the north end of the room, feet pointing south toward the door I keep wanting to walk out of. My left leg is flat, toes relaxed toward the ceiling. My right leg — the one with the reconstructed ACL, the shaved meniscus, the ten-week-old scar still pink and puckered down the front of the knee — is flat too, but it doesn't feel like mine. The quad above it has gone soft. I can see the atrophy when I don't mean to look. Four centimeters smaller. I measured. Then Theo comes in. Theo Lindqvist, who used to run three lanes over from me for six years, who used to count my strides out loud on tempo days. Who now has DPT after his name and a job and a life that kept moving. He is unnervingly attractive in a way that makes me angry, all clean jaw and broad shoulders gone a little thicker with lifting instead of running. And on both forearms, elbow to wrist, he is wearing those ridiculous compression sleeves from our old training group — faded teal and magenta diamonds, frayed at the thumb holes. I want to laugh and I want to hit him. "Hey, Mara," he says, too professional. "Right knee today. Flexion's stuck at a hundred?" "Something like that." He stands on my right side, on the east side of the table, facing me. He doesn't waste time. "We'll start supine. Hamstring first, then we'll push flexion." He slides his left hand under my distal calf, palm cradling the posterior muscle just above my Achilles, fingers warm. His right hand settles on the front of my thigh, just above my kneecap, to keep the joint locked straight. The patterned fabric of his sleeve brushes the back of my knee as he moves. "Relax the leg into my hand. I'm going to lift." He lifts my entire right leg off the table in one plane, knee extended, flexing my hip. My heel rises south to north, then up. At sixty degrees I feel the pull behind the knee, a broad hot band. At seventy-five it sharpens. "Tell me where we are. One to ten." "Four. It's — tight, not sharp." He holds me there, my leg suspended in his two hands. His right hand presses down lightly on my anterior thigh to prevent the knee from bending, and I can feel each finger individually through my shorts. My hamstring starts to tremble, a fine involuntary vibration under his palm. I hate that he can feel it. "Breathe out and let the weight go," he says. His face is very close to my shin, his breath warm on my calf. I stare at the ceiling tiles and count the perforations so I don't think about the heat traveling up the inside of my thigh where his forearm nearly rests against it. I am acutely aware that I am attracted to him, and that it is humiliating. I focus on hating recovery instead. What is the point of lengthening a hamstring for a leg that will never hold a block start again? He eases my leg a degree higher. The stretch flares to a six, a clean burn from ischial tuberosity to back of knee. My toes curl without permission. My breath hitches. "Good. That's enough." He lowers my leg back down, slow, guiding my heel to the table until the back of my knee and calf are flat again. My skin stays warm where he touched. "Now flexion," he says. "Heel slide. You'll do active, I'll assist at end range." I bend my right knee, sliding my heel north along the paper toward my buttock. My hip flexes as my knee flexes. At about ninety degrees of knee bend, the joint feels full, pressurized, like there's a fist inside. My quad fires to guard — I can feel it lock. He steps closer, his hip against the edge of the table. He cups my heel in his left hand, fingers around the posterior calcaneus, and places his right hand lightly over the front of my shin, just below the tibial tuberosity, not pushing yet. "Keep going. I'm just following." I drag another inch. Pain spikes to a seven, sharp and deep at the anteromedial joint line. I gasp before I can stop it, and my left hand grabs the edge of the table. "Hold there," he says quietly. "Don't fight it. Let me take the weight." He takes over. He supports the full weight of my lower leg so my hamstring can release, then guides the heel another two centimeters north. Hip now at about ninety degrees flexion, knee at maybe one-ten. His right hand stabilizes the tibia so it doesn't rotate outward. The stretch is nauseating — not muscle now but capsule, a deep ache behind the patella. Sweat prickles at my hairline. My glute on that side clenches hard, an involuntary bracing, and my breath comes short through my nose. I can smell him — soap and laundry and faint menthol from the lotion. His chest is over my bent knee, his patterned sleeve pressed against my lateral calf. I notice the vein in his forearm and hate myself for noticing. He is looking only at my knee, jaw tight, maintaining the clinical distance with visible effort. A flush climbs his neck that has nothing to do with exertion. "Back down," he murmurs, and extends my leg for me, straightening the knee, sliding the heel south until the leg is flat again. Relief floods so fast it feels almost sexual. My whole right leg tingles. "Flip prone for rectus femoris," he says, stepping back to give me space. "I'll show you first." He demonstrates standing on one leg, grabbing his own left ankle behind him. "Hip extended, knee flexed. Keep pelvis tucked so you don't dump into lumbar extension." He does it cleanly, the old athlete still in him. It hurts to watch how easy it is for him. I roll over, now prone, forehead resting on my folded hands, head north, feet south. My legs extended behind me. He moves to my right side again. "I'm going to bend your right knee. Tell me when." His left hand wraps the front of my ankle, just above the malleoli. His right hand presses flat over my sacrum, over the waistband of my shorts, to lock my pelvis to the table and prevent my lower back from arching. He flexes my knee, bringing my heel up and then north toward my right buttock. At ninety degrees it's just pressure. At one-twenty my rectus femoris — that long quad muscle from hip to knee — goes taut as a cable down the front of my thigh. Because my hip is extended flat on the table, the muscle is pulled at both ends. Pain blooms, a six turning to an eight, hot and sour above the knee. My pelvis wants to lift. His right hand holds it down, firm, warm through fabric. My hamstring cramps slightly and my foot involuntarily plantarflexes, toes pointing, trying to escape. I make a small sound into my hands. "Breathe," he says. His voice is lower. "I know. Two more seconds at end range, then release." His sleeve is against my calf now, that old neon pattern absurdly bright against my skin. I am hyper-aware of his left hand encircling my ankle, of his right hand's weight on my lower back, of my own body held in this bent, exposed position and unable to straighten itself without his permission. The pain and the proximity blur. I feel goosebumps rise on the back of my thigh that have nothing to do with cold. He slowly extends my knee back down, lowering my foot south until my leg is flat, and lifts both hands off at once. The absence of his hands is louder than the touch. We both stay very still for a beat. My heart is hammering against the table. His breathing is audible. "Range is better," he says, stepping back, all business again. "Ice ten minutes." I stare at the frayed magenta diamond on his wrist and think: he got to keep moving forward. I just get to get better at being broken.

+ Historical fiction: High Seas and Low Vices — Score: 84.8
Prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors. Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit. Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell had not yet rung when I woke, my shirt stuck to my back with sweat. Whampoa in August. The air below deck did not move. It smelled of bilge and damp wool and the vinegar the surgeon had the boys swab the mess with. Through the stern port I could hear the Pearl River slapping the hull, and somewhere ashore a dog barking itself hoarse. "You look like hell, sir." Midshipman Ellis stood in the doorway with my coat over his arm. Sixteen, Kentish, still pink about the ears. "I feel like hell, Mr. Ellis," I said. "What is the hour?" "Near six bells. Mr. Collins asked if you will take the muster." I sat up too fast and the cabin tilted. The cough came up from deep then, tearing. I tasted copper on my tongue, bright as a penny. Ellis stepped back. "Are you ill, sir?" "Sea air on the lungs," I said, and wiped my mouth. "It settles in the damp. Tell Mr. Collins I have papers to carry ashore to the Factory. For the Captain." "Aye, sir. Shall I have Dawson lower the gig?" "No. I'll take a chop boat from the landing. No need to waste the men." He frowned, but he was too young to argue with a lieutenant's stripe. "Very good, sir." --- The river at morning was the colour of cold tea. Heat already shimmered off it. As the boatman sculled me toward the American anchorage and then Canton, the smell thickened — river mud at low water, night-soil barges, drying fish laid out on mats, coal smoke from the galley fires, and underneath it all the sweet rot of fruit left in the sun. My coat was too heavy. Sweat ran from under my hat down my neck. My hands shook where they rested on my knees, and I tucked them under my thighs so the boatman would not see. "You navy, master?" he asked in his pidgin. He was old, his back knotted from the oar, a straw hat low over his eyes. "Yes." "You go Hog Lane? Plenty girls, plenty —" "Thirteen Factories," I said. "British flag." He laughed through his teeth. "Everybody go Hog Lane first." --- I did not go to the Factory. I went around it, down the narrow lane behind Hog Street where the cobbles were slick with thrown wash-water and the walls sweated lime. The tea-shop was shuttered, but the boy at the back knew my knock. Inside it was dim and cooler. Incense from the shrine fought with boiled tea and lamp oil and unwashed bodies. A fan turned lazily overhead, moved by a coolie boy with a rope. Harrow was already there, out of uniform, his waistcoat unbuttoned. Once commander of a sloop. Now agent for Matheson, or so he called himself. "Merrick," he said. "Christ. You missed a good night." "I have duties," I said. He poured me tea. The cup was chipped and burned my fingers. "You have debts, you mean. Quill was asking for you." My stomach turned. "Tell Quill he'll have his money." "He's tired of telling. He says the price of your paper has gone down." Harrow leaned forward. The veins in his nose were broken red. "You still copying those coastal soundings?" "They keep them locked now," I said. "Collins keeps the key." "Then find another key." He smiled without humour. "You know what the Americans pay for a signal book? Even an old one?" I coughed again. It rattled the tea in my cup. Copper flooded my mouth. Harrow watched me. "Consumption?" "Sea air," I said. "This damned estuary. It never leaves the chest." "Sea air." He repeated it flatly. "Right." --- Ah Lum did not receive me in the shop. He took me through the courtyard where a woman was gutting eels into a wooden bucket, the blood bright against the grey flesh, flies loud as rain. Upstairs, in a room with blue shutters closed against the glare, the scales were already out. He was a thin man in a clean grey gown, nails long, eyes tired. No theatre about him. That was worse. "Lieutenant," he said in good English. "You are late. My other customers do not make me wait." "The tide," I said. "And the watch." "You have the silver?" I set the pouch on the table. It clinked too lightly and we both knew it. He weighed it without comment, then pushed a small paper parcel forward, no larger than my thumb. "That is half," he said. "Half? Last month that money bought double." "Last month opium was twelve dollars a catty. Today fifteen. Governor sends soldiers to burn dens in Fatshan. Supply is fear. Price is fear." He folded his hands. "You want more, bring more silver." "I can bring you something better than silver," I said. My voice sounded strange to me. "British charts. Whampoa to Bocca Tigris. Depths. Sandbars shifted after the rains. Your smuggling lorchas could run at night without a pilot." Ah Lum looked at me for a long time. Outside, a vendor cried salted plums, and the eel-woman cursed the flies. "I do not want charts," he said at last. "Charts bring warships. I want silver. Or I want what Mr. Quill has — permission to load tea at night without the Hoppo's chop. Can you sign that?" "No." "Then bring silver tomorrow. Full weight." He slid the parcel an inch closer. "Or do not come." I took it. The paper was warm from his hand. My fingers steadied for the first time that day around it. "You squeeze a sick man, Lum." "I sell medicine to sick men," he said. "You English taught us the appetite." --- Quill's warehouse on the Creek smelled of new hemp rope and Bohea tea and the camphor they packed the chests with. Clerks shouted in English and pidgin. Dust hung gold in the light from the high windows. Quill himself was sweating through his linen, a ledger open like a bible. "Merrick. Harrow said you might show." He did not offer me a seat. "You owe me forty-two Spanish dollars." "You'll have it at month's end, when pay comes." "Pay!" He laughed. "Your pay wouldn't cover your laundry. No — you'll do a job for me tonight. A fast job." "What job?" "A manifest needs to change. A brig from Bengal carries chests listed as rice. The Custom House comprador will inspect at nine. You will keep him drinking in the Factory parlour until ten. You wear the King's coat. He will be flattered. He will stay." "That's all? Delay a man over brandy?" "That's all." Quill tore a page from his book and wrote a figure. "Do it, and I give Lum his silver for you. Fail, and I tell your Captain why his lieutenant is always ashore." The cough rose again. I turned toward the bales to hide it, and when I straightened my handkerchief was spotted pink. I folded it quickly. Quill saw. "Sea air?" he said, mocking. "Sea air," I said. He pushed a flask toward me. "Rum. Steady yourself. Be at the parlour at eight. Shaved. Sober enough to stand." I took the flask. The rum burned the copper away for a moment. --- At eight I was there, as ordered. At ten I was still there, telling the comprador stories of Trafalgar I had not witnessed, laughing too loudly, pouring too freely, while outside on the dark river men moved chests from one boat to another without lanterns. By midnight I was in Lum's back room again, on the low couch with the mat worn smooth by other shoulders. The lamp hissed. The smoke was sweet and acrid at once, catching the back of my throat, then smoothing everything — the shaking hands, the debt, Ellis's pink face, the pink on my handkerchief. For an hour the river did not stink. My chest did not ache. I did not cough. When I walked back to the landing at three, the tide had turned. The water slapped clean against the stone. My uniform was damp and strange on me, and the parcel in my breast pocket was empty. Tomorrow I would need silver again.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and atmospheric writing that effectively captures the degradation of a naval officer caught in opium addiction in 1830s Canton. The author successfully creates an immersive historical setting through careful attention to period details, from the naval hierarchy to the complex colonial trading environment. The characterization of Lieutenant Merrick is particularly well-handled. His decline is shown through physical symptoms (the persistent cough, shaking hands, bloody handkerchief) and moral compromises (selling naval secrets, lying to subordinates) rather than explicitly stated. The progression from his morning deception to his evening corruption feels organic and believable. The dialogue serves multiple functions effectively - it reveals character relationships, advances the plot, and provides historical context without feeling expository. Each character has a distinct voice, from Ellis's naive formality to Ah Lum's pragmatic directness to Quill's predatory confidence. The use of period-appropriate language and pidgin English adds authenticity without becoming distracting. The sensory details are particularly strong, creating a vivid sense of place through smell, sound, and texture. The descriptions of Canton's heat, the river's stench, and the various locations feel researched and authentic. The writing maintains a consistent tone of decay and desperation that mirrors Merrick's internal state. The structure works well, following Merrick through his day of increasingly compromising situations. The cyclical nature - beginning and ending with his physical symptoms and need - reinforces the addiction's grip without being heavy-handed. However, the piece occasionally relies on familiar addiction narrative beats, and some of the historical details, while accurate, feel slightly predictable for the genre. The ending, while thematically appropriate, doesn't offer much surprise beyond the expected trajectory of an addiction story. The prose is generally elegant and controlled, avoiding purple prose while maintaining literary quality. The pacing is well-managed, and the emotional complexity emerges naturally from the character's circumstances rather than being forced. Prompt:
Sisyphus Gives Advice Write a comedic scene in the style of Terry Pratchett featuring Sisyphus, who has started an advice column while continuing his eternal boulder-pushing. Rather than being bitter about his punishment, Sisyphus has developed a comfortably zen emotional intelligence and wisdom from his centuries of repetitive labor. Not in the cliche ways you might expect -- he's actually very grounded, warm & connected with the everyday human plight. He dictates responses to "Crow," his feathered familiar who serves as both scribe and mail carrier. The piece should include Sisyphus thoughtfully answering several advice-seekers' letters about everyday problems (relationship troubles, work-life balance, dealing with difficult people, life purpose doubts) while periodically returning to his boulder-pushing duties. His advice should be surprisingly insightful and practical. The humor should emerge naturally from the messages he receives, from mundane to risque. Sisyphus should genuinely enjoy helping others, finding meaning in this new pursuit while maintaining his boulder routine. The humour should be *understated and not forced*. Contrary to expectation, almost none of his advice involves boulder rolling metaphors (though he does sneak *one* subtle in there), nor a treatise on stoicism. We are also going against the obvious fish-out-of-water trope; in fact, he's surprisingly a natural at this. In all of this , it's important to *show, don't tell*. The format should be largely epistolary, with the occasional interjection for scene setting. 1000 words.
Model Output:
It is a well-known fact that Hell is bureaucratic. People imagine fire and screaming, but mostly it is queuing. Sisyphus's hill was on the third level, between the Flatterers (who have to lick envelopes for eternity) and the Department of Ironic Punishments, which was still waiting for planning permission. His hill was steep, grey, and entirely without shade, which seemed like an oversight until you realised it was the point. He was halfway up it when the crow arrived. The crow landed on the boulder, which was technically cheating, and dropped a sack tied with string. "Post," said the crow. "Ah," said Sisyphus, leaning his shoulder into the stone and finding the old groove where his hands went. "Lovely. Give me a moment, Crow. Nearly at the flat bit." He pushed. There is a technique to pushing a boulder that you only learn around year four hundred. Knees bent. Breathe out on the shove. Don't fight it on the loose gravel. He reached the flat bit*, rested his forehead briefly against the warm rock, and sat down. > *There wasn't really a flat bit. There was a bit that was slightly less not-flat, which after three thousand years feels like a meadow. "Right," he said. "Wipe the beak. Dictation voice." Crow extracted a stylus with the air of a bird who had done secretarial college and resented every minute of it, and flipped open a wax tablet. Crow also stole shiny things, swore in three dead languages, and could find any soul in Hades in under an hour for half a sandwich. This made him, by Underworld standards, a postal service. --- **DEAR SISYPHUS,** *My wife and I have been married eleven years and very happily, except we have read in a Corinthian pamphlet about Spicing Up The Marriage Bed with olive oil and a feather duster. I am VERY keen to try it. She says she would rather clean an actual chicken. Who is right? — ANXIOUS IN ARGOS* "Hmm," said Sisyphus. "Tell him to buy a smaller duster," said Crow. "Quiet. Dear Anxious —" Sisyphus stared up at the clouds, which in Hades are mostly other people's sighs. "Your wife is right, and so are you, which is annoying but common in marriages. Wanting is fine. The oil-and-duster is not the point. The point is: did you ask her what *she* finds spicy? Not in the pamphlet way. Over supper. With clothes on." Crow scribbled. "Tell her you don't need the duster, you need her to enjoy herself too, otherwise it's just you making a mess with condiments. If she says no, that's a full sentence. If she says 'not that, but maybe —' then listen like your sandals are on fire. Yours, S." Sisyphus stood, dusted his tunic, and put his shoulder back to the boulder. He walked it up another twenty paces while Crow rode on top, doing corrections. --- **DEAR SISYPHUS,** *I am a copyist for a grain merchant in Thebes. I work from sunrise to lamp-light and dream about ledgers. My master says if I leave on time I lack ambition. My children have forgotten my face and call me 'the man who snores.' How do I balance? — TIRED* "Oh, love," said Sisyphus, softly. He sat down again at the next ridge and took the waterskin. "Dear Tired. Your master is confusing ambition with availability. They are not cousins." "Tell him to poison the ledger," said Crow. "They get tired when they are copied badly. You know this. So: pick a leaving time and keep it three days out of five. Say it once, pleasantly, and then do it. 'I go at sunset.' No long apology — apologies invite negotiation. Use the hour you gain for nothing useful. Play knucklebones. Let them draw on your accounts. A man who snores in his own bed is better than a ghost at his own table. If the merchant sacks you, a good copyist who can add will find another merchant. Children only make one father. Yours, S." He pushed again. The boulder made its familiar sound, like a large stomach rumbling. Sweat ran into his beard. He did not seem to mind it. A thin, officious shimmering occurred by the path. It resolved into a god in a toga that was slightly too clean. "SISYPHUS!" boomed the shimmer. "It is I! Criticus!" "Hello, Criticus," said Sisyphus, still pushing. Criticus was the god of Unfavourable Reviews and Marginal Notes. His temple was a wall in Athens with two worshippers and a goat that had wandered in. He carried a scroll, which he unrolled with a snap. "I have READ your so-called column," said Criticus. "Circulating among the dead! Unauthorised wisdom! I must protest your tone. Where is the suffering? Where is the *gravitas* of eternal torment? You are supposed to wail. The brochure clearly shows wailing." "I wail on Tuesdays," said Sisyphus. "Crow, note that. Dear Criticus, thank you for writing —" "I did not write, I *manifested* —" "Thank you for manifesting," said Sisyphus pleasantly. "I always value feedback from stakeholders. Crow, file him under C." Crow filed him under the boulder. Criticus followed, still talking, which is easy when you don't have to push. --- **DEAR SISYPHUS,** *My mother-in-law moved in 'for the winter' six years ago. She rearranges my kitchen, tells my husband I am barren as a mule (we have three children), and prays loudly for my improvement. If I object I am cruel. If I don't I will murder her with a soup ladle. Help. — MEDEA (NOT THAT ONE)* Sisyphus winced in solidarity. "Dear Medea-Not-That-One," he dictated, while easing the stone around a rut. "Do not murder with the ladle. It dents, and you will still have to wash it." "Sound legal advice," said Crow. "You cannot change her. You can change the kitchen. Give her one shelf, one chair, one job that is truly hers — the herbs, say — and defend the rest like a small, polite country. To your husband, don't say 'your mother is awful.' Say 'I need an hour in my own house where I am not corrected.' Good men hear that better. And when she prays loudly for your improvement, add, very sweetly, 'And for patience for us all.' It drives them mad because they cannot object. Yours, S." Criticus scoffed. "Domestic trivia! You were a KING! You cheated Death TWICE! And now — *agony aunt*?" "I was a terrible king," said Sisyphus cheerfully, not stopping. "Excellent at banquets. Rubbish at listening. I've had time to practise." He nodded at the scroll. "Do you want to ask something, Criticus? Everyone does, eventually." "I most certainly do NOT — well. My worshippers never polish the altar. The goat licks it. Is that disrespect?" "Give the goat its own small salt lick beside the altar," said Sisyphus promptly. "Then it looks deliberate. People will think it's ritual." Criticus blinked. "...Huh." He vanished, faintly mollified and entirely confused. Sisyphus laughed, pushed the last steep stretch, watched — as he always did — the boulder tip, gather, and thunder back down in a cloud of dust, and began walking down after it. "Last one before supper," he said. --- **DEAR SISYPHUS,** *I am nineteen and studying philosophy. My tutor says the gods have a plan but will not say what it is, which seems inefficient. I look at the stars and feel very small and sick. What is the point of anything? — EPHEMERUS* The smile faded into something kinder. Sisyphus caught up to the boulder where it rested in its hollow, patted it, sat on it. "Ah. Dear Ephemerus," he said slowly. "Your tutor is keeping the plan vague because there isn't one you can fit on a tablet. Feeling small when you look at the stars means your eyes are working." Crow, unusually, did not interrupt. "Don't look for *the* point. Look for a small one for Tuesday. Make soup for someone ill. Learn how to mend a sandal properly. The world is mostly held together by people doing unglamorous things well and not telling anyone. Keep a good grip, watch your footing, and when you get a moment at the top, enjoy the view before you walk back down. That's not nothing. That's most of it. Yours, S." Silence, except for the wind. Crow closed the tablet with a click. "Same time tomorrow?" "If the post comes," said Sisyphus, standing and spitting on his hands. "It always comes." He leaned into the stone again.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates exceptional adherence to the complex prompt requirements. The author successfully captures Terry Pratchett's distinctive voice through dry wit, footnotes, and observational humor about bureaucratic absurdities. The characterization of Sisyphus is particularly well-executed - he's genuinely wise and grounded without falling into cliché stoicism or boulder metaphors (save for one subtle instance as requested). His advice is practical and insightful, showing real understanding of human nature. The epistolary format works effectively, with each letter presenting distinct problems that allow Sisyphus to demonstrate different facets of his wisdom. The advice feels earned through his millennia of experience, and his responses are genuinely helpful rather than preachy. The introduction of Criticus provides excellent comic relief while reinforcing the theme that even minor gods seek guidance. The prose flows naturally with Pratchett's characteristic rhythm. Descriptions are vivid but economical - the "flat bit" footnote is particularly Pratchettesque. The dialogue feels authentic, especially Crow's terse interjections and Sisyphus's patient responses. The humor emerges organically from situations rather than forced jokes. The piece maintains emotional complexity throughout. Sisyphus's contentment feels genuine rather than artificially positive, and his empathy for letter-writers creates touching moments, particularly with "Tired" and "Ephemerus." The ending strikes an appropriate note of quiet satisfaction without being saccharine. Minor weaknesses include some slightly predictable advice column scenarios, though the responses themselves are creative. The piece could have pushed the humor slightly further in places, but this restraint actually serves the understated tone requested. The characterization remains consistent throughout, and the world-building details enhance rather than distract from the central concept. The busker, intrigued by the teenager's quiet intensity and knowledge of music, suggests they grab some sushi at a nearby kaitenzushi (conveyor belt sushi) restaurant. The air in Den Den Town smelled like hot takoyaki oil and old plastic. Every shop was shouting at once — *JUNK! JUNK! RETRO GAME KAITORI!* — and from inside the Taito Station arcade came that endless pachinko clatter, coin-music and idol voices. Hana had come for a secondhand MIDI cable at Janpara. She stayed because of the guitar. It ripped straight through the noise. A wall of distortion playing *Zankoku na Tenshi no Thesis.* She stopped walking. **Riko:** *[finishing with a dive-bomb, grinning wide]* Thank yoooou Nippombashi! Ookini! Tip your local degenerate guitarist, I'm saving up for strings and karaage! *[scattered applause, coins in the case. Her eyes land on Hana, who hasn't moved.]* **Riko:** Hey! Hey, you! Front row synth-girl! Yeah, you with the big headphones around your neck! **Hana:** M-me? A-ah — s-sorry! I — I was just — sorry, I'll move — **Riko:** No no no, don't move! You stood through the whole solo without blinking once. That's either true love or heatstroke. Which is it? **Hana:** U-um. True — I mean — that was really — um, good. Really good. Sorry. That sounded weird. **Riko:** *[laughs, sitting on her amp to unplug]* Weird's good! Weird sticks around and actually talks to me. I'm Riko. What's your name, starer? **Hana:** H-Hana. Sixteen. I mean — I'm Hana. Not — not sixteen years — I am sixteen, but — sorry. **Riko:** Hana-chan! Nice to meetcha! You always apologize to strangers, or am I just lucky? **Hana:** S-sorry — I mean! Um. No. I just — your guitar — **Riko:** My beautiful gremlin here? She's a secondhand Fernandes I rescued from Hard Off. Name's Akemi. Say hi, Akemi. **Hana:** H-hi... Um, on the bridge part — before the second chorus — you did that pinch harmonic, and you bent it up a perfect fourth? Like — **Riko:** Oh? **Hana:** Like — s-sorry, this is nerdy — but like hide's live version from '94? Most people just play it straight from the tab, but you — you added the — the squeal, and then you cut the delay off really fast — **Riko:** *[stops coiling her cable]* ...Whoa. Wait, say that again? You caught that? **Hana:** A-ah! Sorry, I talk too much about — I didn't mean to — **Riko:** No! That's sick! Nobody ever catches that! Dudes will stand here and film me for TikTok and they don't hear *anything*. You got ears, Hana-chan. You play? **Hana:** N-no! Not guitar. I can't — people looking at me, I can't. I just — synths. At home. I have a microKORG. A-and my brother's old MS-20 mini that kind of — kind of broken, the filter crackles — **Riko:** Knob-twiddler! I *knew* it. The headphones gave you away. What, you make tracks? **Hana:** ...Kind of. Just — just covers. Anime songs. I try to rebuild them with only oscillators. Like, no samples. It's stupid. **Riko:** That's not stupid, that's the coolest shit I've heard all week. Can I hear sometime? **Hana:** Oh — um — no one’s ever — I mean, they're not good, the mix is — my room is really small so the bass is always — **Riko:** Hana-chan. Breathe. *[grins]* You're doing that red-face thing. It's cute, but you're gonna pass out in front of Akemi and she'll get a big head. **Hana:** *[small laugh]* S-sorry — okay. I'll stop saying sorry. Maybe. **Riko:** Good girl. Hey — you eaten? I'm fucking starving. I played Evangelion like four times and a bunch of middle-schoolers requested *Gurenge* and then left without tipping. Capitalism is dead. **Hana:** Um — no, not yet — **Riko:** Perfect. There's a Kura Sushi right around the corner past the Animate. Come with me. My treat if you keep telling me nerdy music stuff. **Hana:** E-eh? Really? I — I don't want to bother — you were busking, you need the money — **Riko:** And I need company that isn't a drunk salaryman yelling 'play *Erika*.' Come on. Thirty minutes. If I'm weird you can fake a text from your mom and run. **Hana:** ...Okay. Okay, thirty minutes. --- Inside Kura Sushi it was cold and smelled like vinegar rice and green tea powder. Everything rattled and beeped. Hana slid into the booth stiffly, backpack on her knees, while Riko immediately started stacking plates like she owned the place. **Riko:** Rule one of kaitenzushi with me: you gotta drink the matcha first. Watch a master. *[presses the hot water button]* Pow! See? No burns. I'm basically an adult. **Hana:** You — you come here a lot? **Riko:** When I get a good corner. Bad corner, it's convenience store onigiri. Today was a pretty good corner thanks to you bringing me luck, Starer. **Hana:** I didn't do anything — **Riko:** You stood there looking intense as hell. People think, 'oh, that girl's watching, must be good, let's stop.' You're my lucky charm. Eat! What do you like? **Hana:** Um — tamago. And — and inari. The cheap ones. **Riko:** Respect. A fellow broke legend. But I'm getting you a tuna too. You can't just eat egg at sushi, Hana-chan, the sushi gods will cry. *[She snags two plates off the belt. The lane pings.]* **Hana:** Th-thank you. Um — Riko-san — how long have you been playing on the street? **Riko:** Riko is fine! No -san, makes me feel like a teacher. Uh, about a year? Dropped out of music senmon gakkou 'cause tuition was insane and teachers hated my tone. Too 'noisy.' Now I just play loud anime shit for tourists and kids. Way more fun. **Hana:** But — aren't you scared? Just — playing, with everyone staring? **Riko:** Oh, I'm terrified every time. First chord my hands still shake. But then I'm like, well, already making noise, might as well make *more* noise. You get it, right? When you're inside a song you don't really — think about the staring? **Hana:** ...Yeah. Yeah, on synth, when I get the arpeggio right — I forget my room is small. I forget everything. **Riko:** See? Same brain. Different weapon. *[A plate with a gray, unassuming nigiri slides by. Hana lights up a little.]* **Hana:** Ah — aji! Oh, I love aji — **Riko:** Grab it grab it! Oi, fast hands! Nice! **Hana:** *[quietly humming while she pours soy sauce, almost to herself]* ...mm-mm-mm... **Riko:** Wait. Wait wait wait. What was that you just hummed? **Hana:** Huh? N-nothing! Sorry, I do that when I'm nervous — **Riko:** No, that melody — sing it again? That floaty, sad synth thing? **Hana:** Um — like... *du-duu... du-duu...* It's just — **Riko:** *Kiri?* From *Lain?* **Hana:** *[freezes, chopsticks mid-air]* ...You know *Lain?* **Riko:** Do I *know* Lain?! Girl, *Serial Experiments Lain: Cyberia Mix* raised me! Nobody knows that OST! Everyone's like 'Duvet, right? The opening?' and I'm like no, bitch, track seven, *Kiri,* that five-minute hollow drone with the broken music box? That song rewired my brain at fourteen! **Hana:** Yes! Yes! The — the detuned pad underneath, it sounds like it's underwater, and then the high sine comes in just slightly out of tune and it feels lonely but — but not bad lonely? I tried to remake it on my microKORG for three months and I couldn't get the filter to breathe right — **Riko:** Because Takizawa used a real Prophet-5 with a busted chorus, I swear! Oh my god, I finally found another Lain kid in the wild! We're like endangered animals! We should mate for life — I mean, musically! Platonically! Sushi-ly! **Hana:** *[laughing for real this time, hand over mouth]* You — you're weird. **Riko:** And you're smiling! Victory! The shy synth gremlin smiles! **Hana:** It's just — no one at school knows Lain. They all like... normal stuff. When I say I like old synth soundtracks they look at me like I'm speaking alien. **Riko:** Then they're boring and we're right. Hey. Seriously. Next Saturday I'm playing Den Den Town again, same spot. What if you bring your microKORG? Just — plug in with me? We could do the Lain opening, guitar + synth. It'd sound haunted as hell. People would cry. **Hana:** E-eh?! I can't — outside — with people — I would mess up, my hands would — **Riko:** So what if you mess up? I'll mess up louder to cover you. That's what friends are for. **Hana:** Friends...? **Riko:** Duh. You bought into my sushi bribe, you're legally stuck with me now. Gimme your LINE. I'll send you a demo of my *Kiri* guitar arrangement. It's rough, don't judge my tone. **Hana:** ...Okay. Okay! Um — just — don't laugh if my icon is a cat in a spacesuit. **Riko:** Hana-chan, I will only love you more if your icon is a cat in a spacesuit. *[The belt keeps turning. Outside, Den Den Town keeps shouting. But in their little booth, stacked with empty egg plates, it had gone surprisingly quiet and easy.]*
