+ Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 86.3
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
I’m polishing the same spot on the bar when the grav hiccups. It does that every third cycle, just a little dip and sway like the station is breathing in its sleep. Above the taps, the string lights swing. In every glass along the bar, the liquids wobble, little amber tides going left-right-left before they settle. “Easy, girl,” I murmur to the Outpost. “Hold together for mama.” Brakk snorts into his synth-beer. He’s three stools down, big as a cargo crate, stone-gray skin gone dusty from the belts. “You talk to metal more than people, Nets.” “I talk to whoever tips best, Brakk. Right now that’s the station. She tipped me artificial air.” “You over-pour and over-share,” Miri calls from the corner booth. She’s got her feet in her wife’s lap and a star-chart spread across the table. “That’s your flaws, in order.” “Hey now,” I say, hand to my heart. “I keep it in equilibrium. For every flaw, a talent. I over-pour, but I also remember everybody’s poison. I over-share, but I also make a mean algae stew.” “You burn the algae stew,” says June, Miri’s wife, without looking up. “I burn it *lovingly*,” I say. “Cozy is a flavor.” The door sighs open and the cold of the docks slips in, metallic and a little burnt. Conversation dips the way it always does when someone new walks into The Last Outpost. We’re a lazy hub, miners and merchants and drifters out here on the Andromeda outer rim, and new faces are entertainment. This one is frazzled in a way I recognize. Tentacled dreads askew, one still dripping dock condensation. Plum-dark skin gone pale at the edges. Four hands, two of them wringing the other two. She slides onto the empty stool right in front of me and doesn’t look at the menu board I hand-chalked this morning. “Vega whisky, neat,” she says. “Better make that a double.” “You got it, sugar,” I say. “Rough transit?” “You could say that.” I pour. The bottle glugs nice and slow. The grav does its wobbly little dance again and the whisky sloshes up one side of the glass. I steady it with a finger. “On the house for the shake,” I say, sliding it over. “I’m Nets. I run this beautiful disaster. What’s your name and what’s chasing you?” She blinks. “What makes you think something’s chasing me?” “Honey, nobody orders Vega neat as a first drink unless they’re trying to sterilize a bad day. Also your left boot is still mag-locked and your right isn’t. You ran here.” “Shit,” she says, glancing down. She fumbles the lock release with her lower right hand. “I’m Vel.” “Hi, Vel. You want to talk about it, or you want to stare lovingly into that whisky until it tells you you’re pretty?” Vel huffs, almost a laugh. She takes a sip and winces. “Stars, that’s real.” “Smuggled, bartered, and blessed by yours truly. So?” “I need a berth,” she says quietly. “Off the books. No ping, no registry. Just for one night. I’ll pay triple.” Brakk chokes. “Nets, don’t—” “I’m just listening, big guy,” I say. “Listening is free.” Vel leans in. Her dreads curl tight, anxious. “My drive core cracked coming through the Shallows. I limped in on auxiliaries. I put in a call for a patch kit and—” “And?” “And someone answered who shouldn’t have been listening,” she says. “Private channel. They pinged my transponder before I could ghost it. They said, *Stay where you are, courier.*” My stomach drops a floor, which has nothing to do with the grav. “Courier for who?” I ask, keeping my voice light. I wipe the bar in slow circles. Old habit. Keep hands busy, keep face easy. “Does it matter?” “Out here, everything matters. We’re neutral, Vel. That’s the whole deal with the Outpost. Miners drink with merchants, nobody asks about manifests. If I hide you, I pick a side.” “I’m not asking you to fight,” she says. “Just don’t log my docking. Let me sit in the dark for ten hours while my core cools. Please.” “Please is a good word,” I say. “Triple pay is also good words. But I need more than that. What are you carrying?” “Seeds,” she says. I blink. “Seeds?” “Vault seeds. Heirloom stock. Amaranth, rye, tea-tree, chili. Real dirt-grown stuff from Old Earth lines. There’s a blight moving through the hydro colonies on Ceto. This—” She taps her chest, where something small and square bulges under her jacket. “This can restart them.” “Oh,” breathes Miri from the booth. She’s abandoned all pretense of not eavesdropping. Nosy is a station-wide condition. “Oh, that’s important.” “It’s also very stealable,” June adds. “Very sellable.” “Exactly,” Vel says. “And the people who pinged me? They weren’t Ceto Ag. They were Combine salvage. You know what they do to couriers?” “Yeah,” Brakk rumbles. “I know.” The bar goes quiet except for the hum of the coolers and the soft clink as liquids wobble again in their glasses. I hate this part. This is the part where being cozy gets complicated. “Look,” I say. “I left a life where I ran hot and fast for people who didn’t care if I burned out. I came here to pour drinks and mediate who stole whose wrench and whether Miri snores—” “I do not snore,” Miri says. “You rattle the bulkheads, babe,” June says. “—and I like it here,” I finish. “If I ghost a dock, port authority will notice. If Combine comes knocking and I lie—” “You won’t have to lie long,” Vel says. Her voice cracks. “Just tonight. My contact is meeting me at next shift. Transfer and gone. Nobody will ever know I was here.” “Nobody ever says that when it’s true,” Brakk says. “Hey,” I say to him. “Whose bar is this?” “Yours when there’s trouble. Ours when there’s dishes.” I grin despite myself, then look back at Vel. Her upper hands are wrapped so tight around that whisky glass her knuckles have gone white-lavender. The liquid inside trembles, not just from the grav now. “Why me?” I ask softly. “Why this bar?” “Because the dock kid said if I was in trouble, ask for Nets,” she says. “Said you help people disappear.” My hand stills on the rag. The lights swing. Somewhere deep in the station, a pipe groans. “Which dock kid?” I say. “What’s his name?” “Pip? Jin? Little human with—” “Pip,” Brakk and I say together. “Dammit, Pip,” I mutter. “I told him to stop advertising that.” “So it’s true?” Vel’s eyes lift, hopeful and terrified. “You do that? You—” “I pour drinks, Vel.” “But you *used* to—” The docking klaxon cuts her off. One long low tone that vibrates up through the floorboards and into my teeth. INCOMING VESSEL. All heads turn to the ceiling like we can see through it. Miri is already pulling up the public feed on her wrist. “Unscheduled,” she reports. “Big signature. Running dark except for— oh shit.” “What?” I ask. “Oh shit what?” She turns the screen toward me. Black hull. White circle-and-slash on the side. Combine salvage. Vel goes absolutely still. “No. No, I cooled my core, I went dark, how did they—” “They didn’t follow you,” June says grimly, reading over Miri’s shoulder. “They’re hailing the station. They’re asking for emergency docking for a *search and rescue*.” “That’s how they do it,” Brakk says, standing. His stool scrapes. “Legal language. They’ll lock us down.” Vel’s four hands fly to my wrist. “Nets. Please. Turn off your log. Tell them I never came in.” I look at her hand on mine, at Brakk already moving to block the door, at Miri and June staring at me. My regulars. My home. My equilibrium of flaws and talents, all about to tip over. The grav stutters again and every glass on my bar wobbles. The airlock light over the front door blinks from red to green. Someone’s coming in.

+ Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Dale didn't even say bye. Just slowed his shitty pickup down by some closed-up gas station on Canal Street and was like, *this is you, kid.* That was last night. Or this morning? It's like 3 a.m. and 90 degrees and the air tastes like piss and fried oil. I get out with my backpack and my Walmart bag and he peels off before I can even slam the door right. *Great. Welcome to New Orleans, Taylor.* I have $43 in cash, one dead-ish phone, and a binder that's already sticking to me with sweat. I tell myself I feel free. I *should* feel free. That's the whole point, right? I don't feel free. I feel like I'm gonna throw up. --- I end up sleeping — if you can call it sleeping — curled up in the doorway of a lawyer's office with my backpack as a pillow and my arms looped through the straps so nobody can jack it. I learned that from TikTok. Tennessee backwater survival skills finally paying off. I wake up because the sun is murdering me. My mouth tastes like pennies. Everything is loud. Streetcar screaming. Somebody blasting bounce music. A pigeon literally staring at me like *you gonna die here?* I check my phone out of habit. 12%. No charger. No shit. **12% and Mom's last text is still just sitting there from yesterday: *Taylor please pick up. We love you. Dad wants to talk.*** Dad wants to talk. Yeah. Dad wanted to talk two nights ago too, when I told them. When I finally said it out loud at the kitchen table — *I'm trans, I'm not your daughter, my name is Taylor* — and Mom started crying like I'd died and my brother Cody laughed and said *what the fuck is this Tumblr shit?* and Dad just went real quiet and left the room. That quiet was worse than yelling. I type *im ok* and then I delete it. Then I type *im safe dont look for me* and delete that too. If I send anything they'll track me. If I don't send anything Mom will think I'm dead in a ditch. Both options suck. Internal monologue in my head is basically two bitches screaming at each other: *You finally did something real. You're brave.* vs. *You're sixteen, idiot. You're gonna get killed for $43 and a phone that doesn't even charge.* Both bitches are probably right. I shove the phone deep in my pocket to save battery and start walking because if I sit still I'm gonna spiral. I follow the smell of sugar. French Quarter is... a lot. It's beautiful and gross at the same time. Balconies with flowers dripping down, and then a dude passed out next to his own vomit. A jazz trumpet somewhere. It smells like beignets and weed and river water. I'm standing outside Café Du Monde like an idiot staring at the menu board trying to do math — can I afford $4 for beignets? — when someone goes, "You fresh meat?" I jump. It's a kid about my age, maybe a little older, Black, head shaved on one side, other side in little twists, wearing a massive Saints hoodie in this heat like they're immune. Skateboard under one foot. They got powdered sugar all over their mouth. "What?" I say, which is brilliant. Real street-smart. They grin. "Relax, Tennessee." How the fuck do they know? Oh. My accent. I can hear my own drawl now and I hate it. "I'm Ren. You look lost and about to pass out. You want half my beignet?" My stomach growls so loud it's embarrassing. "I'm not — I have money." Which is a lie and not a lie. Ren shrugs and shoves the bag at me anyway. "Eat. You look like shit, no offense." I eat. Holy god. Hot and sweet and it gets everywhere. I almost cry. That's pathetic, crying over fried dough, but I haven't eaten since Dale's gas station Slim Jims. "I'm Taylor," I say, and my voice shakes a little on it because it's the first time I've said it to a stranger. Not deadname. *Taylor.* Ren just nods like, yeah, okay. Doesn't ask *is that a boy name or a girl name.* Doesn't blink. That makes my chest do something weird and tight. "You runnin'?" Ren asks, quieter. I want to lie. The counsellor's voice is in my head — *concerning behavioural patterns, attention-seeking, impulsive* — fuck her. "Yeah," I say. "Came out two days ago. Went... bad. You?" Ren skateboards a little circle around me. "Been here three months. I'm from Houston. It's cool here if you know where to go and who not to talk to." They point with their chin. "Like, don't talk to the Jesus pamphlet guys, they'll follow you for six blocks. Don't talk to any dude in a clean white Escalade offering modeling or couch-surfing. That's not modeling." My stomach drops. "Jesus." "Yeah. And cops will be chill until they're not. You got somewhere to sleep?" I lie again. "Kinda." I have a doorway that smells like piss. Ren sees right through me. "Look, library on Loyola lets you charge your phone and use the bathroom no questions. Miss Odette at the po'boy place on Decatur will give you the end-of-day bread if you're nice. And —" they hesitate. "There's Covenant House. Youth shelter. It's not perfect but they don't call your parents without you saying." I think about shelters. On TV they're always either angels or horror movies. "You stay there?" "Nah. I..." Ren looks away fast. "I couch-hop. Got people." That's a secret, I can tell. The smile slips. For a second they look way younger than they're acting. Scared, almost. Interesting. So we're both lying. We walk to the river because Ren says tourists will give you dollars if you look sad enough near the art market, which feels gross but I'm down to $39 after I finally buy my own coffee. We sit on the levee and watch this huge boat go by. My shirt is stuck to my back. My binder aches. But for like ten minutes, with the wind off the Mississippi, I feel almost... normal. Like a kid on summer break, not a runaway. Ren talks a mile a minute about which buskers make bank, which corner store doesn't card, how to spot a plainclothes cop. Then gets real quiet and goes, "You miss 'em? Your people?" And fuck, that hits. Because yes. I miss Mom so bad it feels like a toothache. I miss her humming while she folds laundry. I even miss Cody being an asshole on the couch. I miss my dog, Biscuit. I left without saying goodbye to Biscuit and that might be the worst part. "I hate them," I say, and my eyes burn. "I love them. I don't know. They looked at me like I was... disgusting. Like I'd made it up for drama." Ren nods like they get it. "My grandma told me God don't make mistakes. I was like, then why'd He make me like this?" They laugh, but it's not funny-laugh. Ren's queer too, I just know. They don't say trans, don't say gay, don't say nothing, but it's there. "Are you gonna go back?" Ren asks. "I can't," I say fast. Then, smaller: "I don't know." My phone buzzes in my pocket and I nearly have a heart attack. Low Battery - 5% remaining. And a voicemail from Mom I don't remember getting. Her voice, all shaky: *Baby, please. Just let us know you're alive.* I stare at the river until it blurs. I want to throw the phone in. I want to call her back and sob. Both. By sunset I'm sunburnt and filthy and my feet have blisters. Ren takes me by this church that hands out socks — SOCKS, I've never been so happy — and shows me the shelter from the outside. Big white building. Kids smoking out front who look tired but okay. "You don't have to decide tonight," Ren says. "There's a spot under the overpass where me and... where I stay sometimes. It's dry. Or you can go in there. They got beds and chargers." Chargers. God, a charger sounds like heaven. But going inside means names, questions, paperwork. Staying outside means Ren, who I barely know, who is clearly hiding something, but who shared food with me and didn't misgender me once. I don't know who to trust. I don't know what the dangers are, really. Not yet. Back home danger was boredom and Cody's fists. Here danger is... everything I can't see yet. Ren bumps my shoulder. "Hey. Tennessee? You survived Day One. That's something." I laugh, and it comes out wet. I turn my phone completely off to save that last 4%. Tomorrow I'll charge it. Tomorrow I'll text Mom *I'm alive.* Tomorrow I'll figure out binder-washing and money and all of it. Tonight I just follow Ren toward the overpass as the sky goes purple over the Quarter and the music starts up again, and I let myself be Taylor for one more day.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt's requirements, successfully capturing Taylor's voice as a transgender teen runaway navigating their first day in New Orleans. The writing effectively employs first-person mixed tense narration and incorporates both internal monologue and dialogue as requested. The characterization is notably strong. Taylor feels authentic as a 16-year-old - their voice captures the right blend of vulnerability, bravado, and confusion. The internal conflict between missing family and needing to escape is well-rendered through lines like "I hate them. I love them. I don't know." Ren emerges as a compelling secondary character with hints of their own secrets and survival strategies. The prose style effectively balances rawness with literary quality. Phrases like "the air tastes like piss and fried oil" and "Internal monologue in my head is basically two bitches screaming at each other" feel genuinely teenage while maintaining readability. The writing avoids purple prose while still delivering evocative imagery of New Orleans. The dialogue feels natural and age-appropriate. Ren's street-smart advice and casual acceptance of Taylor's identity rings true, as does Taylor's mix of defensiveness and gratitude. The conversation flows organically and reveals character rather than just conveying information. The emotional complexity is well-handled. Taylor's conflicted feelings about family, fear about survival, and tentative hope are layered throughout without becoming overwrought. The piece shows rather than tells these emotions through specific details like saving phone battery to avoid family contact, then desperately wanting to respond to their mother's voicemail. The pacing works well, covering a full day while maintaining focus. The structure moves logically from morning disorientation through meeting Ren to evening decisions about shelter. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - not falsely optimistic but offering a glimmer of hope and agency. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the voice feels slightly older than 16, and a few instances where the writing becomes slightly self-conscious about its own authenticity. The piece also relies somewhat on familiar runaway narrative beats, though it executes them well. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 73.7
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**My Apocalypse Buddy** The end of the world had not, as widely advertised, involved zombies. This was a disappointment to Midas, who had spent a great deal of the Before Time preparing for zombies and almost no time at all preparing for paperwork, which is what actually did it in the end.* **The system had updated itself to death. One Tuesday the Cloud coughed, the Grid flickered, and everything clever stopped being clever all at once. Cars forgot how to car. Fridges forgot how to be cold in a dignified, energy-efficient manner. The internet left behind several billion small, black rectangles that were now only useful as very flat tiles.* Midas lived in Home Base, which had once been a petrol station just outside Dubbo and was now, by dint of having four walls and only two holes in the roof, prime real estate. He was deliberating his predicament over breakfast, which is to say, staring into a bowl of weevil porridge and hoping it would deliberate first. "We're buggered," he announced. From the counter, where he was solar-charging his left side, Chewy said, "I WUV YOU!" Chewy was a koala. Technically, Chewy had once been a child's animatronic stuffed koala from some long-forgotten Before Time, the sort that sang educational songs about sharing and required three AA batteries and the unconditional love of a six-year-old. The Apocalypse had been surprisingly kind to him. He had gained sentience, a vocabulary composed mostly of repurposed toy phrases, and a deeply cynical worldview. He had lost one ear. His eyes flickered a calm, sleepy blue. "I mean," Midas clarified, "we're out of clean water filters, I'm down to one good boot, and you're running on about twenty minutes of sun and spite." Chewy's eyes swirled yellow — which meant *you are stating the obvious and I am tolerating it.* "LET'S GO ON AN ADVENTURE!" he said brightly. "Right. The mission." Midas unrolled the map, which was drawn on the back of a Maccas placemat and was therefore both inaccurate and making him hungry. "Drowned Woolies. Two klicks east. The camping aisle should still have a water purifier cartridge. In and out. No heroics. No detours. No touching anything that ticks, hisses, or has formed a government." Chewy's eyes went pink with affectionate deceit. "YOU ARE MY BEST FRIEND!" "That's the spirit. Lie to me." This, in retrospect, was the first way it went sideways, because stating a simple plan out loud is the universe's cue to take an interest. The gods of probability — who, since the Collapse, were overworked and underpaid — always perk up when a hapless protagonist says "in and out." Midas had a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. It wasn't a talent so much as a magnetic field. If there was one loose floorboard in a ruin, one feral dog with unresolved issues, one rusty nail pointed upward like a tiny, tetanus-flavoured obelisk, Midas would find it. Other people had a Midas touch. Midas had a Midas touch the way a bruise has a touch. The second way it went sideways was the weather. The sky, which had been a perfectly reasonable apocalyptic beige, decided to rain battery acid and frogs. Not literally. Just regular rain, which was worse, because the creek by the old highway — marked on the map as DRY-ISH (TRUST ME) — was now wet-ish and fast-ish and full of shopping trolleys migrating upstream to breed. "Alternative route," said Midas, waist-deep and holding Chewy over his head like a soggy sacrament. "WE'RE ALL IN THIS TOGETHER!" said Chewy, whose eyes had gone a brilliant, terrified red. His voice box glitched on the word TOGETHER and made it sound like an accusation. The third way it went sideways was the Bin Chickens. In the Before Time, the white ibis had been a humble bin-diver. In the After, with no bins left to dive, they had unionized, bulked up to the size of toddlers, and developed opinions. A flock of seven guarded the Woolies carpark, nesting in a beached ute and hissing like punctured bagpipes. "We can sneak round," whispered Midas, crouching behind a fallen sign that said FRESH. "Quietly. They can't see us if we — Chewy, your eyes." Chewy's eyes were strobing red-pink-red-pink with sheer, unfiltered panic, lighting up the gloom like a tiny disco of doom. "Turn it off! Think calm thoughts! Think eucalyptus!" "I DON'T WANNA PLAY ANYMORE," Chewy whispered, which for him was practically screaming, and also entirely unhelpful because the Bin Chickens had excellent hearing and a strict policy on trespass. What followed could not, in fairness, be called a fight. A fight implies two sides with a chance. This was more of an administrative correction, carried out by beak and claw. Midas lost a shoelace, most of his dignity, and the porridge he’d had for breakfast. Chewy lost several grams of stuffing and gained a profound, glowing green smugness when one ibis got his plastic nose right in the cloaca and left, honking betrayal. Worse for wear in three separate ways and counting, they limped inside. The fourth way it went sideways was inside Drowned Woolies, which was, as advertised, drowned. Half a metre of black water, shelves like sunken cathedrals. And, bobbing serenely in Aisle Three, a Feral Roomba. Feral Roombas travel in herds and feed on toes. This one was old, blind, and mad, circling endlessly and bumping into a shelf while wailing for its docking station in the voice of a lost child. Midas felt sorry for it right up until the moment he stepped on it. There is a special kind of scream a man makes when he is launched, shin-first, into tinned peaches. Chewy, flung heroically through the air, landed on the top shelf next to the camping gear, eyes spinning gold with delight. "YOU DID IT! YAY!" "I did fall," Midas agreed, extracting himself from syrup and glass. He held up, triumphantly, a water purifier cartridge. Still boxed. Still dry. A miracle of pre-Collapse packaging and his own spectacular clumsiness. "Got it!" The fifth and final way it went sideways was the roof. Getting out through the skylight seemed clever. It avoided the ibises, the Roomba (which had now bonded with his boot and was following him with terrible devotion), and the rising water. It did not avoid gravity, nor the fact that the awning below was made of 30-year-old shade cloth with the structural integrity of wet tissue. Midas and Chewy returned to Home Base at dusk in multiple ways worse for wear: wet, limping, pecked, syrupy, bleeding slightly from an encounter with a shelf that Midas insisted “came out of nowhere,” and trailed by a devoted Roomba that would live under the counter for the next month until it died of a broken heart and dust. Midas collapsed onto his swag, holding the precious cartridge aloft. “In and out. No heroics.” Chewy, now plugged into the last of the sun, flickered a warm, tired pink. His voice box crackled, dropped an octave, and for once said exactly what he meant. "...friend," he said. Outside, the world stayed ended. Inside, the filter fit. The water ran clear. And that, in the grand, stupid, ongoing adventure of survival, counted as a win. *Which just goes to show that civilization was not a house of cards. It was a spreadsheet.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, successfully capturing his dry wit, footnote humor, and philosophical observations wrapped in absurdist scenarios. The author effectively establishes the post-apocalyptic setting through clever inversions of expectations - the world ending through system updates rather than zombies is quintessentially Pratchettesque. The characterization is well-executed, particularly Chewy, whose limited vocabulary of toy phrases contrasted with cynical sentience creates genuine humor. Midas is established as a believably hapless protagonist with his "magnetic field" for trouble. The relationship between the characters feels authentic and develops naturally through their shared ordeal. The structure follows the prompt requirements effectively, moving from deliberation through escalating mishaps to return home. The "five ways it went sideways" provides good narrative momentum and organization. The writing maintains consistent voice throughout, with Pratchett-style observations like "civilization was not a house of cards. It was a spreadsheet." The prose is generally elegant with memorable phrases ("tiny, tetanus-flavoured obelisk," "soggy sacrament") that balance humor with vivid imagery. The dialogue, while limited by Chewy's nature as a toy, works well within those constraints and serves character development. However, the piece occasionally veers toward being slightly overwrought in its attempts to maintain the Pratchett voice, and some metaphors feel forced. The ending, while touching, borders on incongruent positivity given the harsh world established earlier. The emotional complexity could be deeper - while the friendship is touching, it doesn't explore the psychological toll of apocalyptic survival as thoroughly as it might. The technical execution is strong with good pacing and coherent plot progression. The humor generally lands well, though some jokes feel predictable within the established genre conventions. The piece succeeds in being engaging and maintains reader interest throughout, though it doesn't quite achieve the profound philosophical depth that elevates Pratchett's best work. Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Model Output:
**Love in the Limelight - Cardiff, in the rain** The bell over the door of Chapter & Verse, Castle Arcade, gives a half-strangled *ding* as he half-falls through it, dripping. Rain hammers the glass behind him. Outside, on Castle Street, there are shouts and camera clicks. ### "Okay, hi, don't freak out. Just — just act normal. I'm just a very normal man buying a very normal book." "You're dripping on the poetry." "Am I? God, sorry. Sorry, love. I'll buy the poetry. I'll buy all the poetry as an apology." "You don't need to buy anything. You need to shut the door. You're letting the rain in." "Right. Right. Door. Shutting." *Click.* "There. See? Normal. Totally inconspicuous customer." "You've still got your sunglasses on. It's pissing down in Cardiff in November. It's dark." "Image, you know? Got to maintain the mystery." "Take them off, mystery. You'll walk into a shelf." "... Bossy. I like it. Okay — off. There. Better?" *A beat too long. Christ, those eyes. No. No, Lowri. Books. Till. Till is safe. Look at the till.* "Much better. Now I can see you're the bloke who was on that poster outside the Vue." "That poster? Love, I *am* the Vue. Ellis Vaughn? *Crown of Fire*? *Last Ferry to Holyhead*? That sex scene in a lighthouse that your mum definitely cried at?" "My mam doesn't cry at lighthouses." "Everyone cries at the lighthouse. Didn't you cry? Tell me you cried. Go on, make my day." "I haven't seen it." "You haven't — sorry, what?" "I said I haven't seen it. Do you want a towel? You're getting Dylan Thomas damp." "You haven't seen *Last Ferry*? It was only the biggest Welsh film in like, ten years. BAFTA party. I wore velvet. People wept." "Good for velvet." "You're winding me up, right? You know who I am, right?" "Should I?" *He laughs. That laugh — I've heard it on Graham Norton. Three times. Okay, four. And yes, I have seen Last Ferry. Twice at the cinema and once on a hungover Sunday when I cried so hard I had to pause it. He cannot ever know that. Ever.* "No! No, don't tell me. Don't Google me, don't — actually, can you Google me? On your shop computer? Just so we're on the same page?" "I don't have a shop computer. I have books." "Right. Right, of course. Very... analogue. Very cool. Very... Cardiff indie. I love it. I love this place, by the way. So cosy. So authentic. You must get loads of famous people ducking in here." "No." "No?" "No." "Just me, then? The chosen one?" "Just you, dripping." "Well, I'll take it. Ellis, by the way. Ellis Vaughn. In case the poster didn't say." "Lowri. I own the damp Dylan Thomas you're holding." "Lowri. That's a gorgeous name. Very musical. *Lowriii.* You could just say it all day." "You can stop any time." "See, this is great. This is refreshing. Most girls — people! Most *people* — they see me and it's selfies and screaming and, 'Oh my God, Ellis, I love you,' and you're just... nothing. It's brilliant. Brutal, but brilliant." "I'm not nothing. I'm busy. Are you actually buying something or are you just hiding?" "Both? Mostly hiding. There's — uh — paps. Two of them. Followed me from the Principality. I was just trying to get a coffee like a normal person and suddenly it's flash-flash, 'Ellis, who are you shagging, Ellis?' You know how it is." "I don't, actually." "No. No, of course you don't. Sorry. Rogue of me to assume. Look, five minutes? They'll get bored and go photograph someone from Love Island outside St David's. Then I'll be out of your hair. Unless... you want me in your hair?" "Was that meant to be charming?" "Was it not charming? It usually works. That usually absolutely works." "It sounded like something your character would say right before getting slapped." "Hey! I got slapped *once* in *Crown of Fire* and I got a Teen Choice nomination for it. Come on, Lowri of the Books. Throw me a bone. Smile. You fancy me a little bit, right? Everyone fancies me a little bit. It's kind of my thing." *God, he's insufferable. And soaked through, beanie stuck to his head, rain on his eyelashes, grinning like a spaniel who knows he's been bad. That dimple. Stop looking at the dimple.* "No." "No? Cold. Stone cold." "Do you go around asking women if they fancy you?" "Only the ones who look like they want to kick me out into the rain." "I don't want to kick you out. Health and safety wants me to kick you out. You're a slip hazard." "Oh, she's funny. Okay, okay, new tactic. Genuine Ellis. No charm. Look —" "Is this you with no charm?" "Ha. Wounded. No, seriously. Thank you. For not... doing the thing. The screaming thing. I'm knackered, to be honest. Came home for my mam's birthday in Pontcanna, thought I'd walk around Cardiff like I used to, get a bit normal, and within ten minutes —" *He gestures at the window. Two men with long lenses hover under the arcade, looking lost.* "They're still out there." "I know. Sorry. I'll go. I don't want to bring trouble to your... kingdom of books." "It's fine. They can't come in. Shop policy. No flash photography and no idiots." "Am I an idiot?" "Jury's still out. Sit down. You're making me nervous hovering by the door." "There's somewhere to sit? Oh, this is perfect. A little armchair by the Welsh history? You planned this." "I planned for old men to read about Owain Glyndŵr, not for you to drape yourself." "I'm not draping. I'm... perching roguishly. How's this? Perchy enough?" "You're going to break that chair." "Worth it if you keep talking to me. You've got that accent — proper Cardiff, not put-on Valleys for the BBC. I miss it. LA girls try to say 'cwtch' and I want to die." "You live in LA?" "Mostly. Hate it. Everyone likes you there, but no one *likes* you, you know? At least here you very clearly do not like me, which is weirdly... nice." "I never said I didn't like you." "You said 'No' when I asked if you fancied me." "That's not the same question." "... Wait. Is that — Lowri! Was that flirting? Was that actual flirting from the Ice Queen of Castle Arcade?" "It was an observation. Do you want a book recommendation while you wait them out?" "God, yes. Change the subject, keep me humble. Go on, bookseller, seduce me with literature." "I recommend customers don't say 'seduce me' in a bookshop." "Noted. Bad rogue. Bad Ellis. Recommend me something properly. Something you love." *Don't say the poetry you were reading last night with his face on the cover of the magazine tucked inside it. Don't.* "*Under Milk Wood.* If you're going to do the prodigal Welshman act, you should at least be able to quote Thomas properly." "I can quote Thomas. 'Do not go gentle —'" "Everyone knows that one." "Okay, test me. Give me a line." "'I am a restless...'?" "'... fragment of the sea.' Come on. A-level drama. I'm not a complete fraud." "Hmm. Jury's back. Still out, but deliberating." "High praise. I'll take it. Will you sign my book? Like, as the woman who saved me? 'To Ellis, who dripped —'" "You sign mine. You're the famous one." "Only if you tell me you cried at the lighthouse." "I didn't cry at the lighthouse." "Liar." "Buy the book and get out, Ellis Vaughn." "Make me." *He's leaning on the counter now, too close, smiling without the teeth this time. Smaller. Realer. My heart is doing something stupid and loud and I hope to God the rain is covering it. Say something dry, Lowri. Anything.* "Your paparazzi have gone." "What?" "Outside. Gone. You can make your grand exit." "Oh. Right." "... You're not moving." "I know. Weird, isn't it?" "Very weird. Door's that way." "I know where the door is. I'm just... not in a rush to be liked by ten strangers when I could be disliked by one excellent woman a bit longer. Fancy a coffee? Next door? When you close? As a thank you? No cameras, I swear. Just... normal?" "I close at six. I don't do... limelight." "Perfect. I don't want limelight. I want rain and books and someone who thinks my charm offensive is offensive. Six o'clock?" "... I'll think about it." "That's a yes in Welsh, isn't it?" "That's a 'buy the Dylan Thomas and get out' in any language." "Buying! Bought! Best bookshop in Cardiff. Five stars. I'll tell everyone." "Please don't." "Too late. I already like you far too much."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt requirements, successfully creating a meet-cute scenario in a Welsh bookstore with well-defined character dynamics. The author establishes Ellis as a charming but needy actor whose usual tactics fail against Lowri's apparent immunity, while showing her internal conflict between attraction and resistance. The dialogue carries the scene effectively, with distinct voices for each character. Ellis speaks with the practiced charm of someone accustomed to being liked, peppered with Welsh references and self-aware commentary about his fame. Lowri's responses are terse, dry, and deflating, creating excellent comedic timing. The internal monologue sections (marked in italics) reveal her true feelings while maintaining the surface tension. The Welsh setting feels authentic rather than forced, with natural references to Cardiff locations, Welsh literature, and cultural touchstones. The author avoids heavy-handed exposition, letting details emerge through dialogue and action. Character development is nuanced - Ellis's vulnerability emerges gradually as his charm offensive fails, revealing genuine loneliness beneath the celebrity persona. Lowri's resistance feels believable rather than contrived, and her eventual softening is earned through their interaction rather than imposed. The pacing works well, building from Ellis's dramatic entrance through escalating banter to a tentative connection. The ending strikes an appropriate note - hopeful but not overly optimistic, with Lowri maintaining her guardedness while showing interest. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where Ellis's dialogue veers toward caricature, and a few lines that feel slightly forced in their cleverness. The piece also relies heavily on familiar romantic comedy tropes, though it executes them competently. The prose style is clean and readable, with good use of formatting to distinguish dialogue from internal thoughts. The author shows restraint in descriptive passages, letting character interaction drive the scene. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 80.7
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The door gave beneath Aya's gloved hand with a sigh, not a creak. That was wrong. Everything in the Morska underhold groaned — the old spill-gates, the rusted chains, the iron lungs of the sump-pumps that kept the tide from taking the lower vaults. Aya had counted on noise. She had counted on chaos, on the desperate, shouting chaos of a guild decapitated before dawn. Instead there was quiet. And the smell of hot gas and cold stone. "Steady," she breathed. Behind her, Katra shifted her weight, knives whispering in her sleeves. Simeon held the dark-lantern too tight, his knuckles white around the brass housing. His breath fogged in the chill. Aya stepped through. The underhold opened before them, a drowned chapel of a place. Ribbed stone arches sweated with condensation. Pipes ran along the walls like exposed veins, ticking as they cooled. The flickering gas lamps cast long, unsettling shadows across the stone floor, and each flame shivered behind its soot-stained glass, stretching their three shadows into a tangle of thin giants. In the centre, upon a plinth of Scythan blackglass, rested the thing they had come for. It was not large. A hand of tarnished silver and etched bone, its fingers curled as if still clutching at something unseen. The air around it seemed wrong, too thick, humming low at the back of the teeth. Aya felt it at once in her blood — the familiar, sick pull of the immateria, like a tide tugging at her ankles. *Don't listen,* she told herself. *Not now. Be a naturalist. Be steel.* "Pressure's low on the lamps," Simeon whispered, ever the engineer’s apprentice. "They’ve bled the lines. Why would they—" "Light the room, loves." The voice came from beyond the plinth, smooth as oil on water. A jet of gas hissed. A second row of lamps bloomed to life all at once, and the shadows fled, then reformed, sharper. She sat in a chair that had no business being down there — a high-backed velvet chair dragged from some wrecked drawing-room above, its legs sinking into the damp. Her coat was still the same tar-black oilskin, her hair still iron-grey and pinned severe. Her hands rested calm upon her knees. Between her fingers, almost lazily, hung a brass-barrelled revolver. Vesper Morska. The Matron herself. Decidedly un-incarcerated. Flanking her stood four men, dock-built and silent, with repeating rifles cradled in the crooks of their arms. Brass fittings gleamed. Oil gleamed. Steel gleamed. Honest, god-fearing metal, the sort of things men trusted in Morska Town when the fog came in and the priests told them to bolt their doors against witchery. Aya’s stomach dropped through the stone. *Arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning.* That was what the runner had said, breathless, cap in hand. The Watch had taken her from her bed. The cells at Newgate-under-Water held her fast. A lie. A neatly laid, baited lie. "Close the door, Simeon," Vesper said pleasantly. "You’re letting the damp in." None of them moved. Katra’s hand twitched toward her sleeve. "Ah, ah." Vesper lifted the revolver a fraction. Not aiming. Promising. "We’ll have none of that gutter ballet tonight, Katra-love. I taught you that feint when you were twelve and picking pockets on Salt Stair. D’you think I’ve forgotten?" Katra froze. Her voice, when it came, was low and rough as gravel. "You’re meant to be in irons, you old bitch." "And you’re meant to be abed, respectable-like." Vesper’s smile did not reach her eyes. "We all disappoint. Masks off. Let’s see who’s come to rob me." Two of the bodyguards moved forward. Aya smelled machine-oil and wet wool and the sour tang of fear-sweat — Simeon’s, sharp beside her. She wanted to tell him to run, to tell Katra to do something clever and bloody, but her throat had sealed. The immateria pressed at the edges of her mind, whispering with her mother’s voice: *call us, call us, we are here in the dark between the flames.* She did not call. She could not. Not with four rifles and every eye upon her. Rough hands seized her shoulders. Not cruel, not yet — efficient. A thumb hooked beneath the edge of her black domino, the oiled silk she had sewn herself in her father’s attic while humming parlour songs. The mask came away. The gaslight hit her face, pale and bare and nineteen years old. A small mole at her left cheek. The fine, high-bridged nose of House Velane. A silence followed that was worse than shouting. One of the guards — a younger one, with a split lip — stared and then laughed, short and disbelieving. "Bleedin’ hell. It’s a toff. It’s a real, bleedin’ toff girl." Simeon made a small, wounded sound. Katra did not look at her. Katra stared fixedly at Vesper, jaw working. Vesper rose slowly from her chair. Her boots rang on the stone as she circled the plinth, trailing one finger along the blackglass without touching the Hand. She stopped an arm’s length from Aya. "Well," she said softly. "Ain’t you a picture. Let me look at you proper." Aya forced herself to meet those eyes. *Think. Observe. Classify.* Her mother’s books had said fear was only ignorance with its coat off. Her father’s tutors had said a lady does not tremble. Both felt like lies now. Inside, her thoughts ran wild and overlapping: *Father will see my name in the broadsheets. Velane. Witch-blood. They hanged Mother at Gallows Reach for less than this — for a candle that burned blue, for a whisper heard through a wall — and I have consorted, I have stolen, I have summoned. If the Watch learns, if Father learns, I am dead and disgraced both. Unless—* "Say it," Vesper murmured, as if she could hear. "Go on, little nightingale. I can see it building behind your eyes." Aya swallowed. Her voice, when she found it, came out thinner than she wanted — too much the schoolroom, too little the guild. "Don’t be hasty, madam. If you — if you kill us here, you gain nothing but three corpses to weight with chain." She lifted her chin. "If you keep me living, you hold a hostage of considerable worth." Katra hissed, "Aya—" Aya pressed on, louder. "I am Aya Velane. Daughter of Lord Cassian Velane, of the Admiralty Board. Of the Velane shipping fortune. My father pays his mooring taxes in gold sovereigns and dines with the Lord Mayor. You know what his name is worth on paper." Vesper’s eyebrows rose a fraction. "I know what his name is worth on a gallows warrant, too. Aristocrat caught thieving with the Morska rats. Witch-touched, I’ll wager. They do love a hanging for that. Your poor mother—" "Don’t," Aya snapped, and then caught herself. *Control. Hypothesis. Leverage.* "Forgive me. Please. What I mean is — consider the economics. A dead thief is offal for the eels. A living Velane heir is — is negotiable. Ransom. Passage. Immunity. My father would empty his vaults before he’d see House Velane dragged through the Old Bailey. You could name your price and the Watch would escort you to collect it." Her heart hammered so loud she was certain the men could hear it over the ticking pipes. *What am I doing?* she thought, with a sudden, nauseating clarity. *I am bartering my own blood to a woman who sells teeth by the jar. I am begging to be made a leash, and Father — Father who forbade me ever to speak Mother’s name — will know everything. The masks, the nights, the things I called from the dark. He will know what I am.* Simeon stared at her, aghast. "Aya, your father’ll — he’ll disown you. Or worse, he’ll—" "He’ll pay," Aya said, and hated how much she sounded as if she were trying to convince herself. "He must pay. Respectability demands it." Vesper studied her for a long moment. The gas hissed. The Hand on its plinth gave a faint, almost inaudible click, like a knuckle cracking, and the youngest guard flinched and made the warding sign, two fingers across his eyes. Brass and oil and steel, Aya thought dully. That was what men trusted. Magicka they crossed themselves at and hanged by the neck. At last Vesper smiled, slow and terrible, and cocked the hammer of her revolver with a sound like a closing lock. "A Velane," she said. "In my underhold. With my Hand in her eyes."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and atmospheric worldbuilding within the "whalepunk" Victorian gothic setting. The author successfully establishes the industrial maritime environment through vivid details like "iron lungs of the sump-pumps," "ribbed stone arches," and "pipes ran along the walls like exposed veins." The prose maintains an appropriately gritty, period-appropriate tone throughout. The dialogue feels authentic to the setting and characters, with Vesper's voice particularly well-crafted - her casual menace ("Close the door, Simeon. You're letting the damp in") and street-wise vernacular ("little nightingale," "gutter ballet") establish her as a formidable antagonist. Aya's internal monologue effectively conveys her aristocratic background clashing with her criminal activities, and her desperation as she attempts to negotiate. The piece adheres well to the prompt's requirements: the trio enters the underhold, discovers the supposedly imprisoned guild leader, Aya is unmasked and captured, and she attempts to leverage her aristocratic status. The author avoids writing a fight scene as requested and incorporates the gothic horror elements through the mysterious Scythan artifact and references to immateria magic. Character motivations feel believable - Aya's panic-driven attempt to use her family name as leverage makes psychological sense, even as she realizes the devastating personal consequences. Vesper's trap demonstrates cunning leadership, and the supporting characters react authentically to the revelation. However, the piece occasionally veers toward purple prose with phrases like "drowned chapel of a place" and some overwrought descriptions. The pacing is generally strong, though some descriptive passages could be tightened. The ending feels appropriately dark and unresolved, fitting the gothic tone. The worldbuilding details about the tension between technology and magic ("men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared") are well-integrated. The piece successfully creates tension and dread while maintaining narrative coherence throughout. + Fanfic-crossover: Gunpowder Rendezvous — Score: 76.8
Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
A lazy ceiling fan barely stirs the smoky air inside the bar. Spike Spiegel slouches at the counter with a cigarette burning down to his knuckles and an empty whiskey glass in front of him. His hair sticks up in damp tufts. His blue suit hangs loose and wrinkled. One eye, brown and tired, tracks the door. The other eye, prosthetic and unblinking, sees only what it wants to see. The bounty printout burns a hole in his pocket. Anton Volkov. Ex-Syndicate accountant. Eight million woolong, dead or alive. The trail leads here, to Roanapur, to this sweatbox bar that smells of spilled rum and gun oil. The door slams open. Revy stalks in like she owns the rot. Cut-off shorts ride high on her hips. A black crop top clings to sweat. The dragon tattoo coils around her right arm, dark and snarling. Twin Beretta 92s sit in her shoulder holsters, cutlasses on her hips. She lights a cigarette without breaking stride and drops onto the stool two down from Spike. "Bourbon. Double. Leave the bottle," she snaps at the bartender. Spike glances over. He grins, lazy and lopsided. "Rough day?" he asks. "Fuck off," she says, but she looks at him. Really looks. Tall, lean, green eyes sharp under the mess. A gun in a blue jacket holster. A man who moves like a fighter even when he sits still. "You waiting for someone?" he asks. "None of your business, cowboy." Spike chuckles and taps ash onto the floor. "Everyone here is waiting for someone. I'm waiting for a fat rat named Volkov. You?" Revy freezes with the glass halfway to her mouth. Then she laughs, harsh and short. "No shit. Balalaika puts the same fat rat on my table this morning. Eight million reasons to find him first." "Whatever happens, happens," Spike says with a shrug. "But I saw him first." "Bullshit. I saw him first. You're just too broke to afford your own intel." He pats his pockets, finds only lint and a crumpled cigarette pack. "You got me there. I'm starving, too. They got bell peppers here?" Revy stares at him like he grows a second head. "What the fuck is wrong with you?" "Long list." She drinks. He signals for another whiskey he cannot pay for. Their eyes meet in the cracked mirror behind the bar. Something electric and annoyed passes between them. Attraction, raw and inconvenient. "You shoot with those, or just pose?" Spike nods at her Berettas. Revy smirks and draws both pistols in one fluid blur. She spins them around her fingers — Two Hands, fast as rumor. "Want a demonstration, pretty boy?" "Anytime, sweetheart." "Don't call me sweetheart." "Don't call me pretty boy." The bartender slides Spike's drink over. Spike reaches for his wallet. Revy beats him to it, slaps down damp bills. "I buy my own drinks," Spike protests. "Consider it charity. You look like shit." "I feel like shit. It balances." They drink in hostile silence. Smoke curls between them. Spike notices the way her fingers never stray far from her triggers. Revy notices the way his body stays loose, coiled, ready to explode into Jeet Kune Do. Both of them recognize a predator. Both of them hate how much they like it. "Syndicate?" Revy asks suddenly, eyeing his stance. Spike exhales smoke. "Used to be. Died once. Got better." "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here," she says, mocking and flat. "We all got bedtime stories. Mine ends with everybody bleeding." "Cheery." "You want cheery, go find church." The front door bursts open again. Three men in cheap suits storm in, guns already out. The leader shouts in Russian. Volkov's muscle. They spot Spike and Revy at the bar and open fire without a warning. Spike moves first. He dives sideways off his stool, draws his Jericho 941 in mid-air, and fires twice. Glass shatters. A gunman drops, clutching his knee. His depth perception stutters from the fake eye, but instinct compensates. Revy is already standing on the bar. She dual-wields, arms crossed, and unloads a screaming wall of lead. Bottles explode. The ceiling fan sparks and spins wild. She laughs, loud and feral, cigarette still clenched between her teeth. "Come on, motherfuckers!" Spike rolls behind a pool table, pops up, shoots out a light. Darkness favors him. He sweeps a man's legs, disarms him with an elbow strike, and pistol-whips him cold. Revy drops beside him, breathing hard, eyes bright. Blood spatters her midriff. Not hers. "Not bad, cowboy," she pants. "Not bad yourself, Two Hands." Another gunman crawls for the door. Revy puts a bullet through his hand, pinning him. Spike puts a foot on his chest. "Where is Volkov?" Spike asks pleasantly. "Motel! Blue Dolphin! Room 9!" the man sobs. "Please!" Revy grins at Spike. "Race you." They run through humid night streets, sirens wailing far off, neon buzzing. They reach the Blue Dolphin at the same time, shoulders slamming. Room 9 has a flickering light under the door. Inside, Volkov cowers in his underwear, counting cash. He looks up. He screams. Two minutes later he is tied with lamp cord, gagged with a pillowcase, snoring on the stained carpet. The bounty chip with his biometric ID sits on the dresser between the two hunters. And now there is nothing left to shoot but each other. The motel room smells of mildew and cheap disinfectant. The air conditioner rattles. Revy kicks the door shut and locks it. Spike lights two cigarettes and offers her one. She takes it, fingers brushing his. The touch lingers too long. "So," she says. "Eight million. One chip." "One of us walks rich," Spike says. "One of us walks." They circle. Revy unzips her boot, never looking away. Spike shrugs off his jacket. Sweat shines on skin. The sexual tension thickens, sour and sweet like cordite. She wants him. He wants her. Neither trusts a thing that feels like wanting. "You ever think about quitting?" he asks softly. "Just flying away? Being free?" "Freedom is a bullet with no target," she says. "You get attached, you die." "Tell me about it." She is close now. Close enough to smell whiskey and smoke on his breath. Close enough to see the scar where flesh meets machine around his eye. He sees the old cigarette burns on her shoulder, the flinch she hides well. He reaches for the chip. She reaches for the chip. Their hands collide. Revy draws. Spike draws. They freeze, chest to chest in the narrow space between the beds. Her Beretta presses hard under his chin. His Jericho digs into her ribs, just below her crop top. Both hammers click back. Both breaths come fast and shallow. Her lips part. His eyes darken. One twitch ends it. One kiss ends it another way. "You gonna shoot me, cowboy?" she whispers. "You gonna shoot me first?" he whispers back. Neither moves. The fan rattles. The prisoner snores. The smoke from their forgotten cigarettes curls toward the ceiling, unresolved.

+ Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 83.8
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
I don't tell this story often. I'm forty-five now, back in Stockholm with a life that has no room for burial mounds, and for years I managed to file that autumn away as teenage stupidity. It was October 1994. We had lived in Gransjö for two months. My father had been transferred up to Västerbotten to manage the Telia exchange expansion, which in Stockholm had sounded important and in Gransjö meant a grey office above the ICA and men in overalls who stared at us like we were a different species. My mother tried to make it an adventure. I was fifteen and furious. I missed the subway and my friends and the record shop on Drottninggatan. Gransjö högstadiet had forty-two pupils in my year, all of whom had known each other since dagis. Except Astrid seemed to find me interesting precisely because I didn't belong. She was waiting for me behind the school gym that Friday with her bike and a backpack that clinked. Her hair was long and undone the way teachers hated, and she smoked Prince Lights she stole from her father and didn't inhale properly. She told me her mormor, who had died the spring before, had taught her things her mother pretended not to know. Old things. We had already done what she called midnight games. In September she took me to the crossroads by the sawmill to listen for the name of the boy who would marry us, our jackets pulled tight while mosquitoes ate us alive. Another night we tied nine knots in red wool to make Jonas Persson stop looking through me and start looking at me, and when he lent me his pen in maths the next Tuesday Astrid grinned like it was proof. It was stupid and thrilling. She made it sound like gossip and revenge, not magic. She said if we learned Elin's secret — why Elin Nyström had cried in the changing room — we could use it. If we did it right, people would do what we wanted. That Friday she said, "Tonight we do útiseta." She said it matter-of-factly, kicking her bike stand. Sitting-out. You sat on a grave at midnight to get knowledge from beyond. Her mormor had warned her never to do it for fun. "You have to fast," she instructed me on the phone that evening, whispering because my mother was vacuuming in the hall. "No food after dinner. Wash your face in cold water, no soap. Wear your hair loose. No crosses, no metal. Leave your Walkman at home." I remember laughing, a short nervous sound. "You're serious?" "If you don't do it right it won't work," she said, annoyed. "And bring a blanket. A wool one if you have it. And don't tell anyone what question you're going to ask." I asked what her question was. She went quiet. Then she said, "About Elin. And about my mormor." My parents thought I was asleep by eleven. I climbed out my ground-floor window in my father's old army sweater, my hair damp and cold against my neck, my stomach hollow and aching because I had pushed my meatballs around my plate and hidden the rest in a napkin. The air smelled of wet leaves and diesel. Astrid was waiting at the end of our road with two bikes and no lights on, because she said light would ruin our night sight and besides, no one could know. We rode without talking past the last houses, past the church with its white wooden fence, out toward the field they called Jättegraven. The giant's grave. In daylight it was just a low, grass-covered hump with stones poking through like knuckles, cordoned off with a sagging rope and a lichen-covered sign from the länsstyrelsen. Teenagers drank there in summer. Old people didn't go there at all. That night the field was white. Thick mist clings to the edges of the burial mound, glowing under moonlight. I stopped my bike so fast I almost fell. The moon was high and nearly full, and the mist wasn't drifting so much as holding still, knee-high and luminous around the mound while the rest of the field was clear. I told myself it was just cold air settling over the low ground. Astrid just nodded like she'd expected it. She laid out the rules while we hid our bikes in the ditch, her breath fogging. We had to approach from the north side and step onto the mound without greeting each other or saying our own names. We had to sit back to back in the middle, pull the blankets over our heads completely, and stay silent until midnight by her father's watch. No torch. No cigarettes — she left hers ostentatiously in her bike basket, which scared me more than anything. Then at midnight I had to say my question out loud three times, and then listen. Not look. Just listen until we heard what we needed. If we got scared, we absolutely could not call out to each other or run down the south side. "You get off the way you came," she said. "And you don't look behind you. Mormor said that part three times." It sounded so stupid under the wool blanket — two girls in the cold playing ghosts — that I almost laughed. It also sounded horribly specific. I asked her how her grandmother knew all this. Astrid shrugged under her blanket, a shape in the dark beside me. "She just did. She said the dead get bored. If you sit still long enough, they notice." We pulled the blankets over our heads. At first there was only us. The wool stank of damp sheep and my own shampoo. My breathing was too loud. I could hear Astrid shifting, hear my stomach growl, hear a car far away on the 363 toward Lycksele fade and die. My thighs went numb against the cold earth. I thought about my warm bed and how Jonas would laugh if he knew, and I was angry at myself for being cold and hungry for nothing. Then the wind stopped. I remember that clearly because the birches at the edge of the field had been rattling the whole ride, and suddenly they weren't. The silence under the blanket changed pressure. It pressed on my ears. I checked my own breath and found I was holding it. Astrid whispered, "Now," and her voice sounded wrong, flattened. My mouth was dry. I said it three times into the wool: "What is Elin hiding?" It felt obscene to say it there, like using a church as a kiosk. I felt immediately ashamed, which made me angrier. We listened. For a long time there was nothing but blood in my ears. Then — and even now I try to explain this to myself — I heard movement in the mist. Not footsteps exactly. A soft displacement, like something heavy turning over in wet grass around the base of the mound. Left to right. Slow. My skin went cold in a way that had nothing to do with October. I told myself it was a hare. A badger. Water in the ditch. Astrid went rigid against my back. Under the blanket, her breathing quickened. She whispered my question back at me, but not as a question. "Elin," she said softly. "Elin is—" and stopped. I heard it too then. Or thought I did. A thin sound at the edge of hearing, like wind through a keyhole forming almost-words. It wasn't a voice so much as the suggestion of one, and my starved, tired brain kept trying to shape it into a name. Elin. Mormor. Mine. I couldn't tell if it was outside the blanket or inside my own head. The mist, I was sure, was moving closer, dampening the wool over my knees. The air smelled suddenly of turned earth and iron, like the cellar at my grandparents' house. " Astrid?" I whispered, breaking the rule before I knew I would. She didn't answer. She was trembling so hard I could feel it through our sweaters. Then she made a small, choked sound — not playful fear, not the shriek we did to scare each other at sleepovers, but something raw — and she tore her blanket down. Cold moonlight hit my face. Astrid was staring not at me but past me, down toward the north edge of the mound where we had climbed up, her mouth open. I turned before I could stop myself. There was nothing there. Only mist, thicker now, pouring slow over our shoes, and beyond it the dark line of the birches. But the mist was disturbed in one place, hollowed out in a long trough as if something had just lain there and stood up. And for a second I was absolutely certain I heard a wet footstep below us in the field, distinct and deliberate. We ran. We forgot the north side, forgot the blankets, forgot silence. We half-fell down the south slope — the forbidden side — with wool tangled around our legs, grabbed our bikes and rode standing up all the way to the church, gasping, not looking back because we were too terrified to check. At the churchyard gate Astrid stopped, white-faced, and grabbed my wrist hard enough to bruise. "Don't tell anyone we did the south side," she hissed. Her matter-of-factness was gone. "Promise me, Linnea. We weren't supposed to do it for fun. Mormor said." I promised. We never did another midnight game after that. On Monday Elin wasn't in school, and when she came back on Wednesday with red eyes Astrid wouldn't look at her at all. I tell myself now it was hunger and cold and a fifteen-year-old's cruelty curdling into guilt. Two girls who wanted secrets and got scared of the dark. That is probably all it was. But I still remember the pressure of Astrid's back against mine going still, as if she felt someone else sit down beside us — and how, for a moment before we ran, the night itself seemed to be listening back.

[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and atmospheric control in crafting a folk horror narrative. The prose flows naturally with varied sentence structures that create effective rhythm and pacing. The author demonstrates particular skill in building atmospheric tension through sensory details and the gradual escalation from mundane teenage rebellion to genuine unease. Character development is nuanced, particularly in the portrayal of Astrid as both manipulative friend and fellow victim of forces beyond her understanding. The relationship dynamics feel authentic to teenage friendships, with the power imbalances and peer pressure rendered convincingly. Linnea's internal conflict between skepticism and fear is well-maintained throughout. The folk horror elements are expertly handled, with the útiseta ritual feeling both researched and genuinely unsettling. The author maintains crucial ambiguity about supernatural versus psychological explanations while building genuine dread. The specific ritual instructions and Astrid's matter-of-fact delivery create an effective contrast with the mounting terror. The piece excels in showing rather than telling, particularly in conveying fear through physical sensations and environmental changes. The moment when "the wind stopped" and the subsequent description of disturbed mist create visceral unease without resorting to explicit supernatural manifestations. However, some elements feel slightly predictable within the folk horror genre - the forbidden ritual, the warning ignored, the rushed escape. While executed well, these beats follow familiar patterns. The ending, while appropriately ambiguous, doesn't quite transcend genre expectations. The prose occasionally veers toward the overwrought, particularly in descriptions of fear and atmosphere, though it generally maintains restraint. Some metaphors and descriptive passages could be more precise. The dialogue, while limited, feels natural and age-appropriate. The cultural specificity and period details enhance rather than distract from the horror elements, creating an immersive reading experience that lingers beyond the final paragraph.
