+ Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 85.7
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
### Love in the Limelight - Hay The rain in Hay-on-Wye didn't fall so much as commit. It sheeted down Broad Street, turned the cobbles black, and sent a gaggle of tourists and one very tall man in sunglasses sprinting for cover. The bell over the door of *Y Ddraig Ddogfennog — The Dog-Eared Dragon* gave its cheerful, traitorous jingle. "Oh, thank God. Lock it. Lock it, please, I'm begging on actual knees." The man flattened himself against a shelf of Welsh poetry, beanie pulled low, rain dripping off a too-expensive coat onto the carpet. Outside, two figures with long lenses jogged past, swearing. Behind the counter, Anwen Davies didn't look up from her stamp. "We don't lock at half three on a Tuesday." "Right. Of course. Very principled. Love that for you." He peered through the window, breath fogging the glass. "Can I just — hide here for five minutes? Just till they bugger off to the castle?" "You've just dripped all over R. S. Thomas." "Sorry." He stepped sideways, dripping somewhere else. He took off the sunglasses. Then, with a flourish, the beanie. Dark curls, that jaw. That smile from the bus-stop poster for *Tidewater*. "Hi." Anwen finally looked. *Oh, no. Oh, bloody hell, no.* "Hi," she said flatly. He blinked. People usually did more than *hi*. "I'm Jude," he said, offering a wet hand. "Jude Calloway." "I know." She didn't take the hand. She handed him a tea towel instead. "You're dripping on the first editions." "Right. Practical. I like that." He dabbed at his coat, grinning. That grin had melted a late-night host on American telly last month. "You're my rescuer, then? My beautiful Welsh bookshop rescuer?" "I'm your shopkeeper who doesn't want warped pages. Dry yourself." A beat. The grin flickered, recalibrated, widened. "Harsh. Fair, but harsh. Do you talk to all your customers like this, or am I special?" "Only the ones who burst in like a spaniel." She came out from behind the counter, took the sodden beanie between two fingers and hung it on the radiator. "Sit. Before you fall over the travel section." "Ordering me about. I like that too." He sat on the little stool by the children's corner, long legs everywhere. "So. Anwen —" he read her badge, delighted to have ammunition — "Anwen. Do you run this whole dragon's den by yourself?" "With Myfanwy." She nodded at the ancient Jack Russell asleep on a cushion of returned paperbacks. "An assistant." "A dog." "Even better. No HR complaints." He leaned forward, elbows on knees, and dropped his voice into that low, roguish purr from the films. "Seriously, though. Diolch. Thank you. You saved my life. Those two out there have been following me since Cardiff. I was filming up in the Beacons and thought, lovely, a quiet book town, no one will notice —" "Everyone noticed. You parked a black Range Rover with tinted windows outside the chippy." He laughed, loud and surprised. "Okay! Okay, fair. God, you're brutal. Is this a Welsh thing or an Anwen thing?" "Both. We're known for our warmth." He was watching her now, properly looking, and Anwen felt it like a thumbprint on her sternum. *Stop it. He does that to everyone. That's literally his job. And stop noticing his eyes are grey like the Wye in winter.* She busied herself reshelving. "You can take your sunglasses off inside, by the way. The strip lighting's not that paparazzi." "Ha!" He pointed at her. "There she is. There's a sense of humour under the Dewey Decimal." "I keep it under Romance. Nobody looks there." "Oh, low blow." He clutched his chest. "Wounded. I'm very sensitive, I'll have you know." "An actor? Sensitive? Never heard of it." He grinned again, but something in it thinned. He stood, wandering the stacks, trailing fingers along spines without quite touching. The performance was slipping, just a fraction. "You really don't care, do you?" he said. "Who I am. It's — refreshing. Most people want a selfie before I've even said bore da." "Bore da was three hours ago. And I care about my carpet." "Right, right." He picked up a battered copy of *Under Milk Wood* and put it down again. "It's just... you get used to people liking you. Or pretending to. You walk in, you do the thing — the smile, the joke — and it works. And when it doesn't..." He shrugged, too casual. "You wonder what's wrong with the wiring." Anwen glanced up. That had sounded — unscripted. "Nothing's wrong with your wiring," she said, before she could stop herself. "You're just wet." He laughed, but softer this time. He sat back down, closer to the counter now. No purr. Just his real voice, a bit London, a bit Cardiff from his mum's side. "Can I tell you something stupid?" he said. "Customers tell me stupid things for free all day." "I was nine. School Oliver! in Pontcanna. Full Artful Dodger, waistcoat, top hat, the works. Opening night, I go on, lights in my face, and I completely blank. Not a word. Just stood there while little Oliver stared at me. Everyone laughed. I ran off and hid in the props cupboard for two hours. My mam found me crying into a fake pork pie." Anwen snorted before she could help it. "A fake pork pie?" " papier-mâché. Still traumatised." His smile was crooked now, not camera-ready. "Thing is, I still feel like that kid sometimes. Like any minute someone's going to go, wait, he doesn't know his lines, he's just bluffing. So I... I do the charm thing. If everyone's laughing *with* you, they're not laughing *at* you, you know?" The shop went very quiet except for rain on the skylight and Myfanwy snoring. *Oh, no,* Anwen thought, her stomach doing something mortifying. *Don't be real. Be the idiot from the posters. I can handle the idiot.* "That's..." She cleared her throat. "That's a rubbish hiding place. Everyone checks the props cupboard first." "Thank you for your sympathy." "You're welcome. Do you want tea? You look frozen." "You offering me tea means you like me a little bit." "It means I don't want you getting pneumonia in Biography." He beamed — a real one this time, lopsided, surprised out of him — and Anwen had to turn very quickly to the kettle in the back nook because her face was doing something hot and treacherous. *Get a grip. He flirts with traffic cones. He's an actor with a fragile ego and cheekbones that should be illegal in Powys.* When she came back with two mugs, he was crouched down scratching Myfanwy's ears, murmuring, "Who's a good girl? Who's far more welcoming than her mother?" "She's not my —" Anwen stopped. "She likes you. She doesn't like anyone." "See? Irresistible." But he said it quietly, almost to himself, like he needed to hear it. She handed him the mug. Their fingers brushed. Neither moved away quite fast enough. "So," he said, looking up at her. "Anwen Davies of the Dog-Eared Dragon. If I wasn't... this —" he waved at himself — "what book would you give me?" She should have said something dry. She meant to. Instead what came out was honest. "Poetry. You strike me as someone who doesn't sit still long enough for novels, but you want to feel big things quickly." He stared at her. The rogue, the wink, the whole offensive — gone. Just Jude, wet-haired, holding tea with both hands like a kid. "Nobody's ever got me that fast," he said. Outside, the rain eased. The street was empty of lenses. The bell, which had betrayed him coming in, now seemed in no hurry to let him out. He didn't stand.

The character dynamics are well-constructed and follow the prompt specifications precisely. Jude embodies the charming rogue with fragile ego - his practiced charm offensive ("My beautiful Welsh bookshop rescuer") gradually gives way to genuine vulnerability when his usual tactics fail. The progression from performative charm to authentic connection feels organic rather than forced. The conversation flows naturally while building romantic tension through verbal sparring and moments of unexpected honesty. The emotional complexity is particularly strong in Jude's monologue about his childhood theater experience. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 82.2
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The door gave before Aya touched it. Not swung, not creaked — gave, as a held breath gives way. The iron was cold enough to ache through her glove, and the quiet beyond it was wrong. Above, the guildhouse still rang with the aftershock of the raid: overturned tables, constables' boot-nails in the floorboards, the sour reek of spilled gin and lamp-oil. Here, down the throat of the underhold stair, there was only damp stone and tallow-smoke and something else, sweet and coppery, like blood left too long in a brass bowl. Aya glanced back. Katra's scarred mouth was set hard beneath her half-mask, knives sheathed but hands empty and restless. Simeon clutched his oil-lantern too tight, his knuckles white, his spectacles fogged with his own breathing. "Too quiet," Katra breathed. Dockside Morska in her voice, all salt and ash. "I don't like it, Wraith. It's like the tide before it turns." *Wraith.* Aya steadied herself on the name. In silks uptown she was Lady Aya Velrane, second daughter, disappointment. Down here she was the Wraith, the girl who could call things out of the dark. "Then we turn first," she whispered. "The artifact. Before the peelers pick the carcass clean." She pushed the door wide. The underhold was lit like a chapel. A dozen gas-jets burned low along the vaulted walls, their mantles hissing, throwing jaundiced light over the old Scythan stone — that black, veined marble the ancients had dredged from God knew where, carved with things that were almost letters and almost faces. In the center, upon a plinth of riveted iron, rested the Heart: a fist-sized knot of glass and bone that pulsed with a slow, arrhythmic light, as if it remembered being alive. And beside it, seated in a chair dragged from the counting-room as if it were a throne, was Dame Ostra Morska. Alive. Unshackled. Decidedly un-incarcerated. Aya's stomach dropped through the floor. *No. They took her at dawn. I saw the Black Mariah. I heard —* "Close the door, loves," said Dame Ostra. "You're letting the damp in." She was a vast woman in a whalebone corset and a coat of oiled sealskin, her grey hair pinned cruelly back, her fingers heavy with stolen rings. Across her lap lay a brass-barrelled scattergun, lovingly polished, its twin hammers cocked. The sort of weapon men trusted in Morska: brass and oil and steel. Honest killing. Behind her stood four bodyguards, dock-butchers every one, with boat-hooks and cudgels and a second scattergun trained steady on the stair. A distant foghorn sounded once in the harbor beyond the guild walls — low, mournful, swallowed by stone. Simeon made a small, strangled noise. Katra swore softly, "Hell and hull —" "Ah," Ostra smiled, showing teeth filed to points, a whaler's affectation. "My little ghosts. Come down. Come admire my Heart." No one moved. Aya's mind raced, cold and too fast, the scholar in her cataloguing even as the thief panicked. *A double. A bribe. The constabulary sergeant drinks in her pocket. Of course she was never taken. The raid was a cull.* The immateria stirred at the base of her skull in response to her fear, whispering, offering. *Let us out, little daughter of the hanged woman, let us unmake them —* She clamped it down. To summon here, now, with steel already levelled, would be suicide. Magicka was feared in Morska precisely because it could not be aimed. "We heard you'd been guested by the Crown," Aya said at last, pitching her voice low through the mask, trying for insolence. "We came to water the flowers in your absence." Ostra laughed, a wet bark. "Did you now, Wraith? Took my keys, did you? Took my spells off poor old Tibb —" she nodded to a crumpled shape in the corner that Aya had taken for sacking and now realized was a man, his throat cut neat as a ledger line, "— and came down to lift my Heart while Mother was away. Naughty children." She lifted one finger. It was not a fight. There was no time for a fight, and Aya would remember that later with a sick sort of gratitude. The bodyguards simply stepped forward, too many and too close in the narrow vault, boat-hook hafts pinning Simeon's lantern-arm to the wall until the glass shattered, cudgel-ends grinding into Katra's wrists before her blades cleared leather. Rough hands seized Aya by the shoulders and hood. "Don't —" Simeon cried, "don't, please, gentlemen —" "Shut it, pen-pusher," one growled. The mask was torn from Aya's face. The cheap tin domino clattered to the flagstones. Gaslight struck her bare skin, her high Velrane cheekbones, her mother's dark eyes. She felt it like a slap, like being stripped in church. Silence. Then Ostra leaned forward, scattergun shifting. "Well. Well, well." Her voice lost its play. "Take a lamp to her. Closer." A lantern was thrust to Aya's chin. She smelled hot oil, saw her own terrified reflection warped in the brass. "I know that face," Ostra said softly. "I've dined across from it. Velrane. Lord Velrane's youngest. The bookish one. The one whose mother danced at the end of a Newgate rope for witchery." Aya's blood turned to slurry. *Mother.* The memory came unbidden and obscene in its clarity: the crowd on Gallow's Rise, the fog, the respectable ladies holding vinegar handkerchiefs to their noses, her mother's bare feet kicking once, neatly, as if startled. Hanged for immateria magick. Outlawed. Barely understood and therefore unforgivable. If her name was spoken upstairs, House Velrane was finished. Her father would disown her corpse before the magistrates took it. Her sisters would wear mourning for a living girl. And she — she would follow her mother, neck-first, or worse, be handed to the Admiralty's crows who cut witches open to see where the dark lives. Katra saw it hit her. "Aya —" she started, then caught herself, too late. "Aya," Ostra repeated, tasting it. "Aya Velrane. My Wraith's got a pedigree." A second time the foghorn sounded, further off, twice-muffled by the vault. "Kill us and you lose," Aya said quickly. Too quickly. Her voice shook and she hated it. She forced her chin up, summoned every elocution lesson beaten into her at the seminary. "Go on, Dame. Think like a Morskan. Like a businesswoman." Ostra raised a brow. "I'm listening, little lady." "You wanted the Heart for leverage, isn't that right? Against the Harbormaster? Against the Crown?" Aya's thoughts tumbled. "It's worthless dead in a vault. You need buyers. You need time. And right now you've got three corpses that buy you nothing but a mess to scrub off Scythan stone." She swallowed. Simeon's eyes were wide on her, pleading. Katra gave a minute shake of her head — *don't* — but Aya pressed on, because the immateria was choking her and steel was louder. "I'm worth more breathing. I'm Lord Velrane's blood. The Admiralty dines at our table. The magistrates owe my father money. Take me upstairs in chains, send word — a ransom, an exchange, a pardon signed and sealed for whatever you like. A live Velrane heir is a key to every drawing-room in the upper city. A dead thief in a mask is just offal for the tide." Her voice cracked on the last word. *Gods, Father will kill me himself. He'll have to. To save the name.* She pictured his study, all mahogany and brass instruments, his voice: *Science is order, Aya. Magicka is rot. Your mother chose rot.* Boredom had brought her down here. Boredom and curiosity and that humming in her veins she had inherited like her mother's eyes. Now boredom had a price, and it was payable in rope. Ostra studied her for a long moment, scattergun steady. The Heart pulsed beside her, casting crawling shadows that were almost hands. The gas hissed. Somewhere water dripped, each drop loud as a coin. "You've a tongue on you," Ostra said at last. "Posh tongue. Been educated past your sense." She stood, massive, the chair groaning, and came close enough that Aya could smell whale-oil and lavender water and blood. A thick finger tilted Aya's chin up, examining her the way a fence examines a jewel. "A hostage," Ostra mused. "My little lady hostage. With witch-blood in her, besides. Oh, your daddy will pay pretty to keep that quiet, won't he? Pay pretty to keep his daughter from the gallows his wife found." Aya forced herself not to flinch, not to call the dark, though it begged. *Live. Live an hour longer. Live to think.* Behind Ostra, the Heart gave a slow, sick throb, and for an instant Aya swore the carved faces in the walls turned to look. A third time, distant and final, the foghorn sounded in the harbor — three blasts for a ship lost in the fog, groping for the light. Ostra smiled, and cocked the scattergun with a clean brass click that echoed like a verdict. "Bind them," she said.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and atmospheric worldbuilding within the "whalepunk" fantasy setting. The author successfully creates a vivid Victorian-gothic atmosphere through careful attention to sensory details - the "sour reek of spilled gin and lamp-oil," the "jaundiced light" of gas-jets, and the tactile description of iron "cold enough to ache through her glove." The maritime setting is well-integrated through dialect ("Hell and hull"), nautical imagery (foghorns, tide metaphors), and cultural details like filed teeth as "a whaler's affectation." The dialogue effectively differentiates characters through distinct voices - Katra's "Dockside Morska" vernacular contrasts sharply with Aya's educated speech patterns, while Dame Ostra's voice carries appropriate menace and authority. The author handles the class dynamics well, showing how Aya code-switches between her aristocratic upbringing and criminal persona. Character motivations feel authentic throughout. Aya's desperation when unmasked drives her to attempt negotiation rather than fight, which aligns with both her scholarly nature and the tactical reality of facing multiple armed opponents. Her internal conflict about her magical heritage and family reputation adds psychological depth. The pacing builds tension effectively, moving from the ominous quiet entrance through the revelation of Dame Ostra's presence to the final capture. The author incorporates all required story beats naturally without feeling forced. However, some descriptions occasionally veer toward overwrought territory - phrases like "down the throat of the underhold stair" and "her thoughts tumbled" feel slightly purple. The magical system could be clearer; while the fear and mystery around "immateria magick" fits the setting, the mechanics remain vague. The ending maintains appropriate darkness for the gothic tone without false hope, and Aya's character development feels earned through the consequences of her choices. The piece successfully balances action, dialogue, and internal monologue while maintaining consistent third-person limited perspective. + Fanfic-crossover: Gunpowder Rendezvous — Score: 79.1
Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Gunpowder Rendezvous** The bar stinks of stale beer, cheap disinfectant, and smoke that never leaves. A neon jukebox in the corner buzzes blue and pink, and it keeps playing the same scratchy rock track on repeat, the guitar riff skipping every third bar like a nervous tic. No one fixes it. No one cares enough to fix it. Spike Spiegel leans at the counter with his long legs crossed at the ankle, a cigarette burning down between his fingers. He is broke, he is hungry, and he is bored, which is a dangerous combination for him. His hair sticks up in a dark green-black cloud. One eye, the real one, tracks the door. The other eye, the prosthetic one, sees everything just a half-second too flat, so the world always looks a little off-center to him. He likes it that way. It reminds him he already dies once, so whatever happens, happens. He nurses a whiskey he cannot afford and waits for information on his mark, a middle-man smuggler with a price on his head big enough to fill the Bebop's fridge for a month. Then the door kicks open and trouble walks in wearing extremely short shorts and a black crop top. Revy strides in like she owns the rot in the walls. Her long dark hair hangs loose, her midriff is bare, and a dragon tattoo covers her right arm from shoulder to wrist, the ink shifting when she moves. She carries two cutlasses in shoulder holsters — her Beretta 92s — and she moves like a woman who solves most problems with violence because violence always answers. A cigarette dangles from her lip. She drops onto the stool two down from Spike, slams her hand on the bar, and shouts, "Whiskey. Double. And leave the fucking bottle." Spike looks at her. He really looks at her. She feels his stare and meets it with a glare sharp enough to cut glass. "What the fuck are you staring at, asshole?" she says. "You order like you mean it," he says, his voice lazy and amused. "I respect that." "Fuck off." He grins and slides his bowl of peanuts toward her. "Hungry?" She snorts, but she takes a handful anyway. Their fingers almost touch. The jukebox skips, crackles, and starts the same damn song over again. The bartender sets her glass down. She downs it in one pull and pours another. Spike watches the line of her throat when she drinks, the way her tattoo flexes around muscle. She watches the way his long fingers tap ash, calm and precise, the hands of a gunfighter pretending to be a slacker. "You here for Kessler too?" she asks at last. Spike lifts an eyebrow. "Six million bounty, last seen heading for the motel strip? That Kessler?" "Eight million where I come from," she says. "Guess we get hired for the same pig." "Guess so." Competitive instinct snaps tight between them, electric as the neon. Neither likes competition. Both love it. "You should walk away," Revy says, lighting a fresh cigarette off the butt of the old one. Chain-smoking, foul-mouthed, eyes too bright. "I'm Two Hands. You don't want to race me." "Two Hands, huh?" Spike exhales smoke through his nose. "I only need one." "Bullshit." "Try me." She laughs, a harsh bark, and for a second something vulnerable flashes under the anger, a girl who learns early that softness gets you hurt. Then it is gone, buried under bravado. Spike recognizes it because he buries his own ghosts just as deep. A woman with a white parasol. A fall from a chapel window. Freedom that feels a lot like loneliness. He likes her. That annoys him. She likes him. That pisses her off. Three more bounty hunters enter, loud and drunk and stupid, talking about Kessler and the motel on Route 9. Revy and Spike exchange a look. Mutual understanding clicks into place without words. Revy moves first. She stands, kicks her stool back, and draws both Berettas in one smooth blur. "Sorry, boys," she says. "That bounty is fucking taken." Spike sighs like this is a chore, but he is already moving, Jeet Kune Do fluid in his limbs. He sweeps the nearest man's legs while Revy pistol-whips the second. Gunfire erupts. It is loud and beautiful. Spike fires his Jericho once, not to kill but to shatter a whiskey bottle above the bar, raining glass. Revy fires twice, left and right simultaneously, putting neat holes in the wall an inch from the third man's ears to make him dance. "Jesus!" the man screams. "Dance faster, motherfucker!" Revy screams back, laughing wild. Spike grabs her wrist before she puts a real bullet in someone and gets them both barred. His touch is light but firm. She freezes, breath hot and fast, eyes locked on his. The jukebox keeps wailing that same scratchy rock track on repeat, now almost drowned by gun smoke and shouting. The attraction hits them both hard — sweat, adrenaline, gunpowder. "You always play this rough?" he asks, close to her ear. "You have no fucking idea," she breathes. They leave the bar together with the bartender shouting about the tab. Outside the night air tastes like rain and exhaust. Kessler hides in Room 14 of the Blue Comet Motel, and they both know it. So they share Spike's battered hammerhead car in uneasy truce, passing a flask back and forth, knees brushing in the dark. Room 14 is empty when they kick the door in, side by side, guns up. Just a rumpled bed, a running shower, an open window with curtains blowing. Kessler runs. Of course he runs. The bounty slips away into the night. Revy curses in English and Chinese and kicks the bed frame hard enough to bruise her toe. "Fuck! Fucking fuck!" Spike closes the door with his foot and locks it. He holsters his gun, but only halfway. "He comes back. They always come back for their stash." Now it is just them in the small motel room. The air conditioner rattles. A pink neon sign outside bleeds light through the blinds in stripes across the bed, across her bare legs, across his loose tie. Unresolved sexual tension thickens the air until it is hard to breathe. Revy sits on the edge of the bed, legs spread, guns still in her hands but pointed at the floor. She looks up at him through her hair. "So. What now, cowboy?" Spike stands across from her, hands loose at his sides, close enough to strike, close enough to kiss. "Now we wait." "That all you do? Wait?" "I drink. I smoke. I watch pretty girls wave guns at me." She stands so fast the mattress squeaks. Now they stand chest to chest in the narrow stripe of neon. She smells like whiskey and cordite and cigarettes. He smells the same. Her dragon tattoo ripples as she lifts her Beretta, slow, deliberate, and presses the muzzle under his chin. His real eye widens. His fake eye reflects pink. Spike smiles that fatalistic, dead-man smile and draws his Jericho and presses it hard against her ribs, right under her crop top, against warm skin. They freeze like that. Lovers and enemies. Mirror images. Both trust no one. Both want someone to trust. "You gonna shoot me?" she whispers. Her voice shakes, just a little. "You gonna shoot me first?" he whispers back. "I'm not a good person, not a bad person," she says. "I'm just here." "Whatever happens, happens," he says. Neither pulls the trigger. Neither steps back. The neon buzzes. Somewhere far away, in their heads, that same scratchy rock track keeps playing on repeat, skipping on the best part and never getting to the end.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and character understanding while delivering on the prompt's specific requirements. The author captures both Spike and Revy's distinctive voices and mannerisms with impressive accuracy - Spike's fatalistic philosophy, chain-smoking, and laid-back demeanor contrast effectively with Revy's aggressive profanity, dual-wielding gunplay, and underlying vulnerability. The atmospheric writing is particularly strong, with the seedy bar setting established through sensory details like the broken jukebox, stale beer smell, and buzzing neon. The prose maintains a noir-influenced tone that suits both source materials well. The dialogue feels authentic to both characters, capturing Revy's crude directness and Spike's dry wit without feeling forced or imitative. The story structure follows a clear progression from initial meeting through competitive tension to the climactic standoff. The bar fight sequence effectively demonstrates both characters' combat skills while building their mutual attraction through shared violence. The unresolved sexual tension builds naturally through physical proximity, shared danger, and their fundamental similarity as damaged individuals who trust no one. However, the piece suffers from some overwrought metaphorical language that occasionally disrupts the flow. Phrases like "trouble walks in wearing extremely short shorts" and "violence always answers" feel slightly forced. The recurring jukebox motif, while thematically appropriate, becomes somewhat heavy-handed by the end. The characterization shows genuine depth - both characters' trust issues and past trauma inform their actions without being explicitly stated. The mutual recognition of kindred spirits feels earned rather than convenient. The ending maintains appropriate ambiguity, avoiding false resolution while delivering the requested tension. The action sequences are well-choreographed and the sexual tension builds effectively without becoming gratuitous. The piece successfully balances the competitive dynamic with growing attraction, making their standoff feel like a natural culmination rather than a contrived scenario. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
I haven't been back to Västerbotten in almost thirty years, but I still dream about that mound. In the autumn of 1994 I was sixteen and furious about everything. Pappa had been transferred from Stockholm to the paper mill at Obbola, which meant Mamma and I were dragged with him to a white wooden house outside a village so small it didn't even have a Konsum. Kurt Cobain had died that spring. I had a Discman with batteries that always died in the cold and a Stockholm accent the other kids imitated until I stopped talking in class. Astrid Lundqvist was the only one who didn't make fun of me. She lived two houses down in a low red cottage with grass growing too close to the walls. Her parents were divorced in a way people in Stockholm weren't, messy and loud, and she mostly lived with her farmor until the old woman died the winter before I came. Astrid had pale eyebrows and bitten nails and she smoked John Silver she stole from her pappa's jacket. She told me her farmor had taught her things. At first they were just what she called midnight games. Stupid stuff, or I told myself it was stupid. In early September she showed me how to drop a needle in a glass of water to hear a boy's name bubble up. We did it in her kitchen to find out if Mattias Nyström liked me. The needle spelled M-A-T, and for a week I was convinced. Then she taught me to put a mirror under my pillow on a Thursday night to dream who I would marry. Then, the week Emma Lindgren wrote HORAN STOCKHOLM on my desk, Astrid got serious. She took a photograph of Emma from the class photo, burned the edges with her lighter, and buried it under a stone behind the school with salt. "So she shuts her mouth," Astrid said, matter-of-fact, as if it were eyeliner advice. Emma got laryngitis the next Monday and missed two weeks. I told myself it was October colds. Astrid just looked at me. Útiseta was different. She'd been talking about it for days in that flat voice she used when she was quoting her farmor. "It's not a game like the others," she said on the Friday we decided. We were smoking behind the bus shelter after school, our breath making small clouds. "It's sitting-out. You sit on the dead. On a gravhög. All night, or till you get an answer. Farmor did it twice. She said you have to really want to know." I asked what she wanted to know. She shrugged. "Where she is now. If she's angry I use her stuff for fun." She said it lightly, but she didn't look at me. I said I wanted to know what Emma and the others really said about me when I wasn't there. That sounded brave and teenage and small enough to be safe. Astrid nodded like a priest. The preparations took all evening. That was part of it. At her house, with her pappa snoring in front of TV4, Astrid laid everything out on the kitchen table and checked them off. No iron, she said. Take off your earrings, your belt buckle, leave your keys. The dead don't like iron. I laughed and she didn't. Pee before we go, because once you sit you can't stand, not till it's over. Bring something wool to sit on. Don't eat after nine. And bring a cloak or a big cloth to pull over your head. "You have to sit with your head covered," she said. "Like in a tent. So you see inward." She gave me her farmor's vadmal shawl. It smelled of damp sheep and old tobacco and something sweet, like dried angelica. She took a black rain poncho for herself. Into her army backpack she put two cigarettes for after, not for during, a thermos of weak coffee she said we wouldn't drink until morning, and a bit of flatbread. "For offering," she explained. "You leave a bite." We waited until her pappa's breathing went heavy and my parents thought I was asleep. There were no mobiles then. We'd agreed I'd flash my bike light twice from my window. At half past eleven I climbed out in jeans, two sweaters, and my winter jacket, my hair still smelling of shampoo. Outside was the kind of cold that makes the stars sharp. October in Norrland, frost already silvering the grass, the bog behind the houses exhaling mist. We walked without our bike lamps after the first road, because Astrid said light would spoil our night eyes. We knew the way. Everyone knew the mound out past the pasture, where the pines thinned. The old gravhög. Viking, the teacher said, or older. A low, broad back rising from the ground, covered in moss and lingonberry and three leaning stones at the top. The municipality had put up a little rusted sign: FORNLÄMNING. No digging. Astrid was all business. "We go from the north side," she whispered. "Don't step on the top until I say. Walk around it first, sunwise? No — against. Farmor said motsols. Three times. Quiet." So we did. Our boots crunched too loud on frozen heather. I felt ridiculous and sick at the same time, like before stealing something. On the third round she stopped on the northern slope, where the ground was flat enough to sit, and spread out the wool blanket she’d brought. The shawl over my shoulders was heavy. Her instructions came fast now, half rebellion, half liturgy. Smoke one now if you want, because after you can't. Sit facing north. Legs crossed, hands in lap. Pull the cloth right over, so no light gets in. Once midnight comes, you ask your question — not out loud, inside. Then you wait and you don't talk, you don't look, even if you hear something behind you. Especially then. Don't greet anything. Don't promise anything. If you get scared, pinch your thigh, but don't get up. Iron keeps them away but it also insults them, so we left it. Understand? I nodded, lit the cigarette she gave me with shaking hands. It tasted terrible and grown-up. Above us the sky was huge and moonless. The pines stood black around the clearing. Somewhere far off a dog barked once and stopped. "Are you scared?" I asked. Astrid snorted. "It's just sitting. Farmor said most people fall asleep and dream the answer and think they made it up." We stubbed out the cigarettes, buried the filters. She poured a little coffee onto the ground at the foot of the mound, crumbled bread. The earth drank it. Then we climbed up and sat, two lumps side by side but not touching, and pulled our coverings over our heads. Under the vadmal it was suddenly warm and dark and close. My own breathing filled it. The wool itched my forehead. I could smell my cigarette on my fingers. I tried to giggle and couldn't. The ground through the blanket was strangely warm for frost weather, as if the mound breathed. I told myself it was my own body heat trapped. We waited. I heard Astrid settle, her poncho crackling, then stillness. My knees ached. Time stretched. I thought about Emma's voice in the corridor, about Mamma crying quietly on the phone to Stockholm, about how much I hated the smell of the mill. Then I tried to do what Astrid said. I asked, inside: What do they say about me? Nothing happened for a long while except the blood thudding in my ears. Then the wind, which had been moving in the pine tops all night, simply stopped. Not faded. Stopped, as if a door closed. The silence under the shawl became total. I became aware of the cold seeping up through the blanket into my bones, and under it, that spot of warmth. And then, from very far away, a distant church bell chimed once at exactly midnight, though no service was scheduled. Lövånger church was kilometers off, locked and dark at that hour in October. Everyone knew that. One single note, low and clean, carried over the frozen bog. It didn't echo. It just ended. After the bell, I heard it. Or thought I did. A soft shifting, like someone turning over in sleep, deep under me. A smell rose — wet stone, tobacco, the sweet angelica of the shawl but stronger, sourer. My scalp prickled. I was sure, absolutely sure, that there was a third weight on the mound with us, pressing down on the far side. I pinched my thigh hard through my jeans until it hurt. I told myself it was Astrid breathing. It wasn't in rhythm with anything human. Then, very close to my left ear, outside the shawl, something whispered my name. Not Astrid's voice. Lower. Wet. *Lin-ne-a.* My whole body locked. I wanted to rip the shawl off and look, and Astrid's warning held me harder than any hand: don't look, don't greet. Under the wool, my breath came short and white in the dark. I thought I felt fingers, light as frost, settle briefly on top of my covered head. I don't know how long I sat there. It might have been minutes. The wind started again with a rush that made the pines hiss. The warmth under me was gone, replaced by ordinary cold biting through. I was crying without sound, tears cooling on my cheeks. Finally Astrid's hand found my arm through the cloth. "Up," she whispered, hoarse. "Now. Walk back the same way, don't look back." We stumbled down, left the bread and cold coffee, walked fast without speaking until the pines closed behind us. Only on the road, under the orange yard light of the first farm, did we stop and smoke the second cigarettes with trembling hands. Astrid's face was grey. "Did you hear—" I started. "Don't talk about it till morning," she cut in, farmor's rule. "That's how you carry it home." We never talked about it in the morning, either. Emma got better and ignored me. Astrid and I stayed friends, but we never did another midnight game. Even now I tell myself it was suggestion and cold and two girls who wanted to be witches for a night, that the bell was a trick of distance, that the whisper was Astrid after all, or my own blood. But I still remember the weight on that mound and the smell of tobacco where no one was smoking, and I know we crossed some line that night, treating something old as entertainment. It answered as if it had been waiting to be asked.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the delicate balance required for effective folk horror. The author successfully creates an authentic 1990s Swedish setting with convincing cultural details - from the paper mill at Obbola to the lack of mobile phones, from John Silver cigarettes to TV4. The voice of adult Linnea recalling her teenage experience feels genuine and appropriately nostalgic without being overly sentimental. The characterization is particularly well-executed. Linnea emerges as a believable displaced teenager - angry, lonely, and vulnerable to peer influence. Her Stockholm accent being mocked, her fury at the move, and her desperate desire to fit in all ring true. Astrid is more complex than she initially appears, moving from seeming manipulator to someone genuinely connected to family tradition, with her own uncertainties about her grandmother's legacy. The prose maintains an elegant simplicity that serves the folk horror genre well. Descriptions are vivid without being overwrought - "the kind of cold that makes the stars sharp" and "the bog behind the houses exhaling mist" create atmosphere without purple excess. The author demonstrates restraint in building tension, allowing dread to accumulate through mundane details rather than melodramatic flourishes. The ritual preparation sequence is particularly effective, blending teenage rebellion with genuinely researched folkloric elements. The specific prohibitions (no iron, sitting facing north, moving motsols) feel authentic rather than invented, and Astrid's matter-of-fact delivery makes them more unsettling than dramatic pronouncements would. The climactic scene maintains the crucial ambiguity that makes folk horror work. The church bell, the shifting beneath the mound, and the whispered name could all have rational explanations, but the accumulation of details creates genuine unease. The author wisely avoids explaining or resolving these elements. However, there are some weaknesses. The pacing occasionally rushes through important moments - the transition from harmless "games" to more serious ritual could use more development. Some of the folkloric elements, while researched, feel slightly inserted rather than organically integrated. The ending, while thematically appropriate, relies somewhat heavily on the "we never spoke of it again" trope. The dialogue, when present, feels natural and age-appropriate. The author successfully captures teenage speech patterns without resorting to caricature. The emotional complexity is well-handled - Linnea's mixture of skepticism, fear, and desperate need for belonging creates genuine psychological tension. + Physical-spatial: Therapeutic Boundaries — Score: 87.0
Prompt:
**"Therapeutic Boundaries"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a former professional athlete undergoing mandatory physical therapy after a career-destroying injury, harboring resentment toward recovery itself. Their physiotherapist is not only unnervingly attractive but also a former training partner from their competitive days who has successfully transitioned to a new career while the protagonist's identity remains shattered. We'll lean into the sexual tension of the scene by having her be attracted to him, but both of them attempting to maintain mental distance while being in physical contact as he shows her stretches & movements & manipulates her body, navigating the thresholds of pain. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—every movement, stretch, and manipulation must be anatomically precise and spatially consistent. Paint an exceptionally vivid sensory picture through detailed attention to pain thresholds, involuntary responses to touch. Capture the suppressed, flaring tension of physical proximity, touch, and the controlled infliction of uncomfortable movements. Physical clarity is essential — readers must understand exactly what is happening with the body during each therapeutic technique. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The paper on the table sticks to the back of my thighs the second I sit down. That's the first betrayal. Cold, thin, crinkling. Mandatory, they said. Ten more sessions or the insurance flags me non-compliant and the settlement review gets ugly. Not because anyone thinks I'll run again. Recovery, now, just means learning how to walk without limping into an early arthritis diagnosis. Over the table, bolted to the cinderblock wall, the muscle man looms. Life-size, front and back, all peeled red fiber. Gastrocnemius, soleus, hamstrings, quads labeled in tiny black lines. His right leg is half-flayed to show the ACL, a pale cord deep inside the knee. I stare at it while I wait because I can't look at the door. Then Jonah comes in. Jonah Reyes. Lane four next to my lane five for six years. Same 6 a.m. track, same ice baths, same protein grit on our teeth. He was good, never great. Now he's Dr. Reyes, DPT, clip-boarded, in navy scrubs that fit too well across his shoulders. Hair cut short. Forearms veined from work. Unnervingly attractive in the way that makes me angry, because I knew him when he had acne on his back and threw up after 400m repeats. He made it out clean. Coaching cert, grad school, a job where he gets to stay inside the sport without it eating him. I did not. "Right knee?" he says, like he doesn't know. Like he didn't watch the video of my plant-and-pop in the semifinal. "Right knee," I say. ACL reconstruction with hamstring autograft, ten weeks post-op. My identity, surgically replaced with a piece of my own leg. He doesn't do pity. He pulls the rolling stool to the right side of the table, at the level of my knee. "On your back. Head up here, hips square." I swing myself back. The table is narrow, vinyl under the paper, a foam bolster at the head. I lie supine, skull on the bolster, shoulders wide against the paper. I bend my left knee up, place my left foot flat on the table to keep my low back from arching — standard. My right leg stays extended flat, toes pointing straight to the ceiling tiles, heel resting heavy. The knee doesn't fully straighten. There's a pillow of swelling still above the patella, and my right vastus medialis, that teardrop muscle just inside the kneecap, is visibly gone. Atrophy like a dent. He stands. I can feel his body heat before he touches me. He puts two fingers just medial to my patella, presses. "Quad set for me. Push the back of your knee down into the table." I try. The back of my right knee — the popliteal space — grinds down a millimeter. My patella should glide up as the quadriceps fires. It barely twitches. His fingers stay there, light, feeling for the contraction that won't come. "Good. Again." His voice is clinical. His thumb brushes the edge of my kneecap. My skin jumps. Not pain. Just the shock of warm human contact after months of only being handled in a surgical, gloved way. I hate that I notice the callus on his thumb. He moves to the first real work. "Passive flexion. I'm going to do the moving, you do the breathing. Tell me when we hit a four, and when we hit a seven." His right hand slides under my right calcaneus — my heel cupped fully in his palm, fingers curled around the sides of the fat pad. His left hand rests flat over my distal anterior thigh, just four inches above the patella, to keep my hip from hiking and to stabilize the femur. "Slide your heel toward you." He lifts my heel an inch off the paper to reduce friction and guides it in an arc toward my buttock. My knee bends. 30 degrees, easy. 60 degrees, tightness pulls behind the knee where the graft harvest site still aches in the semitendinosus. At 90 degrees my heel is under the edge of my bent knee, my right hip flexing to accommodate. The stretch burns along the anterior joint line. "Four," I grit. He holds, doesn't push. His left forearm lies now along the outside of my right thigh, solid weight. I can smell the laundry detergent on his sleeve and the latex of the glove he isn't wearing — he doesn't wear gloves, his hands are bare and clean. My left foot presses harder into the table. My toes on the right foot curl involuntarily. "Keep breathing into it," he says. He eases another five degrees. The pain spikes to a hot wire behind the patella. "Seven," I say, too fast. He stops instantly. Holds me there at maybe 105 degrees of flexion. My hamstring is shaking. The tremor travels up into my hip. I am breathing through my nose, jaw clenched so hard my ears ring. He waits, counting under his breath, then slowly extends my leg back out, guiding the heel away until the knee is straight again. Blood rushes back. I hate the relief. Relief feels like forgiveness and I'm not ready. Next, patellar mobs. He needs my leg straight and relaxed. He places the pads of both thumbs on the superior pole of my patella, fingers splayed to cradle the sides of my knee, and pushes the kneecap down toward my toes, a slow inferior glide to keep it from scarring down. The bone moves under skin with a gritty, nauseating slide. His face is twelve inches above my knee, eyes focused down. I look at the muscle man on the wall instead. The printed fibers blur. When he does the medial glide — thumbs on the lateral edge, pushing inward — his right wrist rests against my inner thigh, just above the knee. Bare skin on bare skin, because I'm in shorts. The weight of it is clinical, necessary for leverage. My adductors flinch anyway. Gooseflesh ripples up my thigh despite the warm room. I feel my breath catch and I turn it into a cough. He doesn't look up, but his jaw tightens. He felt it. He is attracted to me too, I can tell in the way he is overly careful not to linger, the professional distance he puts into his shoulders. We are both pretending this is only a joint. "Straight-leg raise. Hamstring length," he says, standing straighter to reset. He keeps my right knee locked in full extension with his left hand pressed firmly across the front of my knee, just above the joint line, fingers wrapping the vastus lateralis, thumb on the vastus medialis. With his right hand he cups under my posterior calf, just above the Achilles, and lifts my entire straight leg off the table, flexing my hip. Up to 45 degrees. The pull ignites in lines behind my knee and up into the belly of the biceps femoris and semimembranosus. At 60 degrees my low back wants to lift. My left foot stays planted, left knee bent, anchoring my pelvis. "Tell me." "That's — that's enough," I say. Burning, not sharp. A deep elastic ache like the muscle will peel. My right ankle dorsiflexes on its own, toes pulling toward my shin, trying to protect. He holds the leg there, my heel heavy in his hand, his other hand hot on my knee. I am entirely supported by him in that moment. If he let go, my leg would drop. The intimacy of that dependence makes my throat close. I used to be able to lift this leg over a hurdle at full sprint. Now I am shaking from holding still. He lowers me down with control, heel back to paper. "Flip to your stomach for the quad," he says, and steps back to give me room. The loss of contact is abrupt and cold. I roll onto my left side, then push up and turn prone. Now I'm face-down, forehead resting on my folded forearms, hips flat, both legs extended behind me, toes off the end? No — table is long enough, my feet hang just past nothing, ankles relaxed, toes pointed into the vinyl. My right knee is stiff from the front now. He moves to stand on the right side again, at my lower leg level. He places his left hand flat on the back of my right thigh, just above the knee, pressing the femur down into the table to isolate the motion. His right hand cups the front of my right ankle, fingers around the malleoli, thumb over the anterior talus, and bends my knee, bringing my heel up toward my buttock. At 90 degrees flexion, my heel points at the ceiling. The stretch hits the front — rectus femoris pulling from the anterior inferior iliac spine all the way down over the patella. It's a sick, deep ache. He adds a little hip extension by lifting my ankle an inch higher, increasing tension. My glute fires involuntarily to protect. My breath hisses through my teeth into my arms. "Pain?" "Six," I lie. It's a seven edging to eight. I don't want him to stop because stopping would mean he won, or the scar tissue won. I want to be able to hate this cleanly. He holds, steady. I feel the tremor in my own calf against his palm. Sweat prickles at my hairline. The muscle diagram is now behind me, but I can still feel it looming, that perfect body with no fear. He slowly straightens my leg back down until the front of my ankle rests on the table again. He doesn't rub the spot. He steps back, writes the numbers: flexion 105, extension lag 4 degrees. "Same time Thursday," he says. I sit up, legs dangling off the side, right knee throbbing dully. We don't touch again.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates exceptional technical mastery in fulfilling the prompt's demanding requirements. The author delivers anatomically precise physical therapy descriptions while maintaining narrative tension and emotional complexity throughout. The first-person perspective effectively captures the protagonist's resentment and vulnerability, creating a compelling voice that balances clinical detail with raw emotion. The anatomical precision is remarkable - every movement, position, and therapeutic technique is described with medical accuracy. Terms like "vastus medialis," "popliteal space," and "anterior inferior iliac spine" are seamlessly integrated without feeling forced or show-offy. The spatial coherence is flawless; readers can visualize exactly how bodies are positioned and moving through each exercise. The sexual tension is handled with sophisticated restraint. Rather than relying on cheap titillation, the author builds tension through professional boundaries, shared history, and the inherent intimacy of therapeutic touch. The line "We are both pretending this is only a joint" perfectly encapsulates this dynamic. Character development is nuanced and believable. The protagonist's resentment toward both recovery and Jonah's successful transition feels authentic. Jonah's professional demeanor masking personal awareness creates compelling subtext. Their shared athletic past adds layers without requiring exposition dumps. The prose style is controlled and purposeful. Sentences vary effectively between short, clipped observations and longer, more complex descriptions of physical sensations. The voice remains consistent throughout - bitter, observant, reluctantly vulnerable. However, the piece occasionally veers toward clinical detachment that, while thematically appropriate, can distance readers emotionally. Some metaphors feel slightly overwrought ("My identity, surgically replaced with a piece of my own leg"), though they generally serve the narrative well. The ending maintains the established tone without false resolution, which is appropriate given the ongoing nature of both the physical therapy and emotional journey. The piece successfully avoids sentimentality while remaining emotionally engaging. + Historical fiction: High Seas and Low Vices — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors. Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit. Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell had struck seven before I woke, my shirt stuck to my back with river heat. "You'll be late for muster, sir." Midshipman Pike stood in the doorway of my cabin aboard *Hyacinth*, swinging at anchor off Whampoa. He was sixteen and still pink about the ears. "I've a meeting ashore," I said. "With the Hoppo's deputy. Customs duties. Captain Hartley knows." "Shall I tell the Captain you'll be back for evening gun, sir?" "Tell him I'll be back when the tide suits." He frowned. "Sir, yesterday the purser was asking after the signal book—" "Then tell the purser to ask someone else. Pike." "Aye, sir." I dressed with hands that would not keep still. In my right waistcoat pocket I found her — my small jade Guanyin, no longer than my thumb, cold as river water. I rubbed at her face with my thumb until my gut unclenched enough for me to stand. --- The scull-boat was waiting below the chains, the boatman asleep with his hat over his face. "Ah-Lam," I said, dropping into the stern. "Shamian. The factories. Quick." He sat up and squinted at me. "Too early, Taipanese captain. Water police stop. You pay extra two mace." "One mace. The tide's with us." "Three mace. Tide against police, not against me." He spat over the side. The Pearl was brown and slick that morning, carrying tea leaves and night-soil and the smoke of a thousand cooking fires. "You sick, Captain Merrick? You sweat." "Row." He laughed and pushed off. "Sick men pay three mace." The air coming up the river was thick enough to chew — wet coal, drying fish laid out on mats at Honam, pig fat from the breakfast stalls, and under it the low mud smell of the delta. My bowels turned and knotted. I put my hand in my pocket and worked the jade hard between finger and thumb, back and forth, until the carved folds of her robe grew warm. --- Harcourt was on the veranda of the British Factory, in shirtsleeves, copying invoices. "Merrick," he said, without looking up. "Christ. You look like hell." "Good morning to you too." "You missed dinner Tuesday. Mrs. Jardine asked after you." "I was detained." He set down his pen. "Hartley was here yesterday asking if we'd advanced you any pay against the Navy account. I told him we don't do that for King's officers anymore." "I need twenty dollars, William. Until Friday." He laughed once. "You need twenty dollars every day until Friday. What happened to prize money? What happened to your pay?" "The merchants in London take their time." "The merchants in London." He wiped his face. Flies were settling on the inkpot. From inside came the clack of an abacus and someone shouting numbers in Cantonese. "Listen, James. Last month it was twelve for a tailor. I know there's no tailor. Everyone on the square knows." "Then lend it as a friend." "I can't." He lowered his voice. "Go and see Dr. Pearson. He's sending men home with the liver complaint every week. He'll sign you sick and no one will ask." "I'm not sick with the liver." "No. You're not." He picked up his pen again. "I can't help you." My legs had begun to ache, deep in the bone. I held the Guanyin so tight her edge cut my palm. "Then I'll not keep you from your sums." --- The tea shop on Hog Lane was shuttered though it was past nine. I knocked twice, then once more. Chen Po opened it himself. He was fifty, thin as rope, his queue neatly plaited, ink under his nails from keeping books. "Lieutenant," he said in English. "You come early." "Business can't wait." "You bring money today?" He let me in. Inside it was dark and cool, smelling of charcoal and old tea dust and, very faintly, from the back room, that sweet, scorched-sugar smell that made my mouth fill. "Last time you say tomorrow. Tomorrow was three days." "I'll have it tonight. Hartley's releasing funds." "You say that before." He poured tea with steady hands. Mine shook around the cup. The heat of it burned. Outside, a hawker cried salted plums, and a chair-bearer argued over fare. "No money, no pipe, Lieutenant. How many times?" "Just a small lamp. Enough to steady me. I'll pay double tomorrow." "Double of nothing is nothing." He watched me. "You sweat through your coat. You want to smoke here, in front of compradors? You bring police to me?" I put my hand in my pocket. Rubbed. Rubbed. The cramp took my stomach and twisted. "Please, Po. You know I'm good for it." "I know you were good for it. In spring." He sighed. "You bring me something, I give you something. That is trade. You understand trade." "What do you want?" He refilled my cup. "American captain wants the soundings. The Bogue. Your Navy ship makes new survey, yes?" My mouth went dry for a different reason. "That's Admiralty property." "So is opium, by your law. Yet here we are." He shrugged. "Copy me the inner channel. Vane pays thirty dollars. I take ten for debt. You smoke today." "I could be broken for that." "You will be broken anyway." He said it without cruelty. "You decide." --- I found Silas Vane behind the American Factory, overseeing coolies rolling bales of raw cotton that smelled of dust and seed. "Merrick," he said. "You look like a man come to sell his mother." "I've got the Bogue soundings. Hartley's survey, last month. Inner passage past Tiger Island, corrected depths." Vane stopped smiling. "Let's walk." We walked down toward the river wall, where the water slapped green against stone and the sun beat back up off it. A temple bell rang across at Honam. My coat was black under the arms. "You're offering this out of patriotism?" he said. "Thirty dollars. Now." "Twenty. I don't know if it's good." "It's good. I took half the soundings myself." My hand was in my pocket again, worrying the jade, thumb over and over her bowed head. My knee jumped. "Twenty-five, and you throw in your flask." He studied me a moment, then pulled a leather purse from his belt and counted out Mexican dollars onto his palm. The coins were heavy and bright. "You Navy boys. You come here to stop the trade and end up keeping my books for me. Copy it tonight. Leave it with Po." I took the coins. They were cool. My fingers left damp prints on them. "And the flask." He handed it over. The brandy burned going down and came straight back up into my throat with bile. But my hands steadied a fraction. "Jesus, Merrick," Vane said quietly. "Go easy." --- "You got money," Chen Po said when I laid the dollars on his table. It was afternoon then, the light gone amber through the shutters, the lane outside loud with chair runners and roast chestnut sellers and a blind singer. "I got money." He weighed them, bit one, nodded to the boy. "Back room." The back room was low and windowless, six bunks, three occupied. The air was close with lamp oil and sweat and that heavy sweetness. My stomach turned over and then settled, expectant as a dog. An old woman nodded to me. "Lie down, Lieutenant." I lay down. The mat was stained and warm from the last man. Someone coughed wetly in the corner. The boy knelt and worked the lamp, and the bead over the flame bubbled and browned. "Slow," the woman said. "You rush, you vomit." I did not rush. I breathed as she told me. The smoke was thick and floral on my tongue, coating my teeth. The cramp in my gut loosened its fist. The ache drained out of my knees. The sweat cooled on my neck. In my pocket, my hand still held the Guanyin. I realized I had stopped rubbing her. "Good?" the woman asked. "Good," I said. From the front of the shop came the clink of cups, Chen Po laughing with a customer about the price of Bohea. A boat gong sounded on the river. Evening gun would fire soon on *Hyacinth*, and Pike would mark me absent, and Hartley would write another letter. I closed my eyes and let the room tilt gently, like a ship at anchor.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and atmospheric writing that effectively captures the degradation of a British naval officer caught in opium addiction in 1830s Canton. The author successfully creates an authentic historical setting through careful attention to period details, from the naval hierarchy and customs to the economic realities of the opium trade. The characterization of Lieutenant Merrick is particularly well-handled. His desperation manifests through physical details (shaking hands, sweating, the compulsive rubbing of the jade figurine) rather than heavy-handed exposition. The progression from his morning lies to Pike, through increasingly desperate attempts to secure money, to his final betrayal of naval secrets creates a believable arc of moral decay driven by addiction. The dialogue feels authentic to both the period and the characters' social positions. Each voice is distinct - Pike's earnest formality, Harcourt's weary concern, Chen Po's businesslike pragmatism, and Vane's cynical opportunism. The conversations reveal character and advance plot efficiently without feeling forced. The sensory details are particularly strong, from the "brown and slick" Pearl River carrying "tea leaves and night-soil and the smoke of a thousand cooking fires" to the final opium den with its "heavy sweetness" and stained mats. These details create immersion without becoming overwrought. The structure works well, using scene breaks to show Merrick's descent through increasingly compromising situations. The jade Guanyin serves as an effective recurring motif, representing both his attempt at control and his ultimate surrender to addiction. The ending avoids false redemption or unearned transformation. Merrick's temporary relief comes at the cost of betraying his duty, and the final image of him "letting the room tilt gently, like a ship at anchor" while knowing he'll face consequences shows the tragic nature of his choice. Minor weaknesses include some slightly predictable beats in the addiction narrative and occasional moments where the period atmosphere feels slightly constructed rather than organic. However, these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness.
